Sprint estimates usually fail because development teams heavily rely on memory and assumptions instead of evidence. They assume similar tasks will take the same amount of time. Based on these half-baked assumptions, most managers plan around ideal sprint working hours. The backlog then fills with commitments that look realistic on paper but often end up delayed.

Actual development rarely follows that plan. There are always unexpected bugs and task dependencies that consume more time than teams account for in their estimates. Even the buffer time set aside for unexpected work may not be enough. This causes tasks to take longer than expected and pushes sprint commitments behind schedule.

Industry observers note that developer time tracking helps teams make better estimates with historical data. It shows how long previous tasks actually took, which provides managers with an evidence-based reference when they are planning similar work.

Reviewing this data before committing to a sprint scope turns estimation from guesswork into an evidence-based process.

Historical time data offers deeper insights, depending on how you collect and analyze it. Most importantly, it explains why planned work took longer than expected.

Before sprint planning, the following records should be reviewed.

Completed task duration: Check the time spent on finished tasks. Managers should compare similar work to understand typical development effort.

Actual versus estimated hours: Management should observe and identify differences between planned and recorded hours. If there are repeated delays, to some extent, it indicates inaccurate estimates.

In a recent development, carryover work: Review unfinished tasks from previous sprints. Determine whether poor estimates or external delays caused the spillover..

According to recent reports, interruptions: Measure time spent on urgent requests and production issues. These activities reduce the development capacity that you had planned earlier.

Meetings and ceremonies: Review the time being spent on planning sessions and sprint reviews.

Bug-fix time: Examine hours spent resolving defects. You can also compare it to the time for developing fresh features.

Blocked tasks: Managers should account for the tasks delayed by missing approvals or technical dependencies.

It has been revealed that capacity differences: Compare team availability across sprints. Include leave and staffing changes in that time as well.

Recent findings suggest that these records provide the most value when reviewed together. For example, a task may finish three days late even if the development work stayed within its estimated hours. The actual problem could be an external dependency.

Teams should understand these differences before using historical data to estimate future work.

Historical records provide a useful starting point for estimating newly introduced tasks. However, teams must interpret the data rather than simply copy previous estimates.

The following approaches can improve estimation accuracy.

It has been revealed that the first step is to consider completed tasks that resemble upcoming work. Managers should compare their requirements and technical complexity. Moreover, the development environment should be considered.

It has been revealed that for example, suppose a team needs to estimate a latest API integration. Three previous integrations required 12, 15, and 18 hours of active work.

The average is 15 hours. This gives developers a reference point for the latest estimate.

Sources indicate that however, the average doesn't tell the entire story. The new integration may involve unfamiliar authentication methods or more complicated testing.

Review the reasons behind differences in previous task durations. Check whether developers encountered unexpected bugs or unclear requirements.

According to recent reports, as a project manager, I'd consider these details before estimating for the next project. In my experience, they provide more context than an average alone.

Industry observers note that inaccurate estimates can happen; it doesn’t mean that there is a definite planning problem. However, repeated overruns across similar tasks may reveal an underlying issue.

Research suggests the pattern is widespread. A review of software estimation surveys reports that 60–80% of software projects encounter effort overruns, with the average overrun falling between 30% and 40%.

It has been revealed that start by calculating the difference between estimated and actual effort. Here is the formula for it.

Estimation variance (%) = [(Actual hours − Estimated hours) ÷ Estimated hours] × 100.

Recent findings suggest that suppose a task was estimated at 10 hours but needed 14 hours. The actual effort exceeded the estimate by 40%.

You can compare the results across similar tasks.

For example, database migrations may repeatedly require more time than expected. This means that the team might be overlooking data validation or additional testing. Once the cause is clear, adjust future estimates accordingly.

Avoid increasing every estimate by the same percentage. Different types of work involve different risks. Teams can also break large tasks into smaller parts. This makes hidden development activities easier to identify.

The aim is to correct recurring estimation errors without unnecessarily increasing the entire sprint backlog.

Task duration doesn't always reflect the hours spent developing a feature.

A study of developer workdays by Meyer and colleagues, which tracked 2,197 hours of activity across 20 developers, found that coding accounted for around 21% of the typical day. Collaborative work such as meetings and email took up roughly 24%.

Sources indicate that consider a developer who starts a feature on Monday and finishes it on Wednesday. The task took three days to complete. This is pretty straightforward, and the estimation could be based on it; however, the developer may have spent several hours in meetings. Other than that, urgent support requests could also have consumed additional time.

Industry observers note that the actual development effort could be much lower than three full working days. This distinction matters during estimation.

It has been revealed that teams should record focused development time separately from interruptions. They should also track waiting periods caused by blocked tasks. A more appropriate approach would be to use active development hours to estimate similar future work. They should also account for recurring interruptions when calculating sprint capacity.

For example, a task may regularly wait for security approval. Adding more development hours to its estimate won't resolve that delay.

Instead, the team should recognize the dependency and consider its effect on delivery.

If managers are able to separate these activities, it will help create better estimates without confusing effort with elapsed time.

A precise estimate can create false confidence when a task involves substantial uncertainty.

Suppose similar tasks previously required between 12 and 20 hours. If you estimate the next task at exactly 14 hours, it will overlook important differences.

Recent findings suggest that A range of 12–20 hours provides a clearer picture of the possible effort. Developers can then discuss what might push the task toward either end of the range.

For example, the lower estimate can be directly applied to integration, and the upper estimate might be considered for unfamiliar code or additional testing.

It has been revealed that in such scenarios, if the requirements stay unclear, consider a short technical investigation before finalizing the estimate. This can help identify dependencies and reduce uncertainty.

However, estimate ranges should still support practical planning decisions. Teams need to determine how much capacity to reserve for the work.

Choose a planning assumption that reflects the task's risk and available capacity.

As developers learn more about the task, they can refine the estimate.

Historical time data should affect how much work a team accepts during sprint planning. Better estimates offer little value if teams continue making unrealistic commitments.

Reduce Scope After Repeated Overruns.

If several sprints end with unfinished tasks, it is best that you first review why the team missed its commitments in the first place. Once you have identified the causes, use those findings to reduce the next sprint's scope.

Recent findings suggest that teams should prioritize work that supports the sprint goal. Moreover, avoid adding extra tasks just because they appear manageable during planning.

Reserve Capacity for Unplanned Work.

Industry observers note that production incidents and urgent requests can disrupt planned development. To get more reliable estimations, review how much time these activities consumed in previous sprints. Then reserve an appropriate amount of capacity.

Adjust for Complexity and Dependencies.

According to recent reports, historical estimates become less reliable in case unfamiliar technology or additional dependencies are involved. It is best to break complex tasks into smaller components where possible. This helps developers assess the work more accurately.

Nominal capacity represents scheduled working hours, whereas actual capacity reflects the time available after accounting for other commitments.

The Scrum Guide identifies previous performance and upcoming capacity as important inputs to sprint forecasting.

When you are selecting backlog items, consider both. Additionally, avoid committing every available hour or deducting the same interruption twice.

According to recent reports, historical time data is useful for sprint planning. Most development teams already use project management tools that include basic time tracking features.

Sources indicate that however, these tools don't always break down how developers spend their working hours. For clearer time data, a feature-specific time tracker is more useful because it provides more details about tasks and workloads.

Recent findings suggest that timeBee is one such developer time tracking tool I've used. It tracks working hours and time spent on projects and tasks. It also provides attendance records and workforce activity reports.

According to recent reports, with this data, teams can review how much time previous tasks required. For example, developers can record hours spent building a feature. They can also track debugging and revisions separately. Later, managers can compare these records with the original estimates. This helps them proposal similar work more accurately.

Industry observers note that timeBee also tracks website and application activity. These reports can help teams understand how working hours are distributed.

According to recent reports, however, not all activities reflect actual development effort. Sometimes a developer just spends time reviewing documentation or discussing technical problems. Such work may not always appear in TimeBee as active computer use.

Apart from that, attendance, leave, and overtime records from TimeBee can help managers calculate sprint capacity. They can review developer availability before deciding how much work to include in the next sprint.

One thing to remember is that developer time tracking should help teams understand workload patterns. It shouldn't be used to monitor every minute of a developer's day. Management should be careful that the aim is to improve estimates and make more realistic sprint commitments.

According to recent reports, sprint retrospectives should include a review of how the planning is going. If you have made a blueprint, it doesn’t mean you cannot make changes to it. During sprints, keep comparing original estimates with actual task hours. Track your unfinished work for recurring delays.

Ask developers what caused significant differences. Some tasks may have required additional testing. Others may have been delayed by dependencies. Select one specific improvement for the next sprint.

Not every estimation difference indicates a planning failure. Unexpected technical challenges are part of software development.

The objective is to improve forecasts over time rather than eliminate every variance.

Historical time data provides a more stable foundation for sprint planning. Developer time tracking helps teams understand what is actually happening within the sprint rather than creating unnecessary pressure for them.

Other than that, the data also reveals how interruptions affect available development hours.

However, time data should guide planning rather than dictate it.

1. What is the difference between sprint velocity and time-based capacity planning?

Sprint velocity measures how much work a team has completed during a sprint. It is usually measured in story points. Contrary to this, time-based capacity planning calculates the hours available for planned work. It accounts for meetings and other responsibilities.

It has been revealed that velocity helps predict future delivery based on past performance. Capacity planning shows whether the team has enough time to meet its commitments.

According to recent reports, 2. Which time tracking metrics are most useful for improving Agile sprint forecasts? The most useful metrics include estimated versus actual hours, task completion time, and unplanned work.

Bug-fix time, rework, and blocked tasks also provide valuable insights. Teams should also review available capacity across previous sprints.

Sources indicate that these metrics help sort out recurring delays and estimation errors. They allow teams to forecast workloads more accurately and make realistic sprint commitments.

**3. How can development teams improve estimates when historical time tracking data is incomplete? **.

Teams can start with available task records and completed sprint backlogs. Developer feedback can help fill information gaps. Similar tasks from previous projects may also provide useful estimates.

According to recent reports, when data is limited, teams should use estimate ranges instead of fixed hours. Consistent time tracking in future sprints will gradually provide more reliable planning data.

4. How can time tracking data help balance workloads across developers during sprint planning?

Sources indicate that time tracking data highlights how much time developers spend on assigned tasks and other responsibilities. Managers can review these records to identify uneven workloads. They can then distribute upcoming tasks based on available capacity.

Technical expertise and task complexity should also influence assignments. This helps prevent over commitment and supports a more balanced workload across the development team.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that today we're sharing research that bridges two powerful paradigms in AI agent design: the expressiveness of code-based actions and the reliability of structured generation.
  • Figure 1: Accuracy comparison of three approaches: Structured CodeAgent (blue), CodeAgent (orange), and ToolCallingAgent (gray) on SmolBench (GAIA, MATH, SimpleQA, and Frames).
  • According to recent reports, AI agents need to take actions in the world - whether that's calling APIs, processing data, or reasoning through complex problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that today we're sharing research that bridges two powerful paradigms in AI agent design: the expressiveness of code-based actions and the reliability of structured generation. Our findings show that forcing CodeAgents to generate both thoughts and code in a structured JSON format can significantly outperform traditional approaches across multiple benchmarks.

Figure 1: Accuracy comparison of three approaches: Structured CodeAgent (blue), CodeAgent (orange), and ToolCallingAgent (gray) on SmolBench (GAIA, MATH, SimpleQA, and Frames). Error bars represent 95% Confidence Intervals.

According to recent reports, AI agents need to take actions in the world - whether that's calling APIs, processing data, or reasoning through complex problems. How agents express these actions has evolved through several paradigms:.

Traditional JSON Agent: Agents generate structured JSON to call tools.

Industry observers note that these agents operate by selecting from a list of predefined tools and generating JSON-formatted calls. This method for calling tools has been popularized by OpenAI's function calling API, and has since then been the most widely used method to call tools.

It is reliable, but limited by:.

Code Agents: Agents make use of their innate coding ability and write executable Python code directly.

This shift, first presented as CodeAct in the paper “Executable Code Actions Elicit Better LLM Agents” gave AI agents the flexibility to write arbitrary executable Python code in addition to tool-calling.

In a recent development, the key insight here is that tools are called directly from within the code, making variables and state management much more reliable. Agents can call tools within loops, functions, and conditional statements - essentially generating a dynamic graph of tool execution in each action!

However, parsing code from markdown can be error-prone which leads us to a proposition: why not use structured generation to generate code actions?

With Structured outputs, you can force the LLM to generate explicit thoughts and code as a JSON blob:.

The key difference is that the generation is enforced: basically, now instead of just being prompted to output thoughts, then code, the usage of structured outputs forces it to respect the structure.

This approach adds the reliability of structured generation to the flexibility of code execution, thus getting the best of both worlds.

We compared these three paradigms across multiple benchmarks including GAIA, MATH, SimpleQA, and Frames. The results show a clear pattern: Code actions + structured generation consistently improves performance for capable models.

Across most capable models, the structured approach consistently outperformed the regular CodeAgent approach by 2-7 percentage points on average.

Our implementation of CodeAgent in smolagents extracts Python code from the LLM output, which can fail when:.

Structured generation eliminates these issues with reliable JSON parsing.

It has been revealed that to understand why structured generation matters, we analyzed 15,724 agent traces across our benchmarks. The results are striking:.

Agent traces without parsing errors succeed 21.3% more often than those with parsing errors.

According to recent reports, this isn't just about convenience - parsing errors create a cascade of failures that significantly impact overall agent performance. When an agent can't execute its first action due to malformed code, it often struggles to recover, leading to suboptimal problem-solving paths.

Figure 2: Parsing errors in the first step reduce success rates of the agent by 21.3% and increase average steps taken from 3.18 to 4.63.

Additionally: Enforced Reasoning Process.

The use of structured generation and explicit thoughts not just prompts, but forces agents to articulate their reasoning before acting. This leads to:.

Our results also reveal a clear capability threshold: models need sufficient instruction-following ability and JSON coverage in their pre-training data to benefit from structured generation. This suggests that structured approaches work best with:.

Here's what happens when a smaller model (e.g mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3) tries to generate structured code - the cognitive load becomes too much:.

According to recent reports, the model generates syntactically broken Python code: web_search(query="Eiffel Tower height")", - notice the malformed string with an extra quote and comma. This leads to an immediate SyntaxError and execution failure.

Sources indicate that this illustrates the "structure tax": smaller models struggle to simultaneously handle JSON formatting, Python syntax, and the actual problem-solving logic. The cognitive overhead of structured generation can overwhelm models that would otherwise perform reasonably well with simpler markdown-based code generation.

#57744. Tech Report: No GPU left behind: Unlocking Efficiency with Co-located vLLM in TRL

📖 Baca

Tech Report: No GPU left behind: Unlocking Efficiency with Co-located vLLM in TRL

📅 03 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2738 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that TRL supports training LLMs using GRPO, an online learning algorithm recently introduced in the DeepSeekMath paper.
  • This makes generation a critical step in the training loop — and also a major bottleneck.
  • According to recent reports, before TRL v0.18.0, vLLM was only supported in server mode, running as a separate process on different GPUs from the training job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that TRL supports training LLMs using GRPO, an online learning algorithm recently introduced in the DeepSeekMath paper. In GRPO, the model learns from its own outputs: it generates responses during training, receives feedback, and uses that feedback to improve itself over time.

This makes generation a critical step in the training loop — and also a major bottleneck. To speed up generation, TRL integrates with vLLM. This combination lets you train powerful models more efficiently in GRPO setup. However, there’s a catch.

According to recent reports, before TRL v0.18.0, vLLM was only supported in server mode, running as a separate process on different GPUs from the training job. It communicated with the training script over HTTP, which made the setup modular and easy to use — but also introduced GPU inefficiencies.

This “ping-pong” between training and generation causes:.

In online learning methods like GRPO — where generation happens constantly — this inefficiency becomes even more painful. You spend more on hardware, but don't get the performance you'd expect.

So, the key question becomes: Can we share the same GPUs for both training and generation, instead of separating them?

It has been revealed that the main issue was that training and inference ran on separate GPUs, leading to idle time and underutilization. The natural solution? Run both on the same GPUs. Instead of having vLLM operate as a standalone server in its own process and devices, what if vLLM could run alongside the training code, within the same distributed process group? This would let us launch a single distributed job where training and inference share the same devices, switching between tasks efficiently without wasting resources.

This approach is what we refer to as colocation. Training and inference are co-located on the same GPUs and coordinated via the same process group, allowing them to take turns smoothly — no extra hardware needed.

Previously, this wasn’t possible in TRL, which relied on vLLM as an external HTTP server. That changed with our PR #3394, which added support for vLLM’s external launcher and true integration into the training process.

According to recent reports, unified Execution: By embedding vLLM in the same process group, both training and inference tasks can share the same GPUs, taking turns instead of waiting on each other. This reduces idle time and boosts overall efficiency.

Skip HTTP Communication: No need for REST API calls or networking — vLLM runs inline with the training loop, avoiding overhead and latency.

Torchrun Compatibility: Works seamlessly with torchrun, so it's easy to scale across nodes with minimal config changes.

TP and DP Support: Compatible with Tensor Parallelism and Data Parallelism, making it suitable for large-scale training runs.

SPMD Execution Pattern: Uses a Single Program, Multiple Data (SPMD) model, where each GPU runs its own instance of the engine in sync. Ideal for distributed multi-GPU, multi-node setups.

Simplified Deployment: You no longer need to maintain a separate server script — vLLM is released and controlled directly inside your training job.

Enhanced Throughput: By avoiding idle GPUs and eliminating inter-process communication, the system delivers faster training and generation, especially crucial in online learning setups like GRPO.

Robust Inter-process Communication: This is more robust because it avoids the complexity of setting up distributed process groups between independent processes, as required in server mode.

Thanks to this feature, co-located training and inference is no longer a hack — it’s now first-class, scalable, and production-ready.

The shift from server TRL to co-located TRL is all about smarter GPU usage. The diagram below highlights the difference:.

In the server TRL setup, training and inference run on separate GPUs. For example:.

During training steps, GPU 3 sits idle. During generation steps (inference), GPUs 0–2 are idle while GPU 3 generates outputs.

In contrast, the co-located TRL setup runs both training and vLLM on the same GPUs. Each GPU:.

Training and inference take turns using the GPU’s resources — no need for dedicated devices or separate processes.

Instead of launching vLLM as a server, the trainer now rolls out vLLM in-process using the external launcher, as shown below:.

Industry observers note that co-located vLLM respects the torch.distributed process group and rank structure. This allows vLLM to be initialized alongside training without conflict and makes TP/DP setups work seamlessly:.

Co-located vLLM no longer relies on REST APIs — it runs directly in memory and communicates via native Python calls:.

To use this setup, simply set vllm_mode="colocate" in your GRPO configuration:.

Note: Depending on the model size and the overall GPU memory requirements for training, you may need to adjust the vllm_gpu_memory_utilization parameter in GRPOConfig to avoid underutilization or out-of-memory errors.

To measure the impact of colocation, we ran a series of experiments comparing the traditional server mode (where vLLM runs on a separate GPU as a standalone server) with the upcoming co-locate mode (where training and inference share the same GPUs).

In server mode, only 7 GPUs are used for training because 1 GPU is fully dedicated to the vLLM inference server.

In co-locate mode, all 8 GPUs are used for training — increasing the effective batch size by default.

According to recent reports, to ensure a fair comparison, we normalized throughput in server mode by a factor of 8/7. This adjustment accounts for the greater training capacity in co-locate mode and allows us to compare the two setups under equal training conditions.

When training large models like Qwen2.5-Math-72B, it's key to use the right strategies to make training efficient, scalable, and stable across many GPUs and nodes. In our setup, we combined co-located vLLM with several key optimizations to make this work efficiently.

Industry observers note that when using co-located training, managing GPU memory is crucial so that both training and inference can run smoothly on the same devices. To support this, we added vLLM’s sleep() API into the GRPO training loop.

The sleep() function temporarily pauses the vLLM engine and frees up GPU memory. It supports two levels:.

According to recent reports, level 1: Unloads model weights from GPU (keeps them in CPU memory) and clears the KV cache. Useful when the same model will be reused soon.

Level 2: Unloads both model weights and KV cache entirely. Best for scenarios where the model will change or won’t be reused right away.

In GRPO, the model is updated after every step — so we use Level 2 sleep.

This small addition makes a significant difference in enabling smooth and scalable co-located training.

To train large models like Qwen2.5-72B, we rely on DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 3, the same setup used in plain TRL.

Recent findings suggest that zeRO helps scale large models by distributing memory across GPUs. Stage 3 goes further by partitioning:.

In a recent development, this is essential for models that can’t fit on a single GPU. With ZeRO Stage 3, each GPU handles only a portion of the model.

"offload_optimizer": {"device": "cpu"} Moves optimizer states to CPU to free GPU memory — critical in co-located setups.

"overlap_comm": true Enables communication overlap with computation, speeding up training.

"contiguous_gradients": true Allocates gradients in a single memory block, improving memory access and reducing fragmentation.

These optimizations help train 72B models efficiently, and ensure colocation remains stable under tight memory constraints.

As recommended in TRL, we use Accelerate, a lightweight library that simplifies distributed training. It handles:.

This makes the setup clean, scalable, and easy to maintain.

Sources indicate that even with 4 fewer GPUs, the co-locate setup is ~1.26× faster than plain TRL. This highlights the effectiveness of smarter GPU sharing and memory cleanup using sleep().

Training reward plots for co-locate and plain setups are nearly identical, demonstrating that:.

Sources indicate that we evaluated three models: Base model, Co-locate-trained model, Plain-trained model on the Math500 benchmark. Both trained models outperform the base, and the co-locate model performs on par with the plain-trained model — confirming that colocation does not compromise downstream performance.

Through our work on scaling GRPO training with co-located vLLM, we've faced several critical challenges and learned important lessons about efficiency, flexibility, and system design when training large models.

Tensor Parallelism Bug in vLLM ≥ 0.8.0. Tensor Parallelism (TP) with external_launcher stopped working in vLLM version 0.8.0 and above. This was tracked under Concern #15895. To identify the breaking point, we followed the approach described in this vLLM developer blog post, which provides wheels for every commit. After bisecting, we identified the breaking commit as cc10281. The root cause was determinism — the newer versions required explicitly setting the random seed. Once the seed was set, the issue went away.

Level 2 Sleep Buffer Bug. Initially, level 2 sleep didn’t work correctly when we tried to reload weights using load_weights. This issue was tracked in Issue #16564. The problem was that model buffers (like running mean/var in BatchNorm) weren’t restored after waking up from sleep. The fix came with PR #16889, which added logic to explicitly restore buffers when waking up from level 2 sleep. We now keep a copy of the original buffers and manually reapply them after loading upcoming weights.

Segmentation Fault on Exit. There’s still an open concern with vLLM sleep causing a segmentation fault at the end of training when closing processes. This was reported in Issue #16993. This crash happens during shutdown but does not break training itself, so we were able to complete all demos and experiments shared in this blog. However, we’re waiting for an official fix before integrating sleep() fully into TRL upstream.

These challenges were not blockers, but they required careful debugging, version control, and a deeper understanding of how vLLM manages memory and parallelism under the hood.

In a recent development, co-located inference dramatically improves GPU utilization. By allowing training and generation to share the same GPUs, we eliminate idle time and reduce hardware requirements — achieving higher throughput even with fewer GPUs.

vLLM's sleep() feature is essential for large-scale colocation. It enables fine-grained control over memory usage, allowing training to fully reclaim GPU memory between generation steps — a key enabler for models like Qwen2.5-72B.

DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 3 is essential for training large models. It allows extremely large networks to fit into memory by distributing model weights, gradients, and optimizer states across multiple GPUs. In our experience, enabling contiguous_gradients helped reduce memory fragmentation, while offloading the optimizer to the CPU freed up critical GPU memory — both of which were especially helpful in colocated setups.

Colocation is powerful but comes with trade-offs. It works best when GPU memory is carefully managed, often requiring manual tuning of memory usage parameters like vllm_gpu_memory_utilization. While it offers clear throughput benefits and reduces idle GPU time, colocation may not be ideal for models with tight memory budgets or when memory fragmentation is not well controlled. When done right, though, it unlocks significant efficiency gains.

TP/DP compatibility, Accelerate, and torchrun support make deployment seamless. Despite the complexity of the underlying architecture, the entire system can be debuted and scaled with standard distributed tools.

Recent findings suggest that co-located training maintains model quality. Across multiple benchmarks (Math500, AIME24), co-located and plain setups produced comparable results, validating that performance isn’t sacrificed for efficiency.

This blog post explored how co-locating vLLM with GRPO training unlocks significant efficiency gains when training large language models — including models as large as Qwen2.5-72B.

Traditionally, TRL only supported vLLM in server mode, which required separate processes and GPUs for inference, leading to wasted compute and idle time. With the introduction of vLLM’s external launcher and the colocation PR in TRL PR #3394, we can now run training and inference within the same distributed process group, on the same GPUs, with full support for TP, DP, and Accelerate.

While challenges remain — such as version-specific vLLM bugs and edge cases such as with sleep() — the overall results show that co-located GRPO is a practical, scalable solution for training large models efficiently. We’re excited to continue refining this setup, integrating features like FSDP, and pushing the limits of large model training — making it faster, cheaper, and more accessible for everyone building the next generation of LLMs.

Recent findings suggest that yesterday, the Trump administration extended the reach of its existing export controls on high-end AI accelerator chips, namely, but not limited to, Nvidia's Blackwell lineup. The updated regulation now requires licenses for renting those chips in large quantities to the entirety of America's D:5 countries list (nations embargoed from arms sales). As expected, the news landed in Beijing like a lead dragon, and its Ministry of Commerce states that China "will take countermeasures to firmly safeguard national sovereignty, security, and development interests.".

The bold move taken by the U.S. arrives at a peculiar time, as President Trump is at the moment visiting the nation for the APEC summit in Shenzhen. Trump is scheduled to meet President Xi Jinping on Thursday, Nov. 19, a tête-a-tête that's bound to be interesting. Both nations were recently embroiled in a bitter trade war, with ever-mounting tariffs and restrictions on both sides until a temporary truce was called in Oct. 2025. Only some restrictions were lifted, though; for example, Chinese semiconductors still face a 50% tariff when imported stateside.

A potential restart of tariff-slapping would all but guarantee an even larger amount of turmoil in U.S. stock markets. Those seas are already choppy enough thanks to Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang's romantic involvement with purported Chinese spy Alice Huang — along with mounting suspicions that the soulmates may have connived to siphon billions' worth of Blackwell chips from her Singaporean outfit Megaspeed onto Chinese AI laboratories.

It has been revealed that nvidia cut off about half of its Asian buyers last July, seemingly in the purview of the export controls, and told data center operators that over 50% of their business must come from non-Chinese companies. Meanwhile, both Malaysia and Singapore have intensified their scrutiny of AI hardware shipments.

In a recent development, china's countermeasures ammo is as of yet unspecified. The nation had restricted the sale of gallium, germanium, and antimony to the U.S. previously, and the truce shelved that bullet until Nov. 2027. Beijing may well choose to simply not renew that agreement when that day comes. Although analysts believe that the nations will be cordial enough during this summit, Trump's perceived provocation may bring China's proverbial nuclear option of restricting rare earth exports back to the loading bay.

Industry observers note that the truce on that particular matter only has a few weeks left, expiring on Jan. 10, 2027. Likewise, super-hard materials and high-density lithium batteries, crucial for the newest generations of EVs, solar power storage, and battery installations, all have white flags that will come down early next year. Analysts also expect that Chinese firms and their government will continue to heavily invest in domestic chip production, namely, but not only, by Huawei.

Broadly speaking, the U.S.' updated chip control regulation means that Chinese firms cannot sidestep the existing control on chip sales by renting them instead, closing one of the main existing loopholes around the export restrictions. Additionally, selling chips to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, or Brazil now also requires a license, as the U.S. Department of Commerce suspects that companies in these nations import Blackwell cards to sell to China.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • View counts on YouTube are still settling from the change earlier this year where YouTube now counts a view after the very first frame of a video plays.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following a change in how it counts views earlier this year, YouTube is now announcing “Co-Views” as a way for the platform to try and guess how many people are watching a YouTube video on a TV, and it counts towards the video’s total view count.

View counts on YouTube are still settling from the change earlier this year where YouTube now counts a view after the very first frame of a video plays. But, even with that, YouTube only counts a single view for each time the video is played.

Now, YouTube says it might count more views with a new “Co-Views” setup on TVs.

In a post, YouTube explains that “Co-Views” include “the estimated number of people watching together on TV” in the view count of a video. This only applies to TVs, with views from a mobile device or desktop still only ever counting as a single video. It applies to long-form videos as well as Shorts and Live videos, and only applies going forward – historical data won’t change.

YouTube states it is making this change to reflect the “over 1 billion hours” spend on YouTube through their TVs “every day” and that the added data will assist creators in channel strategy or brand pitches, while also providing a “more complete picture of how audiences are engaging with’ content, aligning with TV industry standards – including how traditional broadcast and streaming networks estimate the total number of people exposed to content.” But “Co-Views” won’t count towards earnings on the platform, as they’re not “Qualified Views.”.

Recent findings suggest that how is YouTube figuring out what to count here? “Guessing” is not exactly an inaccurate summarization, but Google stresses that it is not using cameras or microphones, but rather a “statistical mode.”.

According to recent reports, youTube doesn’t use devices, cameras, microphones or anything like that. Co-views are estimated using a privacy safe statistical mode, developed by Google research scientists, based on factors like demographic patterns and viewing times, calibrated against ground-truth data sources like industry panels.

This change is rolling out now.

You wrote a good email. You hit send. Then half your list never saw it, because it went straight to spam.

That is a deliverability problem, and it costs more than most teams think. Every email that misses the inbox is a lead you paid for and never reached.

The good part is that deliverability is not luck. Mailbox providers like Gmail, Yahoo and Outlook judge you on a short list of things: who you are, who you send to, and how people react. Fix those and your inbox placement goes up.

This guide covers 10 email deliverability best practices in the order you should fix them, starting with SPF and ending with sender reputation.

Email deliverability is the share of your emails that land in the inbox instead of the spam folder or nowhere at all.

Industry observers note that people often mix it up with delivery rate. They are not the same thing.

In a recent development, you can have a 99% delivery rate and still have most of your emails sitting in spam. That is why your email tool can say "delivered" while your open rate keeps dropping.

The big mailbox providers stopped treating authentication as optional.

Microsoft followed on May 5, 2025. If you send more than 5,000 emails a day to Outlook.com, Hotmail or Live addresses, you need all three records in place or your mail goes to junk.

Send less than 5,000 a day? Follow the rules anyway. The same checks decide inbox placement for small senders too, just without the public warning.

SPF (Sender Policy Framework) is a TXT record in your DNS. It lists the servers allowed to send email from your domain.

When your email arrives, the receiving server checks that list. If the sending server is not on it, the email looks suspicious.

A basic SPF record looks like this:.

DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) adds a digital signature to each email. The receiving server uses a public key in your DNS to check two things: the email came from you, and nobody changed it on the way.

Your email provider gives you the DKIM record. You paste it into your DNS and switch signing on.

DKIM also survives forwarding, which SPF does not. If you can only get one of the two perfect, get DKIM right.

DMARC ties SPF and DKIM together. It tells mailbox providers what to do when an email fails both checks, and it sends you reports on who is sending mail under your domain name.

Start with a monitoring policy:.

p=none means "take no action, just send me reports." It is the minimum Gmail, Yahoo and Microsoft accept from bulk senders.

In a recent development, don't stop there. Read the reports for a few weeks, fix any real sender that is failing, then move up:.

Sources indicate that one more thing: DMARC needs alignment. The domain in your From address has to match the domain used in SPF or DKIM. Plenty of senders have all three records and still fail DMARC because their email tool signs with its own domain.

According to recent reports, if you'd rather not handle this in-house, you can also hire a B2B cold email marketing agency such as IntentSignal, Martal or Belkins. A good agency will set up the domains, mailboxes, warm-up and SPF, DKIM and DMARC records for you, and keep an eye on deliverability while the campaigns run.

A upcoming domain has no history. If it sends 10,000 emails on day one, it looks exactly like a spammer who just bought a domain.

Warm-up means starting small and growing a little each day, so mailbox providers can watch how people react to you.

A simple schedule for a new domain:.

In a recent development, send to your most active contacts first. Their opens and replies are what build trust early. If bounces or complaints jump, hold at that volume until they settle.

According to recent reports, and if you run cold outreach, do it from a separate domain or subdomain. That way a bad campaign can't hurt the domain your invoices and password resets come from.

A bigger list is not a better list. Dead addresses and people who stopped caring pull your numbers down.

Never buy a list. Bought lists are full of spam traps, which are addresses that exist only to catch senders who email people without permission. Hitting a few of them can get your domain blocklisted.

Yes, you lose some sign-ups. What you keep is real people with working inboxes who actually want your emails. That means fewer bounces, fewer complaints and better opens from day one.

It also keeps bots and fake addresses out of your forms, which matters a lot if your sign-up form is public.

Recent findings suggest that most email platforms add these for you. Check that yours does.

These two numbers tell you the most about where you stand.

Industry observers note that the complaint figures come from Gmail's own rules. The bounce figures are the working limits most email platforms use.

Recent findings suggest that A 0.3% complaint rate is only 3 complaints per 1,000 emails. It does not take much to cross that line.

If complaints are climbing, ask three questions:.

Most complaint problems come from one of those three, not from the email itself.

Spam filters got smarter. A single word like "free" won't sink you anymore. Patterns will.

Replies help a lot. When someone replies, the mailbox provider sees a real conversation. Ask a question in your welcome email and you'll get some.

Sources indicate that sender reputation is the score mailbox providers give your domain and IP. Everything above feeds into it. A good score means inbox. A bad one means spam, no matter how good the email is.

You can't see the exact score, but these free tools get you close:.

Check them weekly, and right after any big campaign.

A few habits protect your reputation over time:.

Sources indicate that aim for 95% or higher inbox placement. Below 90% means something needs fixing, usually authentication or list quality.

Sources indicate that the common causes are missing or broken SPF, DKIM or DMARC records, a high complaint rate, an old list with lots of dead addresses, or a new domain that sent too much too soon. Check authentication first because it is the fastest to fix.

Industry observers note that DNS fixes like SPF and DKIM take effect within a day or two. Reputation is slower. Expect two to six weeks of steady, clean sending before inbox placement recovers.

According to recent reports, yes. The 5,000 mark is where Gmail, Yahoo and Microsoft start enforcing openly. Small senders are still judged on the same signals, and Gmail asks every sender for at least SPF or DKIM.

Only if you send enough to keep it warm, roughly 100,000 emails a month or more. Below that, a good shared IP from a trusted provider usually performs better.

According to recent reports, sender reputation covers both your IP address and your domain. Domain reputation is the part tied to your domain name, and it follows you even if you switch email providers. Gmail leans on domain reputation more than IP.

Industry observers note that if you only have an hour this week, spend it on SPF, DKIM and DMARC. Nothing else works until those pass.

Industry observers note that after that, clean your list and keep an eye on complaints. Send emails people asked for, to people who still want them, from a domain that proves who it is. Do that for a few weeks and your emails will land in the inbox again.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, we introduce SmolVLA, a compact (450M), open-source Vision-Language-Action model for robotics that runs on consumer hardware.
  • Sources indicate that over the past few years, Transformers have driven remarkable progress in AI, from language models capable of human-like reasoning to multimodal systems that understand both images and text.
  • In response to these challenges, the field has recently turned to vision-language-action (VLA) models, which aim to unify perception, language understanding, and action prediction within a single architecture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we introduce SmolVLA, a compact (450M), open-source Vision-Language-Action model for robotics that runs on consumer hardware.

Sources indicate that over the past few years, Transformers have driven remarkable progress in AI, from language models capable of human-like reasoning to multimodal systems that understand both images and text. However, in real-world robotics, advancements have been much slower. Robots still struggle to generalize across diverse objects, environments, and tasks. This limited progress stems from a lack of high-quality, diverse data and the absence of models that can reason and act like humans in the physical world.

In response to these challenges, the field has recently turned to vision-language-action (VLA) models, which aim to unify perception, language understanding, and action prediction within a single architecture. VLAs typically take as input raw visual observations and natural language instructions, and output corresponding robot actions. While promising, much of the recent progress in VLAs remains locked behind proprietary models trained on large-scale private datasets, often requiring costly hardware setups and extensive engineering resources. As a result, the broader robotics research community faces significant barriers in reproducing and building upon these models.

SmolVLA addresses this gap by offering an open-source, compact, and efficient VLA model that can be trained on consumer-grade hardware using only publicly available datasets. By releasing not only model weights but also using very affordable open-source hardware, SmolVLA aims to democratize access to vision-language-action models and accelerate research toward generalist robotic agents.

Figure 1: Comparison of SmolVLA across task variations. From left to right: (1) asynchronous pick-place cube counting, (2) synchronous pick-place cube counting, (3) pick-place cube counting under perturbations, and (4) generalization on pick-and-place of the lego block with real-world SO101.

SmolVLA-450M is our open-source, compact yet capable VLA model. It is:.

Inspired by the training paradigms of Large Language Models (LLMs), SmolVLA goes through a pretraining phase on general manipulation data, followed by task-specific post-training. Architecturally, it combines Transformers with flow-matching decoders, and is optimized for speed and low-latency inference with the following design choices:.

Despite using fewer than 30k training episodes—an order of magnitude less than other VLAs—SmolVLA matches or exceeds the performance of much larger models, both in simulation and the real world.

To make real-time robotics easier to use, we introduce an asynchronous inference stack. This technology separates how robots perform actions from how they understand what they see and hear. Because of this separation, robots can respond more rapidly in fast-changing environments.

Figure 2. SmolVLA takes as input a sequence of RGB images from multiple cameras, the robot’s current sensorimotor state, and a natural language instruction. The VLM encodes these into contextual features, which condition the action expert to generate a continuous sequence of actions.

SmolVLA is designed to be easy to use and integrate—whether you're finetuning on your own data or plugging it into an existing robotics stack.

First, install the required dependencies:.

Use smolvla_base, our pretrained 450M model, with the lerobot training framework:.

​​If you'd like to build from the architecture (pretrained VLM + action expert) rather than a pretrained checkpoint:.

You can also load SmolVLAPolicy directly:.

In a recent development, smolVLA is not only a lightweight yet capable model, but also a method for training and evaluating generalist robotics policies. In this section, we introduce the model architecture behind SmolVLA and the asynchronous inference setup used for evaluation, which has proven to be more adaptable and capable of faster recovery.

SmolVLA consists of two core components: a Vision-Language Model (VLM) that processes multimodal inputs and an action expert that outputs robot control commands. Below, we share the details of the main components of SmolVLA architecture and the Asynchronous Inference. More details can be found in our technical report.

According to recent reports, we use SmolVLM2 as our VLM backbone. It’s optimized for multi-image inputs and consists of a SigLIP vision encoder and a SmolLM2 language decoder.

The decoder layers process concatenated image, language, and state tokens. The resulting features are then passed to the action expert.

SmolVLA’s action expert is a compact transformer (~100M parameters) that generates action chunks, i.e. sequences of future robot actions, conditioned on the VLM’s outputs. It is trained using a flow matching objective, which teaches the model to guide noisy samples back to the ground truth. In contrast, while discrete action representations (e.g., via tokenization) are powerful, they often require autoregressive decoding, which is slow and inefficient at inference time. While flow matching allows direct, non-autoregressive prediction of continuous actions, enabling real-time control with high precision.

In a recent development, more intuitively, during training, we add random noise to the robot’s real action sequences and ask the model to predict the “correction vector” that brings them back to the correct trajectory. This forms a smooth vector field over the action space, helping the model learn accurate and stable control policies.

We implement this using a transformer architecture with interleaved attention blocks (see the figure 2), and reduce its hidden size to 75% of the VLM’s, keeping the model lightweight for deployment.

While combining a vision-language model with an action prediction module is a common design pattern in recent VLA systems—such as Pi0, GR00T, Diffusion Policy — we identified several architectural choices that significantly enhance the robustness and performance. In SmolVLA, we apply three key techniques: reducing the number of visual tokens, skipping upper layers in the VLM, and interleaving cross- and self-attention layers in the action expert.

High-resolution images improve perception but can significantly slow down inference. To strike a balance, SmolVLA limits the number of visual tokens to 64 per frame during both training and inference. For example, a 512×512 image is compressed into just 64 tokens, instead of 1024, using PixelShuffle as an efficient shuffling technique. While the underlying Vision-Language Model (VLM) was originally pretrained using image tiling for broader coverage, SmolVLA uses only the global image at runtime to keep inference lightweight and fast.

Rather than always relying on the final layer of the VLM—which can be expensive and sometimes suboptimal—we use features from intermediate layers. Prior work has shown that early layers often provide better representations for downstream tasks. In SmolVLA, the action expert only attends to VLM features up to a configurable layer NN during training, set to half the total layers. This halves the compute cost of both the VLM and the action expert, significantly speeding up inference with minimal performance loss.

Inside the action expert, attention layers alternate between:.

Industry observers note that we found that this interleaved design is both lighter and more effective than using full attention blocks. Models that rely only on CA or only on SA tend to sacrifice either smoothness or grounding.

In SmolVLA, CA ensures that actions are well-conditioned on perception and instructions, while SA improves temporal smoothness—especially critical for real-world control, where jittery predictions can result in unsafe or unstable behavior.

Sources indicate that figure 3. Asynchronous inference. Illustration of the asynchronous inference stack. Note that the policy can be run on a remote server, possibly with GPUs.

Sources indicate that modern visuomotor policies output action chunks—sequences of actions to execute. There are two ways to manage them:.

In a recent development, our async stack decouples action execution from chunk prediction, resulting in higher adaptability, and the complete lack of execution lags at runtime. It relies on the following key mechanisms:.

We are really excited about releasing asynchronous inference because it guarantees greater adaptability and improved performance without changing the model. In short, async inference keeps the robot responsive by overlapping execution and remote prediction.

While vision and language models thrive on web-scale datasets like LAION, ImageNet, and Common Crawl, robotics lacks a comparable resource. There’s no “Internet of robots.” Instead, data is fragmented across robot types, sensors, control schemes, and formats—forming disconnected "data islands". In our previous post, we explored how this fragmentation could be resolved through open, collaborative efforts. Just as ImageNet catalyzed breakthroughs in computer vision by providing a large, diverse benchmark, we believe that community-driven robotics datasets can play the same foundational role for generalist robot policies.

SmolVLA is our first step toward that vision: It is pretrained on a curated mix of publicly available, community-contributed datasets designed to reflect real-world variation. Rather than optimizing for dataset size alone, we focus on diversity: a range of behaviors, camera viewpoints, and embodiments that promote transfer and generalization.

All training data used in SmolVLA comes from LeRobot Community Datasets , robotics datasets shared on the Hugging Face Hub under the lerobot tag. Collected in diverse settings, from labs to living rooms, these datasets represent an open, decentralized effort to scale real-world robot data.

Figure 4. A glimpse of the community dataset. Special thanks to Ville Kuosmanen for creating the visualization. Unlike academic benchmarks, community datasets naturally capture messy, realistic interactions: varied lighting, suboptimal demonstrations, unconventional objects, and heterogeneous control schemes. This kind of diversity will be very useful for learning robust, general-purpose representations.

In a recent development, we used a customfiltering tool created by Alexandre Chapin and Ville Kuosmanen to select datasets based on frame count, visual quality, and task coverage. After a meticulous manual review (special thanks to Marina Barannikov), we curated a collection of 487 high-quality datasets focused on the SO100 robotic arm, standardized at 30 FPS. This yielded around 10 million frames—at least one order of magnitude smaller than other popular benchmark datasets, yet significantly more diverse.

Recent findings suggest that A common matter across community datasets was noisy or missing task descriptions. Many episodes lacked annotations or included vague labels like “task desc” or “Move”, “Pick”. To improve quality and standardize the textual input across datasets, we used Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct to generate concise, action-oriented descriptions.

Given sample frames and the original label, the model was prompted to rewrite the instruction in under 30 characters, starting with an action verb (e.g., “Pick,” “Place,” “Open”).

Another challenge was inconsistent camera naming. Some datasets used clear names like top or wrist.right, while others used ambiguous labels like images.laptop, which varied in meaning. To fix this, we manually went through the datasets and mapped each camera view to a standardized scheme: OBS_IMAGE_1: Top-down view OBS_IMAGE_2: Wrist-mounted view OBS_IMAGE_3+: Additional viewpoints.

We further isolate the contributions of community dataset pretraining and multitask finetuning. Without pretraining on the LeRobot community datasets, SmolVLA initially achieves 51.7% success on SO100. After pretraining on community-collected data, performance jumps to 78.3%, a +26.6% absolute improvement. Multitask finetuning further boosts performance, showing strong task transfer capabilities even in low-data regimes.

According to recent reports, table 1. Impact of Pretraining on Community Datasets and Multitask Finetuning.

According to recent reports, we evaluate SmolVLA across simulation and real-world benchmarks to test its generalization, efficiency, and robustness. Despite being compact, It consistently outperforms or matches the performance of significantly larger models and policies pretrained on higher-scale robotics data.

Industry observers note that table 2. SmolVLA Performance on Simulation Benchmarks.

Sources indicate that in real-world settings, SmolVLA is evaluated on two diverse suites: SO100 and SO101. These tasks include pick-place, stacking, and sorting, with both in-distribution and out-of-distribution object configurations. On SO101, SmolVLA also excels in generalization:.

According to recent reports, table 4. Generalization of SmolVLA to Fresh Embodiment (SO101) vs ACT..

Finally, we evaluate SmolVLA under synchronous and asynchronous inference modes. Async inference decouples action execution from model inference, allowing the policy to react while the robot is moving.

This results in more responsive and robust real-world performance, especially in dynamic environments with shifting objects or external disturbances.

Figure 5. Asynchronous vs. Synchronous Inference in Real-World Tasks. (a) Task success rates (%), (b) average completion time(s), and (c) number of tasks completed within a fixed time window.

Sources indicate that smolVLA is our contribution to building robotics foundation models that are open, efficient, and reproducible. Despite its small size, it matches or outperforms larger, proprietary models across a range of real-world and simulated tasks. By relying solely on community-contributed datasets and affordable hardware, SmolVLA lowers the barrier to entry for researchers, educators, and hobbyists alike. But this is just the beginning. SmolVLA is more than just a model — it's part of a growing open-source movement toward scalable, collaborative robotics.

According to recent reports, together, we can make real-world robotics more capable, more affordable, and more open. ✨.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, at H Firm, we are releasing Holo1, a family of Action Vision Language Models (VLMs) and WebClick, a new multimodal localization benchmark on the Hugging Face Hub.

Surfer-H, a web-native agent that interacts with browsers like a human relies on the Holo1.

Holo1 is the first family of open-source Action VLMs designed specifically for deep web UI understanding and precise localization. The family includes Holo1-3B and Holo1-7B models, with the latter achieving 76.2% average accuracy on common UI localization benchmarks—the highest among small-size models. H Organization has released these models with open-source on Hugging Face, along with the WebClick benchmark containing 1,639 human-like UI tasks.

Sources indicate that holo1 models are based on the Qwen2.5-VL architecture, and are fully compatible with transformers. Here we provide a simple usage example. You can load the model and the processor as follows.

Web automation represents one of AI's most practical applications for businesses, but until now, solutions have often sacrificed cost-efficiency for performance. By making our Holo1 Action Models available in Hugging Face, users can now implement web automation solutions that achieve 92.2% accuracy on real-world web tasks at only $0.13 per task.

Surfer-H relies on the Holo1 family of open-weights models. It is a modular architecture for complete web task automation, which performs reading, thinking, clicking, scrolling, typing, and validating. It is designed to be flexible and modular, composed of three independent components: a Policy model that prepares and drives the agent's behavior, a Localizer model that understands visual UIs for precise interactions, and a Validator model that confirms whether tasks are completed successfully. Unlike other agents that rely on custom APIs or brittle wrappers, Surfer-H operates purely through the browser — just like a real user.

Together, these solutions represent a upcoming frontier in web automation, achieving state-of-the-art localization performance and setting the Pareto frontier in cost-efficient web navigation on the WebVoyager benchmark:.

SSDs, laptops, and phones may get cheaper as consumer NAND spot pricing drops 20%

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (676 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Solid-state drives, phones, laptops, and tablets have all gotten substantially pricier in the last couple of years.
  • Industry observers note that the report observes a 20% drop in spot pricing for NAND chips over just the last month.
  • SED says that according to that note, 512 Gb NAND wafers saw a 32% drop to $14.30 apiece on the spot market, while 1 Tb wafers fell 19% to $24.90.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Solid-state drives, phones, laptops, and tablets have all gotten substantially pricier in the last couple of years. Beyond the stratospheric prices of DDR5 memory, prospective PC builders and consumer electronics buyers have had to deal with upcharges on SSDs of all sizes thanks to the AI boom. That may be changing soon, as spot pricing for consumer NAND chips is reportedly dropping, according to a latest report from Seoul Economic Daily (SED).

Industry observers note that the report observes a 20% drop in spot pricing for NAND chips over just the last month. Its conclusions are bolstered by information from a Bank of America note from Nov. 13, wherein industry sources tell that institution that NAND is due for a market correction.

SED says that according to that note, 512 Gb NAND wafers saw a 32% drop to $14.30 apiece on the spot market, while 1 Tb wafers fell 19% to $24.90. SED quotes another industry source that says: "NAND cannot sustain the steep price gains seen so far.".

Sources indicate that those decreases may be hard to square in a time when enterprise SSDs are getting pricier by the day, but SED notes that the rise in phone and PC prices has led customers to delay upgrades, resulting in a 20% year-on-year decline in shipments for phones alone and making for the lowest third-quarter volumes in 14 years. Meanwhile, PC shipments have also fallen 22.5% year-on-year, according to a Gartner report.

In the face of those consumer decisions, device makers are letting their existing stock drain out and are presumably stocked with NAND chips for the short term, thus resulting in lower prices for new fab shipments on the short-term spot market.

Another factor in the consumer NAND market is that not all flash is equal. Both RAM and NAND makers have been redirecting their chip output to serve the ongoing AI boom, converting their consumer-grade production lines to make higher-spec silicon. Memory factories have been converting DDR5 capacity to HBM at a steady pace, as parts of the process are shared across both types.

But according to the Bank of America note that SED cites, things are different in the NAND world. High-density flash now sits at around 300 layers, and its production requires substantially different tooling compared to the lower-grade silicon deemed suitable for us mere mortals. So the continuing growth in NAND demand from AI data centers may not translate directly into reduced consumer supply.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

In a recent development, beyond those factors, added supply from Chinese NAND maker YMTC is creating additional downward price pressure in the NAND market. SED notes that YMTC has taken a 14% chunk from major players in the NAND market in the second quarter of this year alone.

In a recent development, on net, these forces could result in a bit of relief for consumer tech. SED indicates Bank of America expects consumer NAND prices for PCs and smartphones to fall 5% to 10% on the longer-term contract market in the first quarter of 2027, while enterprise NAND contract prices are expected to hold more or less steady.

Whether those declines translate to lower prices for finished devices and components like SSDs will remain to be seen, and products with those chips inside will require some time to reach the market. But in the ongoing AI supply crunch, any potential relief is worth celebrating.

Alongside the huge list of upcoming updates Google detailed yesterday, the organization also revealed that a “faster and more natural” version of Gemini Live is coming to speakers and smart displays “soon.”.

Google explains this is from Gemini Live moving to the “latest speech-to-speech architecture” and brings “significantly faster response times.” Gemini Live isn’t the default experience when you start a “Hey Google” command, rather hiding behind a “let’s chat” or other similar command to start a session.

Initially, Live sessions were purely for brainstorming or longer conversations and lacking support for commands and other functions mid-session, but Google now says that this upgrade will add support for actions such as smart home controls, setting timers, and more without leaving a Live session. That’s a big deal.

In a recent development, coming soon – A faster and more natural Gemini Live experience: Available with a Google Home Premium subscription, Gemini Live is being upgraded to our latest speech-to-speech architecture for significantly faster response times and a smoother experience. Just say, “Hey Google, let’s chat” to brainstorm dinner ideas or proposal a trip out loud, interrupt naturally to change topics, and perform actions mid-conversation—such as, setting a timer, adding a reminder,or controlling a smart home device—without stepping out of the chat³.

The “catch” is that you’ll still need a subscription to use this. Gemini Live has always required a subscription on Google Home speakers and smart displays, with the functionality looped into Google Home Premium looks which start at $10/month (or bundled into Google One AI Pro). That’s the same subscription that gives you Nest storage.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we have implemented KV Caching from scratch in our nanoVLM repository (a small codebase to train your own Vision Language Model with pure PyTorch).
  • In a recent development, autoregressive language models generate text by sampling one token at a time.
  • This step-by-step generation is inherently sequential:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we have implemented KV Caching from scratch in our nanoVLM repository (a small codebase to train your own Vision Language Model with pure PyTorch). This gave us a 38% speedup in generation. In this blog post we cover KV Caching and all our experiences while implementing it. The lessons learnt are general and can be applied to all autoregressive language model generations. Implementing from scratch on a small codebase is a great learning experience, come along for the ride!

In a recent development, autoregressive language models generate text by sampling one token at a time. During inference, the model processes a given input sequence, predicts the next token, appends it to the sequence, and repeats this process until some stopping criterion:.

This step-by-step generation is inherently sequential:.

It has been revealed that this repetition also leads to computational redundancy. In this post, we explore KV Caching, an optimisation technique that mitigates this inefficiency.

Before diving into caching, let’s revisit how attention operates in transformer models. A Transformer language model consists of stacked layers, each composed of:.

To understand where KV Caching helps, we focus on the self-attention mechanism, specifically within a single attention head.

Let’s walk through a simple PyTorch implementation to visualise the key computations.

For a sequence of T T T input embeddings represented as X∈RT×D X \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times D} X∈RT×D, self-attention is computed as:.

Attention(X;Q,K,V)=softmax(QK⊤⋅Mdk)V \text{Attention}(X; Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\left( \frac{QK^\top \cdot M}{\sqrt{d_k}} \right)V Attention(X;Q,K,V)=softmax(dk​​QK⊤⋅M​)V.

Here’s a minimal PyTorch equivalent using a causal mask:.

In autoregressive generation, the model generates one token at a time. With each step, it recomputes Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V for the entire sequence, even though the earlier tokens haven’t changed.

These checks show that for all but the newest token, K K K and V V V are identical to previously computed values.

Most of the attention computation is repeated needlessly. This gets more expensive as sequences grow.

To eliminate this inefficiency, we use KV Caching:.

This changes generation from full-sequence re-computation to a lightweight, incremental revision.

✅ In practice, this cache is a per-layer dictionary with keys "key" and "value", each of shape (batch_size, num_heads, seq_len_cached, head_dim).

This is the foundation of how modern LLMs can generate long outputs efficiently.

Recent findings suggest that now that we understand the theory behind KV Caching, let’s see how it’s implemented in practice inside our nanoVLM repository. This is an ideal testbed, as it's a super concise and self-contained codebase.

KV caching is enabled across three key components in our model:.

In the LanguageModelGroupedAttention class, we modify the forward function to accept and update a cache of keys and values (block_kv_cache).

Previously, the model recomputed K K K and V V V at every generation step. Now we only compute Knew K_{\text{upcoming}} Knew​, Vnew V_{\text{new}} Vnew​ for the current token, and append them to the cached values.

Industry observers note that in the LanguageModel class, we introduce layer-wise cache tracking. The start_pos argument helps the model compute correct rotary positional encodings for newly generated tokens.

The biggest architectural change is in the generate() method of the VisionLanguageModel.

We split generation into two stages:.

By separating these phases, we avoid redundant computation and dramatically speed up inference, especially for long prompts.

KV caching eliminates unnecessary computation during autoregressive generation, enabling faster and more efficient inference, especially in long sequences and real-time applications. This is a trade-off between speed and memory, and its drawbacks can be more complex code and restricting fancier inference schemes, like beam-search, etc. KV caching is a popular method for speeding up LLM inference, making it possible to run them on consumer hardware, and now you know how it works too!

IP geolocation maps an IP address to a physical location & network details, letting you spot suspicious traffic before it reaches sensitive actions. Used well, it’s an invisible, low-friction risk signal. In this guide, you will learn how to flag high-risk activity and apply soft geo-fencing with step-up authentication.

According to recent reports, today, an IP lookup returns far more than a country & city. It can also reveal several other parameters, like.

Each of these fields acts as a clue telling who is really behind a request.

This data powers anomaly detection. You can start by building a baseline for normal behavior for each user with aspects like.

Then, you can watch for deviations from that pattern. An attacker won’t look like the account’s real owner, so you'll catch them.

Geolocation makes several common attack patterns easy to spot:.

The first is traffic bursts from data center ASNs. These are bots, as real customers don’t browse from cloud servers.

According to recent reports, many accounts created from one IP or subnet. This is a clear sign of fake signups.

Impossible travel, such as logins from two distant locations within minutes.

Industry observers note that timezone vs. IP mismatch. A device’s clock disagrees with its apparent location.

Note: Geolocation is just a signal, not a verdict. VPNs, travel, & mobile carriers can all create false alarms, so it works best when combined with other signals. That’s exactly why a proportional, soft response beats a hard block.

In short, IP geolocation turns a bare IP address into context, helping you separate real users from automated or fraudulent traffic.

In a recent development, not every IP geolocation anomaly deserves the same response. The simplest way to stay consistent is to define a clear risk-signal framework.

That can be a short list of checks. Each check can have a weight that reflects how strongly it suggests fraud.

With risk scoring, you can turn these checks into a decision. You just have to assign each signal a numeric weight.

For example, medium can be 10 & 30 can be high.

Now, you need to add up every signal that comes up & map the total to thresholds like.

A single medium signal passes quietly, but several can trigger action.

A customer who has a US billing address logs in from Germany. This is a strong signal, but not proof of fraud. The user could be traveling, an expat, or a privacy-conscious user using a VPN.

Sources indicate that if you treat this as an automatic block, it would punish legitimate customers. Instead, let it raise the score & you take action only if it stacks with other signals, like a hosting IP or a latest device.

Now that you know how to quantify the risk, here is how you can protect yourself without damaging UX.

Before soft, let us learn about hard blocking. This is where you completely deny or permanently ban traffic from specific geographic regions.
