Voyager 1 spacecraft crosses milestones distance of one-light day from Earth 49 years after launch

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that NASA has confirmed that Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to reach one light-day's distance from Earth, passing the milestone today.
  • According to recent reports, there are many astronomical numbers behind what is an extraordinary feat.
  • Industry observers note that these are probably bigger distances than you are used to fathoming.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that NASA has confirmed that Voyager 1 is the first human-made object to reach one light-day's distance from Earth, passing the milestone today. A countdown at Orbital Radar confirmed that Voyager cruised past the threshold at a leisurely 37,844 mph just after 5 am ET on Wednesday, November 18. It means that Voyager is now more than 16 billion miles away, and that a signal from the spacecraft now takes fully 24 hours to travel the distance.

According to recent reports, there are many astronomical numbers behind what is an extraordinary feat. Sci-fi indicates casually mention light-years as if they are like a trip to the local convenience store. One light-day isn’t a distance to be derided, though. Over the last half century, hurtling through space at a cruising speed of 38,000 mph, the Voyager spacecraft has clocked about 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers).

Industry observers note that these are probably bigger distances than you are used to fathoming. So NASA has kindly provided some context with the distances of various heavenly bodies in miles and light-speeds. For example, the Moon is 238,855 miles distant, or about 1.3 light seconds away from Earth. Due to Mars’ independent orbit around the Sun, it can take between three minutes and 22 minutes for light to travel between the red and the blue planet. Meanwhile, the Sun’s rays reach Earth, about 93 million miles away, in 20 light seconds. Now let us remind you that Voyager 1 is on the brink of being a whole light-day away.

On Wednesday, with this major milestone passed, Voyager 1’s journey will be far from over. NASA states that it is on course for an obscure star called Gliese 445, now in the constellation Ursa Minor. We’ll have to keep the champagne on ice for another 40,000 years to celebrate the fly-past of that star, though.

Voyager 1 carries a copy of the Golden Record. Like sending a message in a bottle, NASA scientists launched Voyager with the hope that someone, somewhere will eventually read the message. Moreover, the receiving aliens will need to source tech to play the record, which contains sounds, music, and the data needed to reconstruct photos that showcase the diversity of life and culture on our planet.

If an alien got hold of the record on Wednesday and managed to rustle up a gramophone player to listen to it, a message sent to Earth via radio waves would take a full 24 hours to be received.

In a recent development, space enthusiasts are also invited to participate in a global event “by creating a wave of golden light.” It sounds rather pointless, but enthusiasts are asked to flash the three-letter call sign for NASA's Voyager mission, VGR, into the night sky - Morse Code style - using their phone flashlights. There’s a website you can open to flash your screen appropriately.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past few weeks, we’ve been working tirelessly on making GUI agents more open, accessible and easy to integrate. Along the way, we created the largest benchmarking suite for GUI agents performances 👉 let us introduce ScreenSuite.

We are very excited to share it with you today: ScreenSuite is the most comprehensive and easiest way to evaluate Vision Language Models (VLMs)across many agentic capabilities!

GUI Agents in action - courtesy of OSWorld.

In short, an AI Agent is a robot that acts in the virtual world. (more thorough definition here).

It has been revealed that in particular, a “GUI Agent” is an agent that lives in a GUI. Think “an agent that can do clicks and navigate on my desktop or my phone”, à la Claude Computer Use.

It has been revealed that this means in essence that the AI model powering the agent will be given a task like “Fill the rest of this Excel column”, along with screen captures of the GUI. Using this information, it will then decide to take action on the system : click(x=130, y=540) to open a web browser, type(”Value for XYZ in 2025"), scroll(down=2) to read further… To see a GUI agent in action, you can try our Open Computer Agent, powered by Qwen2.5-VL-72B.

Industry observers note that A good GUI agent will be able to navigate a computer just like we would, thus unlocking all computer tasks : scrolling through Google Maps, editing a file, buying an item online. This involves a variety of capabilities that can be hard to evaluate.

Sources indicate that the literature, for instance Xu et al. (2025) or Qin et al. (2025), generally splits GUI agent abilities amongst several categories:.

So our first contribution is to gather and unify a comprehensive suite of 13 benchmarks spanning the full range of these GUI agent capabilities.

In a recent development, if you look at the last category listed above, evaluating Multi-step agentic capabilities is especially challenging as it requires virtual machines to run the agent’s environment, be it Windows, Android, Ubuntu... To address this, we provide support both for E2B desktop remote sandboxes, and we created from scratch a upcoming option to easily launch Ubuntu or Android virtual machines in Docker!

In a recent development, we’ve carefully designed our benchmark suite with modularity and consistency in mind, ensuring strong alignment across tasks and environments. When required, especially for online benchmarks, we leverage smolagents as framework layer to streamline agent execution and orchestration.

To support reproducibility and ease of use, we’ve built custom Dockerized containers that allow local deployment of full Ubuntu Desktop or Android environments.

According to recent reports, unlike many existing GUI benchmarks that rely on accessibility trees or other metadata alongside visual input, our stack is intentionally vision-only. While this can result in different scores on some established leaderboards, we deem that it creates a more realistic and challenging setup, one that better reflects how humans perceive and interact with graphical interfaces.

– All agentic frameworks (Android World, OSWorld, GAIAWeb, Mind2Web) use smolagents and rely solely on vision, without any accessibility tree or DOM added (in contrast with evaluation settings reported in other sources). – Mind2Web (Multimodal) originally used element-name-based multi-choice selection based on the accessibility tree and screenshots, but was later adapted to click precision within bounding boxes using vision only, which significantly increases task difficulty.

We’ve evaluated leading VLMs on the benchmark.

Our scores are in general agreement with the scores reported in various sources! With the caveat that we evaluate on vision only, causing some differences, see implementation details above.

💡 Note that ScreenSuite does not intend to exactly reproduce benchmarks published in the industry: we evaluate models on GUI agentic capabilities based on vision. As a result, on benchmarks like Mind2Web where other benchmarks gave the agent a view of information rich context like DOM or accessibility tree, our evaluation setting is much harder, thus ScreenSuite does not match other sources.

The multistep benchmarks requires a bare-metal machine to run and deploy desktop/mobile* environment *emulators (see README.md).

Running consistent and meaningful evaluations easily allows the community to quickly iterate and make progress in this field, as we’ve seen with Eleuther LM evaluation harness, the Open LLM Leaderboard and the Chatbot Arena.

We hope to see much more capable open models in the coming month that can run a wide range of tasks reliably and even run locally!

Pebblebee released its Alert feature in 2025 as a way to use a Clip 5 tracker for Find Hub as a siren in an emergency. The tech giant later added an optional live location-sharing feature to this, and also released “Halo” as an emergency siren first, tracker second with a special design.

Now, “Alert Dispatch” takes the whole system up a notch.

It has been revealed that instead of relying solely on location sharing and the siren, Pebblebee’s Alert Dispatch assigns an actual human being to the situation, with a trained dispatch agent reaching out first over SMS or a call, then pulling in emergency responders if the situation calls for it. The feature works with Clip 4, Clip 5, and Halo.

Alert Dispatch connects Pebblebee owners with a trained dispatch agent when they trigger an Alert, starting with a text and escalating to an Emergency call if they don’t respond. With an attempt to send help when users cannot confirm they’re safe, plus live location sharing and private Check-In calls on Clip 5 and Halo, it adds another layer of support when calling for help isn’t an option.

In a recent development, pebblebee Alert Dispatch runs in partnership with Noonlight, with an alert triggered by disconnecting Halo or rapidly pressing the button on Clip trackers. Pricing is as follows:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A new device on Kickstarter claims to make Game Boy cartridges relevant again by playing soundtracks from your favorite classic Nintendo games. The Retro Song Bird is a box-shaped speaker that supports Game Boy and Game Boy Color cartridges, with support for over 1,900 games. Simply inserting a cartridge into the speaker gives you access to all soundtracks and sound effects, which can be controlled using onboard physical controls including next, previous, and volume.

The Retro Song Bird also comes with a 3.5mm stereo line-out and a USB Type-C port in case you want to connect to other audio equipment. According to the developer, it offers accurate, register-level sound emulation and can be used to sample and remix music from your Game Boy cartridges. It exposes all four audio channels (two square, wave, noise) as separate USB audio streams that can be imported into a DAW. This allows you to isolate individual melodies, waveforms, and sound effects from old games to create your own melodies. There’s even support for LSDj for playing saved chiptune tracks, while two Retro Song Bird units can be synced for DJ-style performances using Game Boy cartridges instead of traditional records.

According to recent reports, in addition to playing retro video game soundtracks, the Retro Song Bird also supports the Game Boy Camera, allowing you to use it as a webcam offering a glorious 128×112 pixels resolution and 5 frames per second speed. Other features include the ability to back up and restore save files, ROMs, flash writable carts, and export any soundtrack or sound effect as WAV onto your PC. The listing also includes other abilities, including an Alarm Mode, a record of every cartridge you've ever plugged in, an open API for developers, and over-the-air updates.

In a recent development, the Retro Song Bird is currently available to back on Kickstarter, with the standard model starting at $79. The introductory $59 Early Bird offer has already sold out, while the developer is also offering a two-unit bundle for $150. Shipments are expected to begin in April 2027.

Industry observers note that the developer notes that only a handful of hand-assembled prototypes right now exist and that the hardware and design still need some refinements. The project also faces potential manufacturing challenges, including component availability, finding suitable manufacturing partners, and producing injection-molded enclosures. Like any other Kickstarter campaign, delivery timelines are subject to change, and backers should be aware that there is no guarantee the finished product will ship as planned.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NVIDIA Isaac GR00T (Generalist Robot 00 Technology) is a research and development platform for building robot foundation models and data pipelines, designed to accelerate the creation of intelligent, adaptable robots.

Today, we announced the availability of Isaac GR00T N1.5, the first major revision to Isaac GR00T N1, the world’s first open foundation model for generalized humanoid robot reasoning and skills. This cross-embodiment model processes multimodal inputs, including language and images, to perform manipulation tasks across diverse environments. It is adaptable through post-training for specific embodiments, tasks, and environments.

In this blog, we’ll demonstrate how to post-train (fine-tune) GR00T N1.5 using teleoperation data from a single SO-101 robot arm.

Technical Blog for GR00T N1.5: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/gear/gr00t-n1_5/.

Now accessible to developers working with a wide range of robot form factors, GR00T N1.5 can be easily fine-tuned and adapted using the affordable, open-source LeRobot SO-101 arm.

This flexibility is enabled by the EmbodimentTag system, which allows seamless customization of the model for different robotic platforms, empowering hobbyists, researchers, and engineers to tailor advanced humanoid reasoning and manipulation capabilities to their own hardware.

Before proceeding to installation, please check if you satisfy the prerequisites.

People can fine-tune GROOT N1.5 with any LeRobot dataset. For this tutorial, we will be using the table cleanup task as an example for fine-tuning.

It's notable to note that datasets for the SO-100 or SO-101 are not in GR00T N1.5's initial pre-training. As a result of this, we will be training it as a new_embodiment.

For this tutorial, you can either begin by creating your own custom dataset by following these instructions (recommended) or by downloading the so101-table-cleanup dataset from Hugging Face. The --local-dir argument specifies where the dataset will be saved on your machine.

AI video generators can now turn a prompt or a character image into a few seconds of animation, and anime is one of the most popular styles people ask for. But anime is also one of the hardest styles to get right: flat colors, thin linework and stylized motion expose the weaknesses of video models swiftly. For developers and designers, the useful question is not which tool is “best”, but what each one actually offers, what it cannot do yet, and how to fit it into a real production workflow.

According to recent reports, this article compares five generators on what their own pages state, covers the problems they all share, asks whether AI anime videos are worth making, and then explains how the models work and how designers and developers can build a practical workflow, including ffmpeg and API-integration examples. “Best” here depends on the job: the tools are listed in no ranking order, each is linked once to its official site for reference, and the comparison is based on public vendor pages reviewed in November 2026. Features, models and pricing change often, so verify current details before relying on any of them.

It has been revealed that we reviewed each vendor’s own site and compared what it states on the same points. This is a documentation-based comparison, not a lab benchmark. Where a page does not state something, we say so instead of guessing.

In a recent development, AI anime video generator by Pollo AI sits within a general AI video platform. On its main site, Pollo describes generating video from text prompts or uploaded images and editing existing videos, such as adding, changing, removing or restyling content. It also offers AI image generation, so a character image and the animation can be made in one place.

Strengths for anime work: text-to-video and image-to-video in the same tool, plus video editing and restyling, which suits experimenting with looks.

Limitations and gaps: the pages we could read do not name the underlying models, list credit amounts or pricing, or describe anime-specific controls such as reference characters or first and last frame inputs. You will need to test consistency yourself.

Fits: creators who want image, video and editing tools in one platform and are comfortable testing results before committing.

Sources indicate that vidu lists text-to-video, image-to-video and reference-to-video modes. For image-to-video you can set first and last frames. Reference-to-video lets you upload several images of a character, object or scene, and saved references can be reused through a My References feature. The site highlights 2D animation and diverse artistic styles, mentions 1080p output and offers an API platform aimed at enterprise use.

Strengths for anime work: the clearest set of consistency tools among the five pages we reviewed, with first and last frames, multi-image references and reusable saved characters.

In a recent development, limitations and gaps: the page does not specify clip durations beyond examples, detail its anime-specific templates, or list prices. Free credits are mentioned without an amount.

Fits: sequences built around a recurring character, and teams that want an API.

Kling AI presents Kling 4.0 for video, described as offering stable dynamic motion and an audio-visual experience, alongside an image model, a Motion Control tool and a node-based Canvas editor for working through scripts, storyboards, images and video. It also lists MCP and CLI support for batch generation and automated production, and an API platform with documentation.

Strengths for anime work: motion-focused tooling and a workflow environment for storyboards and multi-step production, plus automation options for developers.

Limitations and gaps: the page we reviewed does not detail image-to-video specifics, first and last frame controls, camera control, durations, video resolution or pricing, and it gives no anime-specific guidance.

Fits: teams that value motion control and scripted or batch pipelines.

It has been revealed that hailuo AI, from MiniMax, describes creating AI videos and images from text or photos. Its page reveals a reference field and an Omni Reference option, a banner for a model that mentions multimodal generation and editing, and many photo-based templates such as photo-to-motion, transformation and style transfer.

Strengths for anime work: an accessible, template-driven way to animate a still image and try stylized effects promptly.

In a recent development, limitations and gaps: the page does not explain how reference works, or state camera control, durations, resolution, API availability or pricing. Template-driven results may be harder to control precisely than prompt- and frame-driven workflows.

Fits: quick experiments and social clips made from a single image.

Dreamina describes itself as an all-in-one creative platform for images, videos and talking avatars. For video it lists text-to-video, image-to-video, sketch-to-video, cartoon video generation and reference-to-video, using several Seedance models, along with editing examples such as green-screen replacement. It also offers image generation and upscaling.

Strengths for anime work: a broad toolset, including cartoon-oriented generation, references and editing in one environment.

Limitations and gaps: no official maximum duration or video resolution is stated, and the page notes that displayed pricing is for reference only and that final pricing requires signing in. The breadth of features and models can make it harder to know which one to use for a given shot.

It depends on the job and on what you compare them with. Against a full studio production they are limited. Against having no animation at all, they change what a small team or solo creator can attempt.

Industry observers note that treat the generator as a fast prototyping and shot-making assistant, not a replacement for writing, direction and design. Audience reaction also varies, and some viewers are openly critical of AI-made work, so quality and disclosure both matter.

Most current generators are diffusion models extended to video. As in image diffusion, the model starts from random noise and removes it step by step, guided by your inputs. The extension to video, described in research such as Video Diffusion Models, is that the model denoises a whole sequence of frames together, so that motion and appearance stay coherent over time. Many systems work in a compressed latent space rather than on raw pixels to keep generation affordable.

Create an original character sheet with front, side and three-quarter views, a fixed color palette and a clear silhouette. Keep it simple: fewer fine details means less flicker.

Break the sequence into short shots with one action and one camera move each. A four-shot, twenty-second sequence is more realistic than one long generation.

Start each shot from a clean keyframe of your character. Where a tool supports first and last frames or reference images, use them to define the pose and keep identity stable.

Describe subject, action, camera and mood, and add a style anchor. For example: “The girl slowly turns toward the camera, wind moves her hair, petals drift past, gentle push-in, 2D cel shading, clean linework.”.

According to recent reports, scrub through each clip for warped hands, drifting faces and flickering lines. Discard or regenerate failures instead of hoping nobody notices.

Join the best takes, color-match them, add sound and captions, and add disclosure where a platform requires it.

It has been revealed that developers can make the pipeline repeatable. Two patterns help: scripted post-processing with ffmpeg, and a resilient job-based client for any generation API.

Recent findings suggest that the script below extracts a last frame to seed the next shot, normalizes clips to a common size and frame rate so they can be joined, concatenates them, and optionally holds each frame twice for an “on twos” look. Adjust sizes and frame rates to your project.

Video generation is usually asynchronous: you submit a job, then poll or receive a callback. The sketch below reveals the pattern with a timeout and backoff. The endpoints and fields are placeholders, so follow your provider’s documentation for real ones.

Most are diffusion models for video. They start from noise and remove it step by step across a sequence of frames, guided by a text prompt and often a starting image or reference images, until coherent motion appears.

Usually, for consistency. The image locks the character and style, while the prompt only needs to describe motion.

Thin lines and flat color regions make small frame-to-frame changes visible. Simpler designs, slower motion and post-processing reduce it.

According to recent reports, partly. Reference images, saved characters and shared keyframes help, but you should still review every shot for drift.

It has been revealed that for short clips, concept previews and storyboards, often yes. For long, dialogue-driven stories, not yet.

It depends on the tool and strategy. Read the current terms and make sure you have rights to any characters or assets you upload.

Run the same character image and prompt through each, then compare consistency, line stability, motion quality and cost per usable second.

According to recent reports, AI anime video generators are useful, but uneven. The five tools reviewed here differ in input modes, consistency tools, developer access and how much their own pages say, and none removes the core problems of consistency, flicker and limited acting. The practical approach is to test several tools on the same shots, keep your workflow tool-agnostic, design characters that are simple and consistent, and review every clip before it ships. Used that way, they are a capable prototyping and shot-making aid, not a substitute for design and direction.

Nvidia's revenue hits $115.8 billion as Vera Rubin generates $20 billion in another record-setting quarter

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1336 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For the first time in its 33-year history, Nvidia on Tuesday reported quarterly financial results without Jensen Huang at its helm or on the call, after its cofounder and longtime chief executive departed five days ago.
  • According to recent reports, "Our momentum is real.
  • It has been revealed that for the third quarter of fiscal 2027, which ended on October 25, 2026, Nvidia posted revenue of $115.844 billion, an increase of 20% sequentially and 103% year-over-year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For the first time in its 33-year history, Nvidia on Tuesday reported quarterly financial results without Jensen Huang at its helm or on the call, after its cofounder and longtime chief executive departed five days ago. To no one's surprise, Nvidia continues to set latest financial records as demand for its AI accelerators highlights no signs of slowing down. The organization reported revenue of $115.8 billion for the third quarter of its fiscal 2027, with its latest Vera Rubin platform generating $20 billion. Meanwhile, its supply commitments surged to $390 billion.

According to recent reports, "Our momentum is real. NVIDIA is an exceptional technology leader, powered by the relentless innovation of our people," remarked Colette Kress, interim chief executive and chief financial officer of Nvidia. "Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track, and our ambition has never been greater.".

It has been revealed that for the third quarter of fiscal 2027, which ended on October 25, 2026, Nvidia posted revenue of $115.844 billion, an increase of 20% sequentially and 103% year-over-year. The company's net income reached $65.287 billion, up 105% from the same quarter last year, while gross margin hit 74.8%. Revenue from the Compute & Networking segment totaled $106 billion, up 20% quarter-over-quarter and 108% year-over-year. Meanwhile, the Graphics segment generated $9.8 billion, a sequential increase of 25% and 62% compared with the same period a year ago.

As expected, Nvidia's results during the quarter were primarily driven by its Data Center business, which generated $107.6 billion in revenue (and accounted for approximately 93% of the tech giant's sales), up 21% sequentially and 110% YoY. Hyperscale customers accounted for $60.1 billion, an increase of 23% QoQ and 71% YoY, while sales to AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise customers reached $47.5 billion, up 18% sequentially and 195% compared to the same period last year. Although hyperscalers remain Nvidia's largest customer category, demand from AI cloud providers, industrial companies, and enterprises continues to grow considerably faster on an annual basis. Meanwhile, Edge Computing revenue reached $8.2 billion, up 14% sequentially and 42% year-over-year.

One of the main contributors to Nvidia's growth was its Vera Rubin platform, which generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments, which Nvidia described as the fastest product ramp in its history. The company also reported strong demand for standalone Vera CPUs and continued sales growth for Blackwell Ultra. According to Nvidia, its hyperscale partners brought Vera Rubin systems into production in approximately one month, which is two times faster than the previous-generation Grace Blackwell platform.

"Vera Rubin is off to an extraordinary start: in its first quarter of production shipments, the Rubin platform generated nearly $20 billion in revenue, making it the fastest product ramp in Nvidia's history," Kress mentioned. "We continue to see very strong demand for Vera and expect total CPU revenue to more than double in FY2028.".

Sources indicate that to support the expected growth of its AI infrastructure business, Nvidia has substantially increased its long-term procurement obligations. The organization's supply and capacity commitments reached $390 billion at the end of Q3 FY2027, compared with $279 billion three months earlier and $119 billion at the end of Q1. Nvidia attributed the latest increase primarily to multiyear memory procurement agreements.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The organization expects to fulfill $69 billion of these commitments during the remainder of FY2027 (which ends in late January), followed by $203 billion in FY2028 and $92 billion in FY2029. Another $26 billion is scheduled for FY2030 and beyond. In other words, Nvidia has already committed to purchasing $390 billion worth of components and manufacturing capacity through the end of FY2030, though given the fact that its purchases in FY2028 are set to exceed $200 billion, expect its procurements in FY2030 to be higher.

It has been revealed that the commitments reflect Nvidia's efforts to ensure that its suppliers can manufacture sufficient quantities of advanced processors, memory, substrates, and packaging components. In addition to its existing agreements with partners like TSMC, Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, Nvidia on Wednesday revealed latest partnerships with Samsung Electro-Mechanics and Kinsus for substrates, as well as SPIL for advanced packaging. In addition, the company disclosed agreements with Amkor, Ibiden, KYEC, and Unimicron.

Sources indicate that during the earnings call, Kress mentioned that demand for Nvidia's products continues to exceed available supply, prompting the tech giant to work with manufacturing partners to expand production capacity. She also indicated that Nvidia could provide suppliers with prepayments or other financial assistance to accelerate capacity expansion.

Industry observers note that although these procurement commitments are gargantuan, Nvidia expects demand for its AI infrastructure to remain strong, which will justify the expenditures. The manufacturer raised its revenue growth forecast for FY2028 from approximately 70% to 75% due to stronger demand and additional manufacturing capacity that it expects to secure.

In addition to its supply commitments, Nvidia disclosed $32 billion in agreements with neocloud providers that allow it to earn revenue from hardware sales and participate in cloud rental revenue above a guaranteed minimum. Meanwhile, the tech giant's maximum financial exposure under various guarantees reached $118 billion, including $105 billion in credit support for the PORTS-Pike AI data center campus in Ohio, which will serve OpenAI under 20-year leases.

In total, Nvidia's commitments reached $540 billion as of early Q4 FY2024.

Nvidia at the moment absorbs higher component and manufacturing costs to honor existing purchase orders and maintain previously agreed prices for its customers. As a result, the firm expects its GAAP gross margin to decline from 74.8% in Q3 FY2027 to 71% – 72% in Q4, which it considers the bottom of the current margin cycle.

Going forward, Nvidia prepares to introduce revised pricing in FY2028 to help offset higher supply costs and restore profitability, which is when the company expects gross margins to recover to 72% – 73% next fiscal year, although it has not disclosed the magnitude of its planned price adjustments or the products they will affect.

Industry observers note that "We thought about in terms of our prices and pieces of that, and a lot of the costs were some of the things that we absorbed in those numbers that we included," Kress mentioned. "What we provided here in Q4 is our bottom. If you recall, that was our bottom as we honored many of the different POs that we had already received from our customers, and we just wanted to make sure that was held solid as we moved to a newly introduced pricing, as we moved into the new year.".

Perhaps more importantly is that Colette Kress largely sidestepped the question about custom AI accelerators and their potential impact on Nvidia's pricing power. During the conference call, an analyst asked whether Nvidia would accept lower margins to protect its market share against custom AI accelerators developed by hyperscalers. The interim CEO avoided directly addressing whether competition from custom silicon could undermine Nvidia’s competitive position, leaving considerable room for speculation.

For the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, Nvidia projects revenue of approximately $130 billion ±3%, which would represent an increase of about 12% sequentially. The organization expects GAAP gross margin of 71% to 72% and GAAP operating expenses of approximately $11 billion during the quarter. Nvidia’s forecast excludes Data Center compute revenue from China and accounts for an additional week in the quarter. While Nvidia expects its gross margin to decline during the Vera Rubin transition, Kress said that the company anticipates a recovery to 72% – 73% in FY2028.

We're thrilled to share that Featherless AI is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub! Featherless AI joins our growing ecosystem, enhancing the breadth and capabilities of serverless inference directly on the Hub’s model pages. Inference Providers are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for both JS and Python), making it super easy to use a wide variety of models with your preferred providers.

Featherless AI supports a wide variety of text and conversational models, including the latest open-source models from DeepSeek, Meta, Google, Qwen, and much more.

Featherless AI is a serverless AI inference provider with unique model loading and GPU orchestration abilities that makes an exceptionally large catalog of models available for consumers. Providers often offer either a low cost of access to a limited set of models, or an unlimited range of models with users managing servers and the associated costs of operation. Featherless provides the best of both worlds offering unmatched model range and variety but with serverless pricing. Find the full list of supported models on the models page.

We're super excited to see what you'll build with this newly introduced provider!

Read more about how to use Featherless as an Inference Provider in its dedicated documentation page.

The following example demonstrates how to use DeepSeek-R1 using Featherless AI as the inference provider. You can use a Hugging Face token for automatic routing through Hugging Face, or your own Featherless AI API key if you have one.

Install or upgrade huggingface_hub to ensure you have version v0.33.0 or better: pip install --upgrade huggingface-hub.

Sources indicate that for direct requests, i.e. when you use the key from an inference provider, you are billed by the corresponding provider. For instance, if you use a Featherless AI API key you're billed on your Featherless AI account.

For routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the Hugging Face Hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. There's no additional markup from us, we just pass through the provider costs directly. (In the future, we may establish revenue-sharing agreements with our provider partners.).

Key Note ‼️ PRO customers get $2 worth of Inference credits every month. You can use them across providers. 🔥.

We also provide free inference with a small quota for our signed-in free users, but please upgrade to PRO if you can!

Sources indicate that we would love to get your feedback! Share your thoughts and/or comments here: https://huggingface.co/spaces/huggingface/HuggingDiscussions/discussions/49.

#57711. How Long Prompts Block Other Requests - Optimizing LLM Performance

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

How Long Prompts Block Other Requests - Optimizing LLM Performance

📅 12 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (998 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in the previous part of our series on LLM performance, we looked into the differences between the prefill and decode phases during token generation.
  • Since individual decode steps are not compute-intensive, one can increase throughput by batching decodes of multiple requests.
  • Industry observers note that this sequential scheduling of prefill chunks for different requests poses a challenge: whenever a request with a very long prompt is scheduled for prefill, any subsequent request has to wait for the duration of the long prefill before its processing starts; a long prompt blocks the prefill-queue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in the previous part of our series on LLM performance, we looked into the differences between the prefill and decode phases during token generation. In short: for the first output token (prefill step), the entire prompt needs to be processed, which can be parallelized efficiently and can saturate GPU utilization. For all later output tokens (decode steps), only a single additional token needs to be processed, which is less compute-intensive but must be done sequentially. When many requests are processed concurrently, any strategy that aims for low latency needs to run prefill steps for newly arriving requests while the decode steps of previously scheduled requests are still ongoing. Concurrent processing of latest as well as running requests therefore requires careful balancing between the prefill and decode stages, which presents two major challenges, which we will discuss in the following. One is a readily solvable matter, while the other one constitutes a more fundamental flaw.

Since individual decode steps are not compute-intensive, one can increase throughput by batching decodes of multiple requests. For prefill, however, this approach does not work. Because of the parallelized processing of all prompt tokens, a single prefill step can already saturate GPU utilization. Consequently, in the default chunked-prefill strategy of vLLM, each prefill chunk contains only prompt tokens of a single request. The next request in line has to wait until the previous prefill phase has been finished before its own prefill phase can start.

Industry observers note that this sequential scheduling of prefill chunks for different requests poses a challenge: whenever a request with a very long prompt is scheduled for prefill, any subsequent request has to wait for the duration of the long prefill before its processing starts; a long prompt blocks the prefill-queue. (Note that the sequential processing of prefills is the default characteristic of chunked-prefill and only appears when there already is a concurrent request in its decode phase; hence the name "partial prefill".).

In a recent development, unfortunately, this challenge can neither be solved with vLLM-side priority scheduling (see the first article of this series) nor with a more sophisticated upstream scheduler. The reason is that the long prompt can be scheduled before any subsequent requests exist, so there is nothing the scheduler could wait for.

A straightforward solution would be to process prefill chunks of different requests in parallel. This might not be resource-optimized, as single-request prefill chunks could already saturate compute-power. Any additional prefill executed in parallel would likely prolong the prefill duration a bit and slow down any concurrent decode-requests even further. This would be acceptable if it reduced the latency of short requests and made the system appear more responsive. This approach fails, however, when the next request in line has a long prompt too. In such a case, two compute-intensive prefills would be batched together and result in a severe slowdown.

According to recent reports, in one of the latest vLLM updates, an improved strategy has been implemented: it allows for parallel prefills of different requests but with a limit to the number of concurrently processed long prompt requests. An example configuration could enable batching of prefills for four requests, but only one of them may be longer than 10,000 prompt tokens. With such a configuration, the behavior for longer requests is still the same as before: long prompts are processed sequentially. Short requests, however, no longer need to wait for the long prefill of a previous request to finish; short prompts can take a fast lane. These requests no longer suffer from long waiting times and show much lower time-to-first-token metrics.

Of course, parallel prefills can only reduce waiting times; but the time-per-output-token remains elevated during the concurrent long-prefill operation. In this regard, request-parallel prefills show the same behavior and performance as standard chunked-prefill, just with a shorter time-to-first-token.

Whenever prefill and decode of different requests are executed in the same GPU operation, it takes longer than for an isolated decode step. The user experiences an interruption or a slowing down of the token generation by a subsequent request. In particular, a single request with a long prompt is sufficient to slow down all previously scheduled requests that are already in their decode phases.

This is a fundamental flaw in the concurrent processing of prefill and decode on the same GPUs, because there is little you can do:.

The difference between ideal concurrent processing (which would be no different from isolated requests), actual concurrent processing, and a disaggregated prefill strategy is shown by the following measurements:.

Separating prefill and decode eliminates the slowing-down of token generation in presence of other requests to a large extent, which makes it a very attractive strategy. It comes at the price of a second full-size vLLM deployment (e.g. for Llama-3.3-70B, you would need four H100 GPUs for a prefill worker and another four H100 GPUs for a decode worker if you wanted to support a maximum context length of 130k tokens). Another disadvantage is the uneven GPU utilization: because prefill is compute-intensive but decode is not, the prefill worker will likely saturate GPU utilization before the decode worker does. On the other hand, large clusters could consist of different numbers of prefill and decode workers (depending on load patterns), in order to optimize resource utilization.

Sources indicate that disaggregated prefill is not intended to increase total throughput, rather total "goodput" (i.e. the rate of requests that satisfy latency targets). Consequently, it is not the best use of GPU resources if your application is not sensitive to latency of individual requests.

Another caveat: the disaggregated prefill feature in vLLM is still experimental, and some optimizations and features are not accessible yet. For example, there are currently lower limits on context length, and the decode worker doesn't use CUDA graphs consistently, causing the slower decode of the long-prompt request in the figure above. Fortunately, these are not fundamental obstacles and are likely going to be solved in future versions of vLLM.

That makes them useful far beyond screen readers. Developers use them for product voice prompts, marketers for video voiceovers, teachers for course narration and writers for listening back to their own drafts.

Industry observers note that openArt’s AI text to speech tool lives inside a wider creative platform. You open the Audio tab, choose Create voice-over, select a model, paste your script, pick a voice, generate, listen and download. It runs in the browser with nothing to install. According to OpenArt’s page, you can switch between models for each script, including Fish Audio Drama 3, Eleven v4 and Eleven v4 Turbo.

Sources indicate that the direction system is what makes it practical for storytelling. You add notes in square brackets, such as [whispering], [laughs] or [pause], directly in the script. OpenArt indicates Fish Audio Drama 3 gives close control over single words and mid-line changes of mood, while Eleven v4 reads the whole script to infer the emotion of each line and keeps the voice steady when you regenerate a line. Preset voices are labeled by accent, gender and age, and you can upload a recording of your own voice to clone it.

It has been revealed that because OpenArt also makes video and background music, you can build the voiceover, visuals and soundtrack in one place. It describes a Director mode for planning stories up to five minutes, and the voiceover can also be added in any video editor.

Pricing: Upcoming accounts get 40 free credits. Paid looks add monthly credits and watermark-free downloads, and commercial rights apply on eligible paid plans. Check the pricing page for current plans.

Best for: creators who want expressive voiceovers together with AI video and music.

ElevenLabs is one of the best-known names in AI voice. Its text to speech page describes a large voice library, voice design and both instant and professional voice cloning, with the latest model, Eleven v4, positioned as the most expressive. It also lists Eleven v3, Multilingual v2 and a low-latency Flash and Turbo family aimed at real-time use, and it claims support for more than 90 languages and accents, with the exact count varying by model.

Recent findings suggest that for developers, there is a text to speech API with SDKs, which makes it practical for apps, games, agents and automated pipelines. The free plan includes 10,000 credits a month, and paid aims start with Starter at $6 a month, then Creator at $22 and Pro at $99, according to the vendor page, with introductory offers on the first month.

Pricing: Free plan with 10,000 credits a month. Paid aims from $6 a month as listed on the vendor page.

Best for: expressive narration, multilingual content and apps that need a voice API.

In a recent development, murf AI positions itself as a studio for voiceovers. Its page lists more than 200 voices, built with permission and partnership from professional voice actors who earn royalties, and support for 35 or more languages for text to speech, with dubbing in 40 or more. The Studio editor offers pitch, speed and intonation controls and a custom pronunciation library, which helps with brand names and technical terms.

Murf also has an API. Its page describes Falcon 2 for conversational use with time-to-first-audio under 100 milliseconds, priced at $0.01 per minute, and Gen 2 for controllable voiceovers. Gen 2’s “Say it My Way” feature lets you record your own rendition so the model reflects your tone and inflections.

In a recent development, pricing: Free initiative with limits. Paid plan prices are on Murf’s pricing page.

Best for: marketing videos, training and presentations where you want to fine-tune delivery.

Speechify is built around reading aloud. You paste text or upload a PDF, DOCX, TXT or EPUB file, pick a voice, adjust playback speed and listen or download the audio. Its page lists more than 1,000 voices across 60 or more languages, including several regional English accents, and the tool works in the browser and in apps for iOS, Android, Mac and Windows, plus Chrome and Edge extensions.

The use cases lean toward productivity and accessibility: studying, going through emails and documents, language learning and support for people with visual impairments, dyslexia or ADHD. A free account saves your documents and syncs them across devices.

Pricing: You can start free. Paid looks are listed on Speechify’s pricing page.

Best for: students, professionals and anyone who wants to listen to documents and articles.

Industry observers note that wellSaid Labs focuses on professional voiceover for businesses. Its page describes hundreds of voices across languages, accents, tones and styles.

You can highlight a word to see suggested pronunciations and save your choice to a team library that applies to every project, and set pacing, emphasis and pronunciation line by line. WellSaid also describes a Producer product that connects AI assistants to WellSaid through MCP and its API.

Pricing: Contact sales for a quote based on your voiceover volume.

Best for: corporate training, product marketing, courses and advertising where licensing and consistency matter.

Amazon Polly is Amazon Web Services’ text to speech service, and it is aimed squarely at developers. According to AWS, it supports more than 40 languages and language variants with over 100 male and female voices, and it works through APIs in your code. It supports SSML, the W3C standard markup for phrasing, emphasis and intonation, and custom lexicons that fix the pronunciation of acronyms and terms. Output formats include MP3 and OGG.

Pricing is usage-based. AWS lists a free tier for latest accounts, with usage allowances that depend on the voice engine, so estimate your character volume before you decide. A short example highlights how little code a basic request takes:.

Pricing: Usage-based with a free tier for new accounts. See the AWS pricing page for current rates.

Best for: apps, IVR systems, notifications and any product that needs automated speech at scale.

Sources indicate that treat this table as a starting point. Features and limits change often, so test two or three tools with the same script.

Modern text-to-speech systems turn written words into audio through several stages.

Industry observers note that newer expressive systems go further by reading the whole script to infer emotion and context, and by accepting direction in the text itself, such as a bracketed note that states to whisper. That is why a single script can produce very different reads depending on the model and the instructions.

If you use a tool with SSML support, you can make a spoken code or number far clearer:.

According to recent reports, the say-as element tells the engine to read the number digit by digit, and the break and emphasis tags shape the rhythm. Supported tags and attributes differ between engines, so check the documentation for yours.

It has been revealed that what is the best AI text to speech tool? It depends on the job. OpenArt suits voiceovers with video and music, ElevenLabs suits expressive multilingual audio, Murf AI suits studio-style control, Speechify suits listening, WellSaid Labs suits licensed corporate work and Amazon Polly suits developers.

Is AI text to speech free? Several tools offer free prepares or credits, but limits are common. Examples include OpenArt’s free credits for new accounts, ElevenLabs’ free monthly credits and Murf’s limited free strategy, which has no commercial licence.

It has been revealed that can I use AI voices commercially? Often yes on paid aims, but the rules differ by tool. Always check the current licence before publishing.

In a recent development, can AI text to speech clone my voice? Some tools support it, including OpenArt and ElevenLabs, usually from a short recording of your own voice. Only clone voices you have permission to use.

Recent findings suggest that what is SSML? Speech Synthesis Markup Language is a W3C standard that lets you control pauses, emphasis, pronunciation and pitch in synthetic speech. Amazon Polly is one service that supports it.

Industry observers note that which tool is best for developers? Amazon Polly and ElevenLabs both offer APIs, and Murf describes API options as well. Evaluate latency, languages, pricing and SDK support for your use case.

It has been revealed that how do I make AI voices sound less robotic? Write conversationally, add pauses and emphasis, correct pronunciations and split long scripts into short sections. Choose a model that is designed for expressive reads.

AI text to speech is now good enough for real projects, but the right tool depends on what you are making. OpenArt is a strong first stop for expressive voiceovers alongside video and music, ElevenLabs offers a deep voice library and API, Murf AI and WellSaid Labs suit polished, controlled narration, Speechify turns documents into audio and Amazon Polly fits straight into developer workflows. Test two or three with your own script, check the licence and always listen to the full result before it goes live.

We're thrilled to share that Groq is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub! Groq joins our growing ecosystem, enhancing the breadth and capabilities of serverless inference directly on the Hub’s model pages. Inference Providers are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for both JS and Python), making it super easy to use a wide variety of models with your preferred providers.

Groq supports a wide variety of text and conversational models, including the latest open-source models such as Meta's Llama 4, Qwen's QWQ-32B, and many more.

At the heart of Groq's technology is the Language Processing Unit (LPU™), a new type of end-to-end processing unit system that provides the fastest inference for computationally intensive applications with a sequential component, such as Large Language Models (LLMs). LPUs are designed to overcome the limitations of GPUs for inference, offering significantly lower latency and higher throughput. This makes them ideal for real-time AI applications.

Groq offers fast AI inference for openly-available models. They provide an API that allows developers to easily integrate these models into their applications. It offers an on-demand, pay-as-you-go model for accessing a wide range of openly-available LLMs.

In a recent development, you can now use Groq's Inference API as an Inference Provider on Huggingface. We're quite excited to see what you'll build with this newly introduced provider.

Read more about how to use Groq as Inference Provider in its dedicated documentation page.

For routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the Hugging Face Hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that global OLED monitor shipments doubled year over year in the third quarter of 2026, according to the latest market research from TrendForce.
  • Recent findings suggest that ASUS maintained its position as the world's largest OLED monitor vendor, accounting for 21.7% of shipments.
  • According to recent reports, price isn't the only obstacle that OLED manufacturers have been addressing, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that global OLED monitor shipments doubled year over year in the third quarter of 2026, according to the latest market research from TrendForce. Shipments also increased 13% sequentially, reflecting strong demand for OLED displays and improving panel availability. While the market's rapid growth is impressive regardless, there are good reasons why OLED monitors are becoming increasingly popular: they're getting cheaper, better, and considerably easier to justify.

Recent findings suggest that ASUS maintained its position as the world's largest OLED monitor vendor, accounting for 21.7% of shipments. MSI climbed into second place for the first time, capturing 14.5% of the market, while Samsung slipped to third with 11.3%. Both Taiwanese vendors have been particularly aggressive in the gaming monitor market, where increasingly competitive pricing has helped make OLED technology accessible to more buyers, while ubiquitous advertising with tech-conscious gamers has made them highly visible. According to Omdia, mainstream 27-inch QHD 240Hz OLED gaming monitors have seen price cuts exceeding 40% in 2026.

According to recent reports, price isn't the only obstacle that OLED manufacturers have been addressing, though. Earlier generations of OLED monitors had some fairly significant compromises, particularly their relatively limited brightness and unconventional subpixel arrangements that could cause colored fringing around text. Newer tandem OLED panels offer improved brightness and color reproduction, while RGB-stripe OLED layouts bring much cleaner text rendering. These improvements are making OLEDs considerably more attractive as everyday desktop monitors, rather than merely excellent gaming displays with major caveats.

It has been revealed that there's also an interesting macroeconomic angle to OLED's growth. The AI industry's insatiable appetite for memory and storage has made upgrading a gaming PC considerably more expensive. DRAM component prices have increased severalfold, while NAND flash and hard drive availability have also been squeezed by demand from AI data centers—though there are early signs of some relief, at least on the flash memory front. Graphics cards, especially (but not exclusively) at the high end, are increasingly difficult to find at anything resembling reasonable prices.

Monitors, meanwhile, aren't directly subject to the same supply pressures affecting DRAM, NAND, and discrete GPUs. That makes upgrading a display an appealing alternative for gamers who aren't particularly interested in spending a small fortune on an entirely new PC. An OLED monitor can substantially improve the gaming experience without requiring a new graphics card, memory kit, or storage drive. The contrast, response times, and color gamut of OLEDs far outstrip even the best LCDs, and that's to say nothing of their superior HDR reproduction thanks to the inherent self-emissive nature of OLED panels.

Recent findings suggest that with OLED prices falling and the technology's longstanding limitations becoming less noticeable, a new monitor is becoming one of the more compelling upgrades available to PC gamers. Indeed, several of our picks for the best gaming monitors, including the best overall, best 4K, and best ultrawide, are based on OLED technology. Though concerns about burn-in and limited lifespan remain, there's no question that OLED is the best display technology we have right now.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

(LoRA) Fine-Tuning FLUX.1-dev on Consumer Hardware

📅 19 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1709 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in our previous post, Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers, we dived into how various quantization techniques can shrink diffusion models like FLUX.1-dev, making them significantly more accessible for inference without drastically compromising performance.
  • Performing inference is cool, but to make these models truly our own, we also need to be able to fine-tune them.
  • We aim to fine-tune black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev to adopt the artistic style of Alphonse Mucha, using a small dataset.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in our previous post, Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers, we dived into how various quantization techniques can shrink diffusion models like FLUX.1-dev, making them significantly more accessible for inference without drastically compromising performance. We saw how bitsandbytes, torchao, and others reduce memory footprints for generating images.

Performing inference is cool, but to make these models truly our own, we also need to be able to fine-tune them. Therefore, in this post, we tackle efficient fine-tuning of these models with peak memory use under ~10 GB of VRAM on a single GPU. This post will guide you through fine-tuning FLUX.1-dev using QLoRA with the diffusers library. We'll showcase results from an NVIDIA RTX 4090. We'll also highlight how FP8 training with torchao can further optimize speed on compatible hardware.

We aim to fine-tune black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev to adopt the artistic style of Alphonse Mucha, using a small dataset.

The model consists of three main components:.

Sources indicate that in our QLoRA approach, we focus exclusively on fine-tuning the transformer component. The text encoders and VAE remain frozen throughout training.

Sources indicate that we used a diffusers training script (slightly modified from here designed for DreamBooth-style LoRA fine-tuning of FLUX models. Also, a shortened version to reproduce the results in this blogpost (and used in the Google Colab) is available here. Let's examine the crucial parts for QLoRA and memory efficiency:.

It has been revealed that loRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) Deep Dive: LoRA makes model training more efficient by keeping track of the weight updates with low-rank matrices. Instead of updating the full weight matrix W W W, LoRA learns two smaller matrices A A A and B B B. The upgrade to the weights for the model is ΔW=BA \Delta W = B A ΔW=BA, where A∈Rr×k A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k} A∈Rr×k and B∈Rd×r B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r} B∈Rd×r. The number r r r (called rank) is much smaller than the original dimensions, which means less parameters to update. Lastly, α \alpha α is a scaling factor for the LoRA activations. This affects how much LoRA affects the updates, and is often set to the same value as the r r r or a multiple of it. It helps balance the influence of the pre-trained model and the LoRA adapter. For a general introduction to the concept, check out our previous blog post: Using LoRA for Efficient Stable Diffusion Fine-Tuning.

According to recent reports, QLoRA: The Efficiency Powerhouse: QLoRA enhances LoRA by first loading the pre-trained base model in a quantized format (typically 4-bit via bitsandbytes), drastically cutting the base model's memory footprint. It then trains LoRA adapters (usually in FP16/BF16) on top of this quantized base. This dramatically lowers the VRAM needed to hold the base model.

For instance, in the DreamBooth training script for HiDream 4-bit quantization with bitsandbytes reduces the peak memory usage of a LoRA fine-tune from ~60GB down to ~37GB with negligible-to-none quality degradation. The very same principle is what we apply here to fine-tune FLUX.1 on a consumer-grade hardware.

Sources indicate that 8-bit Optimizer (AdamW): Standard AdamW optimizer maintains first and second moment estimates for each parameter in 32-bit (FP32), which consumes a lot of memory. The 8-bit AdamW uses block-wise quantization to store optimizer states in 8-bit precision, while maintaining training stability. This technique can reduce optimizer memory usage by ~75% compared to standard FP32 AdamW. Enabling it in the script is straightforward:.

Gradient Checkpointing: During forward pass, intermediate activations are typically stored for backward pass gradient computation. Gradient checkpointing trades computation for memory by only storing certain checkpoint activations and recomputing others during backpropagation.

In a recent development, cache Latents: This optimization technique pre-processes all training images through the VAE encoder before the beginning of the training. It stores the resulting latent representations in memory. During the training, instead of encoding images on-the-fly, the cached latents are directly used. This approach offers two main benefits:.

Before we launch the QLoRA fine-tune we can save a huge chunk of VRAM and wall-clock time by caching outputs of text encoders once.

At training time the dataloader simply reads the cached embeddings instead of re-encoding the caption, so the CLIP/T5 encoder never has to sit in GPU memory.

By combining this with cached VAE latents (--cache_latents) you whittle the active model down to just the quantized transformer + LoRA adapters, keeping the whole fine-tune comfortably under 10 GB of GPU memory.

For users with NVIDIA GPUs possessing compute capability 8.9 or greater (such as the H100, RTX 4090), even greater speed efficiencies can be achieved by leveraging FP8 training via the torchao library.

After training your LoRA adapters, you have two main approaches for inference.

One approach is to load your trained LoRA adapters on top of the base model.

For when you want maximum efficiency with a single style, you can merge the LoRA weights into the base model.

While we showcased results on an RTX 4090, the same code can be run on more accessible hardware like the T4 GPU available in Google Colab for free.

On a T4, you can expect the fine-tuning process to take significantly longer around 4 hours for the same number of steps. This is a trade-off for accessibility, but it makes custom fine-tuning possible without high-end hardware. Be mindful of usage limits if running on Colab, as a 4-hour training run might push them.

QLoRA, coupled with the diffusers library, significantly democratizes the ability to customize state-of-the-art models like FLUX.1-dev. As demonstrated on an RTX 4090, efficient fine-tuning is well within reach, yielding high-quality stylistic adaptations. Furthermore, for consumers with the latest NVIDIA hardware, torchao enables even faster training through FP8 precision.

The Downfall of Jensen Huang — a timeline of allegations and scandals that brought down the king of AI infrastructure
