    Parquet Content-Defined Chunking

    📅 25 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Reduce Parquet file upload and download times on Hugging Face Hub by leveraging the fresh Xet storage layer and Apache Arrow’s Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) feature enabling more efficient and scalable data workflows.
    • Recent findings suggest that TL;DR: Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) is now available in PyArrow and Pandas, enabling efficient deduplication of Parquet files on content-addressable storage systems like Hugging Face's Xet storage layer.
    • Apache Parquet is a columnar storage format that is widely used in the data engineering community.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Reduce Parquet file upload and download times on Hugging Face Hub by leveraging the fresh Xet storage layer and Apache Arrow’s Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) feature enabling more efficient and scalable data workflows.

    Recent findings suggest that TL;DR: Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) is now available in PyArrow and Pandas, enabling efficient deduplication of Parquet files on content-addressable storage systems like Hugging Face's Xet storage layer. CDC dramatically reduces data transfer and storage costs by uploading or downloading only the changed data chunks. Enable CDC by passing the use_content_defined_chunking argument:.

    Apache Parquet is a columnar storage format that is widely used in the data engineering community.

    Sources indicate that as of today, Hugging Face hosts nearly 21 PB of datasets, with Parquet files alone accounting for over 4 PB of that storage. Optimizing Parquet storage is therefore a high priority. Hugging Face has introduced a latest storage layer called Xet that leverages content-defined chunking to efficiently deduplicate chunks of data reducing storage costs and improving download/upload speeds.

    While Xet is format agnostic, Parquet's layout and column-chunk (data page) based compression can produce entirely different byte-level representations for data with minor changes, leading to suboptimal deduplication performance. To address this, the Parquet files should be written in a way that minimizes the byte-level differences between similar data, which is where content-defined chunking (CDC) comes into play.

    Let's explore the performance benefits of the newly introduced Parquet CDC feature used alongside Hugging Face's Xet storage layer.

    For demonstration purposes, we will use a manageable sized subset of OpenOrca dataset.

    Since pyarrow>=21.0.0 we can use Hugging Face URIs in the pyarrow functions to directly read and write parquet (and other file formats) files to the Hub using the hf:// URI scheme.

    Sources indicate that we can see that the table has been uploaded entirely (total bytes == total transfer) as new data because it is not known to the Xet storage layer yet. Now read it back as a pyarrow table:.

    Note that all pyarrow functions that accept a file path also accept a Hugging Face URI, like pyarrow datasets, CSV functions, incremental Parquet writer or reading only the parquet metadata:.

    To demonstrate the effectiveness of the content-defined chunking feature, we will try out how it performs in case of:.

    According to recent reports, while this use case sounds trivial, traditional file systems do not deduplicate files resulting in full re-upload and re-download of the data. In contrast, a system utilizing content-defined chunking can recognize that the file content is identical and avoid unnecessary data transfer.

    According to recent reports, we can see that no fresh data has been uploaded, and the operation was instantaneous. Now let's see what happens if we upload the same file again but to a different repository:.

    The upload was instantaneous again since deduplication works across repositories as well. This is a key feature of the Xet storage layer, allowing efficient data sharing and collaboration. You can read more about the details and scaling challenges in the From Chunks to Blocks: Accelerating Uploads and Downloads on the Hub blog post.

    First write out the original and changed tables to local parquet files to see their sizes:.

    Now upload them to Hugging Face to see how much data is actually transferred:.

    We can see that only the latest columns and the new parquet metadata placed in the file's footer were uploaded, while the original data was not transferred again. This is a huge benefit of the Xet storage layer, as it allows us to efficiently add new columns without transferring the entire dataset again.

    Same applies to removing columns, as we can see below:.

    To have a better understanding of what has been uploaded, we can visualize the differences between the two parquet files using the deduplication estimation tool:.

    It has been revealed that adding two new columns mean that we have unseen data pages which must be transferred (highlighted in red), but the rest of the data remains unchanged (highlighted in green), so it is not transferred again. Note the small red area in the footer metadata which almost always changes as we modify the parquet file. The dedup stats show / = where smaller ratios mean higher deduplication performance.

    Also visualize the difference after removing a column:.

    Since we are removing entire columns we can only see changes in the footer metadata, all the other columns remain unchanged and already existing in the storage layer, so they are not transferred again.

    Industry observers note that another common use case is changing the column types in the table e.g. to reduce the storage size or to optimize the data for specific queries. Let's change the question_length column from int64 data type to int32 and see how much data is transferred:.

    Recent findings suggest that again, we can see that only the upcoming column and the updated parquet metadata were uploaded. Now visualize the deduplication heatmap:.

    Sources indicate that the first red region indicates the fresh column that was added, while the second red region indicates the updated metadata in the footer. The rest of the data remains unchanged and is not transferred again.

    We are going to append new rows by concatenating another slice of the original dataset to the table.

    Now check that only the upcoming rows are being uploaded since the original data is already known to the Xet storage layer:.

    Since each column gets new data, we can see multiple red regions. This is due to the actual parquet file specification where whole columns are laid out after each other (within each row group).

    Here comes the difficult part as insertions and deletions are shifting the existing rows which lead to different columns chunks or data pages in the parquet nomenclature. Since each data page is compressed separately, even a single row insertion or deletion can lead to a completely different byte-level representation starting from the edited row(s) to the end of the parquet file.

    This parquet specific problem cannot be solved by the Xet storage layer alone, the parquet file itself needs to be written in a way that minimizes the data page differences even if there are inserted or deleted rows.

    Let's try to use the existing mechanism and see how it performs.

    Also visualize both cases to see the differences:.

    It has been revealed that we can see that the deduplication performance has dropped significantly (higher ratio), and the deduplication heatmaps show that the compressed parquet files are quite different from each other. This is due to the fact that the inserted and deleted rows have shifted the existing rows, leading to different data pages starting from the edited row(s) to the end of the parquet file.

    We can solve this problem by writing parquet files with a newly introduced pyarrow feature called content-defined chunking (CDC). This feature ensures that the columns are consistently getting chunked into data pages based on their content, similarly how the Xet storage layer deduplicates data but applied to the logical values of the columns before any serialization or compression happens.

    The feature can be enabled by passing use_content_defined_chunking=True to the write_parquet function:.

    Pandas also supports the new feature:.

    Let's visualize the deduplication difference before and after using the Parquet CDC feature:.

    According to recent reports, looks much better! Since the proof of the pudding is in the eating, let's actually upload the tables using the content-defined chunking parquet feature and see how much data is transferred.

    Note that we need to upload the original table first with content-defined chunking enabled:.

    The uploaded data is significantly smaller than before, showing much better deduplication performance as highlighted in the heatmaps above.

    Vital to note that the same performance benefits apply to downloads using the huggingface_hub.hf_hub_download() and datasets.load_dataset() functions.

    There are cases depending on the reader/writer constraints where larger or smaller row-group sizes might be beneficial. The parquet writer implementations use fixed-sized row-groups by default, in the case of pyarrow the default is 1Mi rows. Dataset writers may change to reduce the row-group size in order to improve random access performance or to reduce the memory footprint of the reader application.

    In a recent development, changing the row-group size will shift rows between row-groups, shifting values between data pages, so we have a similar problem as with inserting or deleting rows. Let's compare the deduplication performance between different row-group sizes using the parquet CDC feature:.

    Datasets are often split into multiple files to improve parallelism and random access. Parquet CDC combined with the Xet storage layer can efficiently deduplicate data across multiple files even if the data is split at different boundaries.

    Let's write out the dataset with three different file-level splitting then compare the deduplication performance:.

    Even though we uploaded the dataset with three different sharding configurations, the overall upload size would be barely larger than the original dataset size.

    So far we've used PyArrow, let’s explore using the same CDC feature with Pandas by downloading, filtering then uploading the dataset with the content-defined chunking feature enabled:.

    Since Parquet CDC is applied at the parquet data page level (column chunk level), the deduplication performance depends on the filter's selectivity, or rather the distribution of the changes across the dataset. If most of the data pages are affected, then the deduplication ratio will drop significantly.

    More details about the feature can be found at:.

    We explored the performance benefits of the latest Parquet content-defined chunking feature used alongside Hugging Face's Xet storage layer. We demonstrated how it can efficiently deduplicate data in various scenarios making parquet operations faster and more storage-efficient. Comparing to traditional cloud storage solutions, the Xet storage layer with Parquet CDC can significantly reduce data transfer times and costs.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (220 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Googleblog

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that in our previous posts - Easy FunctionGemma finetuning with Tunix on Google TPUs and Autonomous LLM post-training with Tunix on TPUs - we indicated how Google Tunix streamlines Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and single-turn Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on Cloud TPUs.
    • We will revisit the Plane Strike board game from an earlier TensorFlow/JAX reinforcement learning blog, replacing the custom MLP policy with Gemma 4 E2B in thinking mode on a single Cloud TPU v6e-8 host.

    Sources indicate that in our previous posts - Easy FunctionGemma finetuning with Tunix on Google TPUs and Autonomous LLM post-training with Tunix on TPUs - we indicated how Google Tunix streamlines Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and single-turn Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on Cloud TPUs. Real-world AI agents, however, rarely finish their job in a single turn. They have to reason over partial observations, invoke tools, observe environment feedback, and adapt their strategy across multiple steps. So in this post, we will walk through how to train a multi-turn, tool-using LLM agent using Tunix's agentic reinforcement learning pipeline on Cloud TPU v6e-8. You can find the complete code in this GitHub repository.

    We will revisit the Plane Strike board game from an earlier TensorFlow/JAX reinforcement learning blog, replacing the custom MLP policy with Gemma 4 E2B in thinking mode on a single Cloud TPU v6e-8 host. Plane Strike is played on a 6x6 grid (A1 to F6) where one 8-cell plane is hidden in one of 4 orientations. Each turn, the agent sees the result of its previous strike and the raw visible board (. untried, X hit, O miss), thinks through candidate placements, and calls the strike(cell="...") tool to strike one cell. The game ends when all 8 plane cells are hit, or after 23 strikes.

    We are glad to announce a long-awaited quality-of-life improvement: the Hugging Face CLI has been officially renamed from huggingface-cli to hf!

    It has been revealed that typing huggingface-cli constantly gets old fast. More importantly, the CLI’s command structure became messy as new features were added over time (upload, download, cache management, repo management, etc.). Renaming the CLI is a chance to reorganize commands into a clearer, more consistent format.

    We decided not to reinvent the wheel and instead follow a well-known CLI pattern: hf . This predictable grammar makes the Hugging Face CLI more ergonomic and discoverable, while also setting the stage for upcoming features.

    To start playing with the new CLI, you’ll need to install the latest huggingface_hub version:.

    and reload your terminal session. To test the install completed successfully, run hf version:.

    Next, let’s explore the latest syntax with hf --help:.

    As we can see, commands are grouped by "resource" (hf auth, hf cache, hf repo, etc.). We also surface hf upload and hf downloadat the root level since they’re expected to be the most-used commands.

    To dive deeper into any command group, simply append --help:.

    Industry observers note that if you are used to huggingface-cli, most commands will look familiar. The biggest change affects authentication:.

    All auth commands have been grouped together with the existing hf auth switch (to switch between different local profiles) and hf auth list (to list local profiles).

    The legacy huggingface-cli remains active and fully-functional. We’re keeping it around to ease the transition. If you use any command from the legacy CLI, you’ll see a warning that points you to the newly introduced CLI equivalent:.

    We couldn’t resist shipping our first dedicated command: hf jobs.

    Recent findings suggest that hugging Face Jobs is a new service that lets you run any script or Docker image on Hugging Face Infrastructure using the hardware flavor of your choice. Billing is "pay-as-you-go", meaning you pay only for the seconds you use. Here’s how to launch your first command:.

    The CLI is heavily inspired by Docker’s familiar commands:.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, TL;DR: Trackio is a new, open-source, and free experiment tracking Python library that provides a local dashboard and seamless integration with Hugging Face Spaces for easy sharing and collaboration. Since trackio is a drop-in replacement for wandb, you can get started with the syntax you already know!

    If you have trained your own machine learning model, you know how important it is to be able to track metrics, parameters, and hyperparameters during training and visualize them afterwards to better understand your training run.

    Most machine learning researchers use specific experiment tracking libraries to do this. However, these libraries can be paid, require complex setup, or lack the flexibility needed for rapid experimentation and sharing.

    At Hugging Face, our science team has started using Trackio for our research projects, and we've found several key advantages over other tracking solutions:.

    Easy Sharing and Embedding: Trackio makes it incredibly simple to share training progress with colleagues or embed plots directly in blog posts and documentation using iframes. This is especially valuable when you want to showcase specific training curves or metrics without requiring others to set up accounts or navigate complex dashboards.

    Standardization and Transparency: Metrics like GPU energy usage are notable to track and share with the community so we can have a better idea of the energy demands and environmental impacts of model training. Using Trackio, which directly gets information from the nvidia-smi command, makes it easy to quantify and compare energy usage and to add it to model cards.

    According to recent reports, data Accessibility: Unlike some tracking tools that lock your data behind proprietary APIs, Trackio makes it straightforward to extract and analyze the data being recorded. This is crucial for researchers who need to perform custom analysis or integrate training metrics into their research workflows.

    Flexibility for Experimentation: Trackio's lightweight design allows us to easily experiment with new tracking features during training runs. For instance, we can decide when to move tensors from GPU to CPU when logging tensors while training, which significantly improves training throughput when you need to track model/intermediate states without impacting performance.

    In a recent development, ok then, so what is Trackio and how do you use it? Trackio is an open-source Python library that lets you track any metrics and visualize them using a local Gradio dashboard. You can also sync this dashboard to Hugging Face Spaces, which means you can then share the dashboard with other users simply by sharing a URL. Since Spaces can be private or public, this means you can share a dashboard publicly or just within members of your Hugging Face organization.

    You can install trackio using pip:.

    In a recent development, trackio is designed to be a drop-in replacement for experiment tracking libraries like wandb. The API is compatible with wandb.init, wandb.log, and wandb.finish, so you can simply import trackio as wandb in your code.

    Industry observers note that after logging your experiments, you can launch the dashboard to visualize your results. Run the following command in your terminal:.

    You can also specify a project name:.

    To sync your local dashboard to Hugging Face Spaces, simply pass a space_id to init:.

    If you are hosting your dashboard on Spaces, you can simply share the URL or embed it anywhere using an iframe:.

    Since Spaces can be private or public, this means you can share a dashboard publicly or just within members of your Hugging Face organization — all for free!

    According to recent reports, when you sync your Trackio dashboard to Hugging Face Spaces, the data is logged to an ephemeral Sqlite database on Spaces. Because this database is reset if your Space restarts, Trackio also converts the Sqlite database to a Parquet dataset and backs it up to a Hugging Face Dataset every 5 minutes. This means you can visualize your logged metrics in a Hugging Face dataset at any time easily:.

    Tip: you can set the name of this dataset by passing in a dataset_id to trackio.init().

    Trackio integrates natively with Hugging Face libraries like transformers and accelerate, so you can log metrics with minimal setup.

    No extra setup needed—just plug it in and start tracking.

    Sources indicate that trackio is intentionally lightweight and is presently in beta. Some features found in other tracking tools, such as artifact management, or complex visualizations, are not available yet. If you'd like to have these features, please create issues here: https://github.com/gradio-app/trackio/issues.

    Given Trackio's lightweight and open-source nature, we'd love to work with the machine learning community to design an experiment tracking product that works for all of us!

    Please let us know any features you'd like to see in Trackio here: https://github.com/gradio-app/trackio/complications.

    Is there a plan to support tracking of LLM calls?

    There are many Open-Source Telemetry services which tracks both the ML and LLM Traces, such as opik, Raga AI Catalyst.

    Recent findings suggest that trackio looks like a very welcome addition to the ML ecosystem... 🚀📊 One of the biggest challenges during model development is keeping track of experiments, hyperparameters, and performance metrics in a way that is simple and reproducible. Many existing solutions are powerful, but they often come with setup overhead or limitations that can slow down rapid experimentation. A lightweight approach from Hugging Face feels like the right balance between functionality and ease of use... 👏.

    What stands out most is the focus on flexibility and accessibility... 💡 Researchers, students, and independent developers often need a tool that works immediately without requiring extensive configuration or expensive subscriptions. Being able to quickly log results, compare runs, and visualize training progress can make a huge difference when iterating on models and testing new ideas. Simplicity is often underrated, especially when experimentation speed matters... ⚡🔬.

    Industry observers note that it's great to see Hugging Face continuing to build tools that lower barriers for the machine learning community... 🌍🤝 Trackio has the potential to become a favorite for practitioners who want effective experiment tracking without unnecessary complexity. Looking forward to seeing how the community adopts it and what new workflows it enables in the future... 📈✨.

    As AWS re:Invent is around the corner, we’re proud to recognize a new group of AWS Heroes. Every Hero finds their own way to give back, whether through sharing what they know, bringing people together, or building tools that help others succeed. What they have in common is a genuine commitment to supporting the builders around them learn, grow, and lead.

    Let us take a moment to meet them!

    Serverless Hero Andres Moreno leads the Cloud del Norte AWS User Group and is a former AWS Community Builder. On his blog, And More Dev, and at conferences and community events, he explains serverless, cloud native architectures, generative AI, and agentic systems in ways that make upcoming technology easier to try. Andres puts special energy into supporting builders across Latin America and helping them explore what’s possible on AWS.

    Community Hero Geethika Guruge is a Principal Consultant at Mantel Group whose work spans serverless, DevOps, cloud infrastructure, and agentic AI. Geethika has shared real lessons from building agentic applications and leading large migration and modernization programs at AWS re:Invent, AWS Summits, and AWS Community Days. At home in Auckland, Geethika organizes local AWS meetups that encourage grassroots innovation and mentors the next generation of cloud architects and leaders.

    Data Hero Jéssica Cristina Coelho is a Database Reliability Engineer and a former AWS Community Builder with more than 15 years of experience in databases, cloud, and data engineering. She leads the AWS User Group in Minas Gerais, hosts DataTalks Brasil, teaches MBA courses, and supports Women in Cloud, DevOpsDays, and AWS Community Day events. She speaks at events such as AWS Summit São Paulo and Web Summit Rio on database modernization and generative AI. At AWS re:Invent 2025, she was recognized as a LATAM Diversity & Inclusion Champion.

    According to recent reports, devTools Hero Kazuho Cryer Shinozuka is an AWS CDK Top Contributor and Trusted CDK Community Reviewer. With 200 merged pull requests, he ranks 18th among more than 1,700 contributors. He has reviewed more than 120 pull requests, has been involved in about 2% of all CDK commits, and has published 10 construct libraries, along with tools such as cfn idle cost. Through talks at JAWS DAYS and CDK Conference Japan and through hands on contribution workshops, he helps more developers in Japan start contributing to open source.

    To connect with these Heroes or find one in your region, explore the AWS Heroes webpage, and join the conversation on AWS Builder Center.

    #57632. 📚 3LM: A Benchmark for Arabic LLMs in STEM and Code

    📅 01 Aug 2025 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (854 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    📚 3LM: A Benchmark for Arabic LLMs in STEM and Code

    📅 01 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (854 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 📄 Paper on arXiv | 📦 Datasets on HuggingFace | 🔧 Code on GitHub.
    • Sources indicate that arabic Large Language Models (LLMs) have seen notable progress in recent years, yet existing benchmarks fall short when it comes to evaluating performance in high-value technical domains.
    • To address this gap, we introduce 3LM (علم), a multi-component benchmark tailored to evaluate Arabic LLMs on STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) subjects and code generation.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    📄 Paper on arXiv | 📦 Datasets on HuggingFace | 🔧 Code on GitHub.

    Sources indicate that arabic Large Language Models (LLMs) have seen notable progress in recent years, yet existing benchmarks fall short when it comes to evaluating performance in high-value technical domains. Most evaluations to date have focused on general-purpose tasks like summarization, sentiment analysis, or generic question answering. However, scientific reasoning and programming are essential for a broad range of real-world applications, from education to technical problem-solving.

    To address this gap, we introduce 3LM (علم), a multi-component benchmark tailored to evaluate Arabic LLMs on STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) subjects and code generation. 3LM is the first benchmark of its kind, designed specifically to test Arabic models in structured reasoning and formal logic which are domains traditionally underrepresented in Arabic NLP.

    3LM is made up of three datasets, each targeting a specific evaluation axis: real-world multiple-choice STEM questions (MCQs), synthetic high-difficulty STEM questions, and translated code generation tasks.

    Recent findings suggest that the Native STEM benchmark consists of 865 MCQs extracted from authentic Arabic educational content, including textbooks, worksheets, and exam banks for grades 8 through 12. Questions span five core subjects: Physics, Chemistry, Biology, Mathematics, and Geography.

    Recent findings suggest that each question is annotated with metadata including domain and difficulty (on a 1–10 scale). The data was sourced using a pipeline that combined OCR (including LaTeX math parsing via Pix2Tex), LLM-assisted question-answer extraction, and manual review. This dataset provides a realistic testbed for evaluating factual and conceptual understanding in Arabic models using real educational materials.

    According to recent reports, to introduce greater challenge and diversity, we created a synthetic subset of 1,744 MCQs using the YourBench pipeline. This component draws from Arabic textbook text, which is chunked, summarized, and used as input to an LLM-driven question generation system. The result is a curated set of questions focused on mid-to-high difficulty reasoning, including conceptual, analytical, and application-based problems.

    Synthetic STEM provides an notable counterbalance to native MCQs by probing deeper reasoning skills and minimizing answer bias. All generated questions underwent filtering based on clarity, structure, and content validity, followed by quality assurance via manual review.

    Industry observers note that the third component of 3LM targets code generation which is a growing area of LLM evaluation. We translated and adapted the widely-used HumanEval+ and MBPP+ benchmarks into Arabic, creating the first code datasets that test Arabic LLMs on natural language prompts for programming.

    Sources indicate that we used GPT-4o for prompt translation and validated the results with a backtranslation pipeline, rejecting low-quality samples based on ROUGE-L F1 thresholds (< 0.8). Additional human filtering ensured prompt clarity and correctness. The code and test suites remain unchanged to preserve scoring fidelity. Evaluations use the EvalPlus framework for pass@1 and pass@1+ metrics.

    Each dataset in 3LM went through a multi-stage development process to ensure data quality, fairness, and representativeness.

    Recent findings suggest that for Native STEM, we collected Arabic PDF sources and applied a dual OCR approach to recover both plain text and math formulas. Questions were extracted using LLM-based chunking and pattern recognition, followed by classification into MCQ format with randomized answer order. Final samples were reviewed by native Arabic speakers with STEM expertise to confirm answer validity and readability.

    Sources indicate that for Synthetic STEM, the YourBench pipeline was adapted for Arabic input. Source documents after ingestion were first summarized, chunked and then fed to a code-controlled generator for MCQ creation. We filtered out image-dependent or ambiguous content, and only retained questions within target difficulty ranges. The result is a set of clean, high-quality synthetic Arabic MCQs for STEM.

    For the Code Benchmarks, our goal was to isolate language understanding while preserving code logic. Prompt translation was handled by GPT-4o with verification via reverse translation. Code and tests were untouched to allow evaluation parity with English versions. The result is a benchmark where Arabic prompts can be evaluated directly with the EvalPlus toolchain.

    We evaluated over 40 LLMs, including Arabic-first, multilingual, and general-purpose base and instruction-tuned models. Evaluation was performed using both multiple-choice accuracy and generative completion metrics.

    According to recent reports, in the MCQ setting, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct achieved top performance across both native (71.8%) and synthetic (67.0%) STEM subsets. For completion tasks, Gemma-3-27B demonstrated the strongest results with 43.2% accuracy on STEM answers.

    In a recent development, in code generation, GPT-4o demonstrated best-in-class performance on both HumanEval-ar (83.5% pass@1+) and MBPP-ar (63.6% pass@1+). These results highlight strong correlation (~0.97) between Arabic and English pass@1 scores, suggesting language-specific prompt quality has a major influence on model outcomes.

    We also examined robustness under distractor perturbation, revealing that instruction-tuned models are significantly more stable than their base counterparts. Prompt engineering and zero-shot design were also shown to meaningfully affect Arabic STEM performance.

    We built the benchmark to be easily reproducible using standard tools:.

    All scripts, configs, and evaluation pipelines are available in our GitHub repository, and can be adapted to evaluate any model compatible with HuggingFace Transformers or OpenAI APIs.

    All three datasets are open-source and hosted on HuggingFace Datasets:.

    If you use 3LM in your research, please cite us:.

    Python parallel debugging comes to HPC thanks to TotalView upgrade

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (706 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • TotalView has supported C/C++ and Fortran.
    • The OG debugger for supercomputer iron has buddied up with the data-science darling now muscling in on HPC: Python.
    • At the SC26 supercomputing show this week (booth #2829), Perforce Software is demonstrating how its TotalView parallel debugging tool now understands Python, easing the path for using the language on large, distributed apps, particularly those in the high-performance computing (HPC) space.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    TotalView has supported C/C++ and Fortran. With the latest quarterly release, it supports Python as well.

    The OG debugger for supercomputer iron has buddied up with the data-science darling now muscling in on HPC: Python.

    At the SC26 supercomputing show this week (booth #2829), Perforce Software is demonstrating how its TotalView parallel debugging tool now understands Python, easing the path for using the language on large, distributed apps, particularly those in the high-performance computing (HPC) space.

    In the HPC community, "Python has grown in popularity,” stated Bill Burns, Perforce vice president of software engineering, in an interview with The Register.

    TotalView is a debugger specializing in picking apart parallel applications for developers.

    In a recent development, built in the late 1980s for military applications, TotalView today largely serves developers in high-performance computing (HPC), where large scientific applications are spread across multiple servers, running in parallel on thousands or even tens of thousands of processes. (Perforce acquired TotalView in 2019 in its purchase of the DevOps-focused Rogue Wave Software.).

    Sources indicate that to date, TotalView has supported C/C++ and Fortran. With the latest quarterly release, the tool now supports Python as well.

    It has been revealed that C/C++ has long had a decent dedicated debugger in GDB, but figuring out what went wrong across multiple threads is a special kind of torture. Each thread needs to be instrumented, and all the output needs to be aggregated and filtered to just highlight the interesting stuff. Regular debuggers get overwhelmed with all this info.

    It has been revealed that “Even if you have 10,000 things going on, if you have one crash in there, TotalView can pinpoint that,” Burns noted. It can look at the state of the process, the threads within that process or the GPU that process is using.

    Recent findings suggest that in the HPC space, computing work has traditionally been written in C/C++. And at least some HPC iron still runs Fortran.

    Industry observers note that thanks to it being easy to learn and use, Python has gained a foothold in this community as well. The mpi4py library bridges a Python program to the Message Passing Interface (MPI), allowing different parts of an application running on different hardware to communicate.

    Python became more amenable to parallel programming at the thread level with version 3.14, released a year ago, which included the ability to use concurrent interpreters, as well as the long-awaited free threading support, thanks to the disabling of the global interpreter lock (GIL).

    “If you have a CPU with 64 cores, you can run 64 independent threads all working in unison on that CPU. Without GIL, those threads will run fully asynchronously,” Burns stated.

    Multinode scientific simulations, distributed AI training, and large applications that would benefit from shared memory have all become fair game for Python.

    Of course, with 500 or 1,000 interpreters all running in parallel, debugging will also get more difficult.

    “Now you're going to end up with lock and thread contention and race conditions and all the things that C++ and Fortran developers have dealt with for years,” Burns stated.

    Recent findings suggest that under the hood, TotalView uses Microsoft's debugpy engine (via the Debug Adapter Protocol) to power its own hierarchical tree server. TotalView can aggregate hundreds of stack traces into a single view, highlighting only those outside of expected bounds.

    To kick off a debugging session, a developer can launch a single-process or parallel program under TotalView’s control. They can then set breakpoints to pause execution and inspect variables and data structures, as well as evaluate Python expressions.

    The package doesn’t offer full cross-language debugging, which would be truly helpful for Python apps that call C/C++ libraries and modules. For now, developers have to choose between debugging the C/C++ side (while viewing the Python stack) or debugging Python on its own — though Burns stated Perforce intends to merge both modes into a single workflow in an upcoming release.

    And though TotalView supports mpi4py and Python’s own multiprocessing module out of the box, future releases will support other Python concurrency frameworks, such as Dask and PyTorch’s torchrun.

    TotalView is priced on a token-based model, where each token buys the capability to debug a process. ®.

    Contributors: David Austin, Raja Biswas, Gilberto Titericz Junior, NVIDIA.

    Recent findings suggest that NVIDIA’s AI-Q Blueprint—the leading portable, open deep research agent—recently climbed to the top of the Hugging Face “LLM with Search” leaderboard on DeepResearch Bench. This is a significant step forward for the open-source AI stack, proving that developer-accessible models can power advanced agentic workflows that rival or surpass closed alternatives.

    What sets AI-Q apart? It fuses two high-performance open LLMs—Llama 3.3-70B Instruct and Llama-3.3-Nemotron-Super-49B-v1.5—to orchestrate long-context retrieval, agentic reasoning, and robust synthesis.

    The AI-Q reference example also includes:.

    The architecture supports parallel, low-latency search over local and web data, making it ideal for use cases that demand privacy, compliance, or on-premise deployment for reduced latency.

    It has been revealed that NVIDIA Llama Nemotron Super isn’t just a fine-tuned instruct model—it’s post-trained for explicit agentic reasoning and supports reasoning ON/OFF toggles via system prompts. You can use it in standard chat LLM mode or switch to deep, chain-of-thought reasoning for agent pipelines—enabling dynamic, context-sensitive workflows.

    One of the core strengths of AI-Q is transparency—not just in outputs, but in reasoning traces and intermediate steps. During development, the NVIDIA team leveraged both standard and fresh metrics, such as:.

    The architecture lends itself perfectly to granular, stepwise evaluation and debugging—one of the biggest pain points in agentic pipeline development.

    DeepResearch Bench evaluates agent stacks using a set of 100+ long-context, real-world research tasks (across science, finance, art, history, software, and more). Unlike traditional QA, tasks require report-length synthesis and complex multi-hop reasoning:.

    The open-source ecosystem is rapidly closing the gap—and, in some areas, leading—on real-world agent tasks that matter. AI-Q, built on Llama Nemotron, demonstrates that you don’t need to compromise on transparency or control to achieve state-of-the-art results.

    Try the stack or adapt it to your own research agent projects from Hugging Face or build.nvidia.com.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, GPT OSS is a hugely anticipated open-weights release by OpenAI, designed for powerful reasoning, agentic tasks, and versatile developer use cases.
    • To make it even better and more impactful for the community, the models are licensed under the Apache 2.0 license, along with a minimal usage policy:.
    • We aim for our tools to be used safely, responsibly, and democratically, while maximizing your control over how you use them.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, GPT OSS is a hugely anticipated open-weights release by OpenAI, designed for powerful reasoning, agentic tasks, and versatile developer use cases. It comprises two models: a massive one with 117B parameters (gpt-oss-120b), and a smaller one with 21B parameters (gpt-oss-20b). Both are mixture-of-experts (MoEs) and use a 4-bit quantization scheme (MXFP4), enabling fast inference (thanks to fewer active parameters, see details below) while keeping resource usage low. The large model fits on a single H100 GPU, while the small one runs within 16GB of memory and is perfect for consumer hardware and on-device applications.

    To make it even better and more impactful for the community, the models are licensed under the Apache 2.0 license, along with a minimal usage policy:.

    We aim for our tools to be used safely, responsibly, and democratically, while maximizing your control over how you use them. By using gpt-oss, you agree to comply with all applicable law.

    According to OpenAI, this release is a meaningful step in their commitment to the open-source ecosystem, in line with their stated mission to make the benefits of AI broadly accessible. Many use cases rely on private and/or local deployments, and we at Hugging Face are super excited to welcome OpenAI to the community. We believe these will be long-lived, inspiring and impactful models.

    OpenAI GPT OSS models are accessible through Hugging Face’s Inference Providers service, allowing you to send requests to any supported provider using the same JavaScript or Python code. This is the same infrastructure that powers OpenAI’s official demo on gpt-oss.com, and you can use it for your own projects.

    Industry observers note that below is an example that uses Python and the super-fast Cerebras provider. For more info and additional snippets, check the inference providers section in the model cards and the dedicated guide we crafted for these models.

    It has been revealed that inference Providers also implements an OpenAI-compatible Responses API, the most advanced OpenAI interface for chat models, designed for more flexible and intuitive interactions.Below is an example using the Responses API with the Fireworks AI provider. For more details, check out the open-source responses.js project.

    Industry observers note that you need to install the latest transformers release (v4.55.1 or later), as well as accelerate and kernels. We also recommend installing triton 3.4 or better, as it unblocks support for mxfp4 quantization on CUDA hardware:.

    The model weights are quantized in mxfp4 format, which was originally available on GPUs of the Hopper or Blackwell families, but now works on previous CUDA architectures (including Ada, Ampere, and Tesla). Installing triton 3.4, together with the kernels library, makes it possible to download optimized mxfp4 kernels on first use, achieving large memory savings. With these components in place, you can run the 20B model on GPUs with 16 GB of RAM. This includes many consumer cards (3090, 4090, 5080) as well as Colab and Kaggle!

    If the previous libraries are not installed (or you don’t have a compatible GPU), loading the model will fall back to bfloat16, unpacked from the quantized weights.

    The following snippet indicates simple inference with the 20B model. As explained, it runs on 16 GB GPUs when using mxfp4, or ~48 GB in bfloat16.

At the time of writing, this super-fast kernel has been tested on Hopper cards with PyTorch 2.7 and 2.8. We expect increased coverage in the coming days.     We recommend you use mxfp4 if your GPU supports it. If you can additionally use Flash Attention 3, then by all means do enable it!

You can test it with the same inference code shown above.

    According to recent reports, GPT OSS models are reasoning models: they therefore require a very large generation size (maximum number of upcoming tokens) for evaluations, as their generation will first contain reasoning, then the actual answer. Using too small a generation size risks interrupting the prediction in the middle of reasoning, which will cause false negatives. The reasoning trace should then be removed from the model answer before computing metrics, to avoid parsing errors, especially with math or instruct evaluations.

    Here’s an example on how to evaluate the models with lighteval (you need to install from source).

    For the 20B model, this should give you 69.5 (+/-1.9) for IFEval (strict prompt), and 63.3 (+/-8.9) for AIME25 (in pass@1), scores within expected range for a reasoning model of this size.

    If you want to do your custom evaluation script, note that to filter out the reasoning tags properly, you will need to use skip_special_tokens=False in the tokenizer, in order to get the full trace in the model output (to filter reasoning using the same string pairs as in the example above) - you can discover why below.

    OpenAI GPT OSS uses the concept of “channels” in its outputs. Most of the time, you will see an “analysis” channel that contains things that are not intended to be sent to the end-user, like chains of thought, and a “final” channel containing messages that are actually intended to be displayed to the user.

    Assuming no tools are being used, the structure of the model output looks like this:.

    Most of the time, you should ignore everything except the text after <|channel|>final<|message|>. Only this text should be appended to the chat as the assistant message, or displayed to the user. There are two exceptions to this rule, though: You may need to include analysis messages in the history during training or if the model is calling external tools.

    In a recent development, when training: If you’re formatting examples for training, you generally want to include the chain of thought in the final message. The right place to do this is in the thinking key.

    Recent findings suggest that you can feel free to include thinking keys in previous turns, or when you’re doing inference rather than training, but they will generally be ignored. The chat template will only ever include the most recent chain of thought, and only in training (when add_generation_prompt=False and the final turn is an assistant turn).

    In a recent development, the reason why we do it this way is subtle: The OpenAI gpt-oss models were trained on multi-turn data where all but the final chain of thought was dropped. This means that when you want to fine-tune an OpenAI gpt-oss model, you should do the same.

    Sources indicate that openAI GPT OSS is unusual because it distinguishes between a “system” message and a “developer” message at the start of the chat, but most other models only use “system”. In GPT OSS, the system message follows a strict format and contains information like the current date, the model identity and the level of reasoning effort to use, and the “developer” message is more freeform, which makes it (very confusingly) similar to the “system” messages of most other models.

    It has been revealed that to make GPT OSS easier to use with the standard API, the chat template will treat a message with “system” or “developer” role as the developer message. If you want to modify the actual system message, you can pass the specific arguments model_identity or reasoning_effort to the chat template:.

    Industry observers note that GPT OSS supports two kinds of tools: The “builtin” tools browser and python, and custom tools supplied by the user. To enable builtin tools, pass their names in a list to the builtin_tools argument of the chat template, as shown below. To pass custom tools, you can pass them either as JSON schema or as Python functions with type hints and docstrings using the tools argument. See the chat template tools documentation for more details, or you can just modify the example below:.

    If the model chooses to call a tool (indicated by a message ending in <|call|>), then you should add the tool call to the chat, call the tool, then add the tool result to the chat and generate again:.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Google Quantum AI confirmed on November 19, 2026 that research published on the cover of Science had demonstrated measurement contextuality at scale on its superconducting processors, including a coordination game won 98.3% of the time, above the 88.9% classical limit.
    • Contextuality means that a measurement outcome is not a predetermined value; it depends on which other compatible measurements are performed alongside it.
    • The underlying work was first submitted as an arXiv preprint on December 1, 2025.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Google Quantum AI confirmed on November 19, 2026 that research published on the cover of Science had demonstrated measurement contextuality at scale on its superconducting processors, including a coordination game won 98.3% of the time, above the 88.9% classical limit.

    Contextuality means that a measurement outcome is not a predetermined value; it depends on which other compatible measurements are performed alongside it. Theory suggests that this property may power certain quantum algorithms, but earlier demonstrations had mostly involved systems of only a few particles. The fresh publication reports experiments extending those tests to as many as 105 qubits.

    The underlying work was first submitted as an arXiv preprint on December 1, 2025. The November 2026 development is its journal publication, rather than the initial disclosure of the experiments.

    The preprint’s experimental account begins with the Mermin–Peres magic-square game. Two players, Alice and Bob, can agree on a strategy before being separated. A referee then assigns Alice a row and Bob a column of a three-by-three table. Alice’s entries must multiply to +1 and Bob’s to −1, and the players win when their values match at the intersecting cell.

    According to recent reports, no prearranged classical table can satisfy those opposing constraints for every assignment. The quantum implementation uses a two-by-two square of qubits and two shared Bell pairs, with an ideal noiseless strategy winning every game. The reported experimental average came from nine row-column assignments, each repeated 100,000 times.

    In a recent development, A separate Kochen–Specker–Bell test quantified contextuality with χKSB, a combination of correlations from compatible measurements. The paper reports χKSB = 5.618 ± 0.005, exceeding the classical bound of 4 and approaching the quantum limit of 6, with the remaining difference attributed to experimental errors. Its circuit streamed 180 randomly selected measurement contexts over 1,000 runs.

    Recent findings suggest that to examine contextuality beyond few-qubit states, the team implemented an N-player GHZ parity game. Each player corresponded to one qubit, and the group shared a GHZ state entangled across those qubits. Each player received a binary question and returned a bit; to win, the parity of their combined answers had to match a value determined by the questions.

    The paper reports tests through 71 qubits, with the quantum winning probability above the classical probability at every tested size. Its advantage nevertheless narrowed as players were added. For each player count, the researchers tested 20 games across 50 qubit configurations, repeating each configuration 1,000 times to distinguish performance from statistical fluctuations as the margin contracted.

    A separate two-dimensional hidden-linear-function task asked the processor to find a hidden bitstring associated with a symmetric matrix. The experiments used Willow superconducting processors and controlled-Z gates as the native entangling operation, testing sizes from 9 qubits up to the largest device. At each size, the team measured 1,000 random matrices and ran each matrix 100 times.

    An error-free implementation returns a correct bitstring after four effective two-qubit-gate layers. To quantify hardware errors, the researchers converted the fraction of correct outputs into an effective depth, a time-to-solution measure reflecting the extra runs needed to obtain a correct answer. The paper reports that this measure rose to about six layers on the largest grid.

    The authors propose contextuality-based algorithms as processor benchmarks and report that the many-body versions exposed subtle coherent errors absent from random unitary operations. That gives the tests a hardware-diagnostic role beyond their game scores.

    Recent findings suggest that google presents that error-detection capability as a step toward future chemistry and materials-science applications. Those are stated potential uses; the reported experiments do not simulate either application.

    The scope of the quantum-classical separation is equally important. The paper states that no unconditional proof of quantum advantage exists for a general computational model; its results concern particular tasks with bounded resources. For the hidden-linear-function comparison, the established classical lower bound becomes relevant only at roughly one million qubits. The logarithmic near-term classical-depth bound shown against the experimental results is expressly a conjecture, so the measurements do not establish an unconditional advantage over every classical implementation at current processor sizes.

    In a recent development, the immediate value is a sharper way to evaluate quantum hardware: contextuality supplies scalable tasks tied to a proposed source of computational advantage, while their sensitivity exposes errors that can remain hidden in less structured tests. At the same time, the shrinking GHZ-game margin and rising effective depth show that preserving the quantum benefit becomes harder as more qubits participate.

    With a theoretical and deeply intellectual perspective, Aster examines research emerging from quantum labs, academic institutions, and national research programs. They focus on how machine learning models assist in managing quantum noise, calibrating hardware, and navigating the immense complexity of quantum systems, while remaining clear about the limitations and uncertainties that still define the field.

    • In a recent development, "So last week in some sense was really a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world," mentioned Nadella.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    At Ignite, the Windows-Azure giant is all about Copilot.

    Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella's Ignite conference keynote on Tuesday was all about trust. He opened by promising to earn back trust after last week's massive M365 outage and went on to focus on the need for organizations to trust their AI models.

    In a recent development, "So last week in some sense was really a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world," mentioned Nadella. "We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve.".

    Speaking at San Francisco's Moscone Center, Nadella described three areas of focus for the company as it works to build what he referred to as a frontier ecosystem: "Keeping the human at the center of it all, ensuring that you have ownership over your organization's intelligence and learning, and trust.".

    Recent findings suggest that anthrocentrism is a tough sell just weeks after offering buyouts to 60,000 employees. Describing the shift from hand-written code to agent-written code, Nadella suggested developers have moved from building software artifacts to building software factories that build those artifacts.

    "The notable thing here though is to remember still that that human intent, that judgment, that experience, skills, expertise all very much matter," he said.

    People may judge development work, but ask them whether they have the same sense of ownership as when they wrote every line.

    According to recent reports, as to ensuring that organizations have ownership over their intelligence, that borders on heresy for a organization with massive cloud computing commitments specifically to run AI workloads. If everyone really owned their machine learning models and ran them in their own data centers and on employee computers, Azure would be in trouble.

    Sources indicate that "In the age of AI, the key question is how do individual firms continually build and own their learning and tacit knowledge?" he said. "For an economy to remain an economy where many firms exist and thrive, intelligence by definition needs to be broadly distributed versus just collapsed into a couple of models.".

    Suffice to say that Nadella is promoting client control over AI data that's processed mostly on equipment rented from Microsoft, with some allowance for customer-controlled infrastructure. But that still ought to concern frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI that favor a white-glove, black-box service model where they are the arbiters of access.

    As for the third pillar of Nadella's vision, that's trust, which remains missing in action.

    "How can you even trust all this powerful technology?" Nadella asked. "And the reality is, by definition, you can't. In other words, it becomes an architectural imperative to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. And so our goal is to build a stack that addresses these three architectural imperatives.".

    Microsoft's original stack was built on ownership of the operating system. But the manufacturer's commitment to AI is such that it now describes Copilot in the terms once reserved for Windows.

    "Copilot is the fresh operating system for work," said Nadella.

    Sources indicate that fifteen years ago, venture capitalist Marc Andreessen famously observed that software is eating the world. Now AI, including Copilot, is eating software.

    It has been revealed that "Apps are just plugins to Copilot," Nadella mused. "That's why we in fact have brought all of Office, all of its richness, right built into Copilot.".

    In a recent development, copilot is eating other companies too. Nadella said Microsoft is extending Copilot to take on specific roles by providing skills, connectors, and plugins for industry-specific tasks. Toward that end, "Copilot is the new front door to Dynamics 365," which now offers CRM plugins. And Nadella announced a partnership with Salesforce called Copilotforce that brings Salesforce context into Copilot, Teams, and Fabric.

    He also talked up Microsoft IQ, the company's upcoming enterprise context management platform.

    "The idea behind IQ is to help every organization build, retain, and continuously improve your own intelligence across the organization," said Nadella, describing it as an externalization of the context system underlying Copilot.

    Recent findings suggest that nadella went on to announce a new model family for GitHub Copilot Fusion, its code hosting subsidiary's model orchestration and routing play. He noted that Copilot Fusion today is ranked above Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 at less than half the cost on Terminal Bench, a measurement of how well AI agents complete tasks using a terminal.

    In a recent development, then there's Copilot Workspaces, which Nadella described as a multiplayer version of Copilot. Instead of a chat window where one person interacts with a model, it's an interface for team collaboration that shares context with a model.

    Microsoft's decision model, intended to challenge TypeSafe AI's Jev, debuted about a month ago and now Decisions 1.1 is generally available.

    "We have improved performance, making decisions more accurate and responses faster," said Nadella. "Already over 4,000 customers have used it.".

    He then said that Microsoft Foundry would offer OpenAI's GPT-6.2, which may have caused some confusion because at that point, OpenAI had no such model. A short time later, OpenAI confirmed GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol.

    Microsoft also rolled out fresh coding models, in the form of Code 2, Code 2 Flash, and Cyber 2 Flash, and remarked its next-gen Cobalt 200 VMs are generally available.

    After rattling off the various products and services Microsoft has prepared to help organizations with intelligence ownership, Nadella returned to the question of trust.

    "Today we can see almost everything that models touch, but you cannot see what happens inside a model," he stated. "And really what's worse is that we know that what a model tells us about itself is not even independent evidence and therefore cannot be trusted.

    Industry observers note that "And one model monitoring another model has the same concern. So you essentially have these unacceptable nested sets of black boxes, which we now need to make transparent and verifiable.".

    Sources indicate that microsoft's bid to bridge the trust gap is the Microsoft Transparency Initiative. The firm claims this will involve engagement with the National Institute of Standards and Technology's "SI Agent Standards Initiative.".

    According to recent reports, whether Microsoft AI will be compatible with NIST SI remains to be seen. That  initiative also calls for collaboration with other organizations to develop accountable, verifiable, vendor-neutral AI transparency standards, and for Microsoft to incorporate this work into Microsoft AI, Foundry, and Copilot. Check in next year to see whether transparency is achieved. ®.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Vision Language Models (VLMs) are getting stronger, but aligning them to human preferences still matters.
    • These go beyond pairwise DPO, extracting richer signals from preference data and scaling better with modern VLMs.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Vision Language Models (VLMs) are getting stronger, but aligning them to human preferences still matters. In TRL, we already showed how to post-train VLMs with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). This time, we’re going further.

    tl;dr Here’s what’s fresh in TRL:.

    These go beyond pairwise DPO, extracting richer signals from preference data and scaling better with modern VLMs.

    We’ve also extended existing methods to support VLMs:.

    This enables more efficient and scalable multimodal alignment.

    It has been revealed that traditionally, you would take a base model, apply SFT to follow instructions, and then apply DPO to align it to preferential data. Previously, we adapted this approach to Vision Language Models (VLMs) and validated it on IDEFICS2, showing improvement in model responses.

    DPO works by optimizing preferences between pairs of model responses using a contrastive loss: you have a chosen and a rejected answer and you optimize your preferences based on what you want and don’t want.

    Industry observers note that but in the last year, new multimodal alignment methods have gained popularity, GRPO and MPO, that can push VLM performance even further. At the end of the blog post you can find a table that showcases the differences between model responses.

    It has been revealed that aligning multimodal models with SFT to do reasoning tasks falls short due to distribution shift. Meanwhile, models aligned with DPO fail to generate coherent rationales and might generate repetitive responses. To address this, there’s a fresh technique called Mixed Preference Optimization (MPO) specifically made for multimodal models. This method is essentially an extension of DPO with multiple losses: preference loss from DPO (sigmoid), quality loss from Binary Classifier Optimization (BCO), and generation loss from SFT. According to the paper, simply switching to this combined loss results in 6.2 pts improvement in MathVista!

    Since this is only modifying the loss, we added combined loss support to TRL's DPOTrainer class. To use it, you can initialize the DPOConfig as follows:.

    According to recent reports, group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is a cutting-edge alignment method initially introduced in DeepSeek Math paper and later integrated to DeepSeek R1, the groundbreaking LLM. It’s an addition to PPO where the policy updates are done over groups (batches of trajectories that represent how a dialogue rolls out). This feature makes it more robust to reward noise, as the noise averages out within groups. Since the model learns broader sense of a good response rather than singular high reward samples, this method also makes the model highly performant.

    In TRL, we now introduce GRPO support for vision language models. We will not provide a full training script example, as you can find it in the notebook. Instead, we'll focus on highlighting the key component and concepts.

In order to really see improvements in the latter reward, you would need a rather maximalist setup, where you have relatively larger models, a lot of generations, and a high-quality, diverse dataset.

It achieves a more stable training computing importance sampling weights at the sequence level instead of per-token. Its benefits are more relevant in MoE style models.

    vCluster Adds Self-Service Private Clouds for Dedicated AI Hardware

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (846 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • vCluster Labs has introduced vCluster Platform v5.0 in limited availability, giving AI cloud providers a way to offer self-service environments on dedicated physical servers.
    • The November 19 release addresses a practical problem for operators that have already committed to supplying bare-metal capacity.
    • According to recent reports, the release brings physical servers into an inventory maintained by vMetal, the provisioning component beneath the platform.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    vCluster Labs has introduced vCluster Platform v5.0 in limited availability, giving AI cloud providers a way to offer self-service environments on dedicated physical servers. Customers can provision machines from their allocated capacity, select an operating system image and launch Kubernetes, Slurm or inference clusters without asking the provider to handle each request.

    The November 19 release addresses a practical problem for operators that have already committed to supplying bare-metal capacity. A customer may rent a block of GPU servers but still depend on the provider’s operations team to get machines ready for new projects. The new platform moves some of those decisions to the customer while leaving hardware ownership and capacity allocation with the provider.

    According to recent reports, the release brings physical servers into an inventory maintained by vMetal, the provisioning component beneath the platform. An operator assigns capacity to customers or leaves it available on demand, then decides which machine types, images and cluster templates each customer can use. The platform adds an explicit customer boundary, called a tenant, above individual projects. Quotas limit how much capacity a customer can claim, and customers cannot see inventory they have not been granted.

    It has been revealed that for a customer platform team, that means several internal groups can draw from the same contract without each needing a new allocation from the provider. A research group could set up a scheduled Slurm environment while an application team uses Kubernetes for an inference deployment. The provider decides which configurations it supports, and the customer can choose among them. How much control a customer has therefore depends on what is included in its allocation and which templates the provider makes available.

    The firm notes providers can use its console or build a branded portal on the same underlying API. That distinction matters to operators selling infrastructure under their own brand: the interface can differ without requiring a separate inventory and provisioning system for each type of service.

    It has been revealed that bare metal provides access to physical servers rather than instances that share a host with unrelated customers. That can be attractive when buyers want a known hardware configuration, dedicated accelerator capacity or control over the software environment. But a physical reservation does not by itself provide a usable cloud service. Someone still has to set up the operating system, configure access and prepare the cluster.

    Industry observers note that vCluster’s approach combines dedicated machines and per-customer networking with self-service provisioning. A provider may use the same inventory for simple server rentals and more managed products. The business case is that a smaller number of steps handled by a provider’s staff could make each customer easier to onboard, while buyers that prefer a managed cluster can purchase a different level of service. The release does not establish how much either side would save, and the economics will depend on how heavily the hardware is used and what support customers require.

    It also matters how operators handle hardware that sits idle between projects. Reserved capacity gives buyers predictability, but those machines can remain unavailable to other customers even when idle. An on-demand pool can increase flexibility, though only when the provider can reliably meet demand. The platform lets providers offer both models; it does not remove the need to set reservation terms or blueprint for shortages.

    Sources indicate that version 5.0 is not generally available. The vendor’s documentation recommends retaining the existing long-term support releases, Platform v4.12 and vCluster v0.37, for current deployments. Operators considering the upcoming version still have to assess compatibility with their provisioning and networking tools, and verify that customers can move from a machine allocation to a usable cluster without new support bottlenecks.

    The immediate test is operational: how quickly a provider can deliver working infrastructure after allocating hardware, and how often customers need assistance afterward. If those measures improve without making dedicated capacity harder to manage, self-service could become a meaningful distinction between AI cloud providers selling similar hardware.

    GPU giants throw HPC people some tasty crumbs

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Nvidia unveils an HPC-optimized Rubin GPU to challenge AMD's 288 teraFLOPS MI430X.
    • At Supercomputing 2026 this week, Nvidia unveiled a new variant of its Rubin GPUs aimed at – you’ll never believe it – high performance computing (HPC).
    • Recent findings suggest that the creatively named Rubin HPC promises more than 50,000 CUDA cores, nearly twice that of the AI-focused version of the chip that Nvidia unveiled earlier this year.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Nvidia unveils an HPC-optimized Rubin GPU to challenge AMD's 288 teraFLOPS MI430X.

    At Supercomputing 2026 this week, Nvidia unveiled a new variant of its Rubin GPUs aimed at – you’ll never believe it – high performance computing (HPC).

    Recent findings suggest that the creatively named Rubin HPC promises more than 50,000 CUDA cores, nearly twice that of the AI-focused version of the chip that Nvidia unveiled earlier this year. It will arrive sometime in 2028.

    According to Dan Ernst, Nvidia’s senior director of supercomputing, the newly introduced chip offers a rebalanced architecture optimized for the kinds of simulation, engineering, and high-performance analytics workloads common in the HPC and scientific computing communities.

    In a recent development, this is not the first time Nvidia has introduced specialized hardware. Last year, the company optimized its B300 accelerator for AI inferencing workloads.

    In a recent development, “Rubin HPC is the same idea,” Ernst told El Reg. “Within the Rubin platform, but we’re building variants to really focus on a specific sub domain of applications.”.

    It has been revealed that details remain remarkably thin. Nvidia hasn’t disclosed peak performance memory capacity or bandwidth. That said, the chip will likely include features which show Nvidia can think beyond AI and still cares about the HPC community.

    Fearing that Nvidia could ignore HPC is reasonable becuase beginning with the launch of Blackwell Ultra (B300/GB300), the company traded double-precision matrix acceleration for higher throughput at lower-precisions.

    The result was a chip that at FP4 churned out 15 petaFLOPS of AI compute, but just 1.3 teraFLOPS at FP64. That's good for AI, but less useful for scientists.

    When Nvidia unveiled Rubin, it seemed the GPU-slinger would continue this trend. At 33 teraFLOPS, the chip was not only slower at FP64 than the Blackwell GPUs it replaced, but slower than Nvidia’s now four-year-old Hopper accelerators as well.

    Nvidia contended that for sparse vector-heavy workloads measured by the High Performance Conjugate Gradients (HPCG) benchmark, the higher ratio of memory bandwidth to compute should deliver meaningful performance gains.

    Meanwhile, for dense matrix-heavy workloads, for which benchmarks like High-Performance Linpack (HPL) are representative, Nvidia adopted a latest strategy: FP64 emulation.

    We discussed the pros and cons of this technique in greater detail earlier this year, but in a nutshell it uses an algorithm derived from the so-called Ozaki Scheme.

    The algorithm works by decomposing FP64 matrix operations into a string of INT8 operations that, when run on Nvidia’s tensor cores, achieve higher-than-native performance.

    Nvidia, we’re told, isn’t using INT8, but it is unlocking substantial performance gains, at least for certain workloads. According to Nvidia, Rubin can churn out up to 200 emulated FP64 matrix teraFLOPS.

    While Ernst didn’t offer any specifics, he assured us that Nvidia’s HPC hardware should offer native FP64 matrix performance and customers won't have to rely entirely on emulation.

    It has been revealed that assessing the new chip's vector performance is much easier. With more than 50 thousand CUDA cores (by our calculation, it should be closer to 53,248), the chip should deliver at least 86 percent higher vector performance at double precision.

    According to recent reports, AMD is also cooking up newly introduced HPC chips. In a blog post published late last week, AMD revealed the HPC-tuned version of its MI400-series GPUs.

    The Instinct MI430X boasts 432 GB of HBM4, 23 TB/s of memory bandwidth and a whopping 288 teraFLOPS of peak double precision grunt.

    AMD isn’t relying on FP64 emulation. Instead, AMD took advantage of its modular chiplet architecture to build two distinct versions of its MI400-series accelerators: one optimized for AI and another designed to excel in HPC and scientific computing workloads.

    AMD has shared predictions as to how the chips will perform in several of the Top500’s headline benchmarks. In a total non-surprise, the House of Zen says systems like EuroHPC’s Alice Recoque and Oak Ridge National Laboratories’ upcoming Discovery supers would enjoy significant performance gains if they upgrade from its earlier Instinct MI300A and MI250X-based offerings. ®.

    #57617. OpenRun v1.0 - declarative deployments for internal tools on Docker or Kubernetes
