    OpenRun v1.0 - declarative deployments for internal tools on Docker or Kubernetes

    📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1150 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openrun

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • After over three years of development, over 2000 commits, 170 releases and with multiple customers running OpenRun in production, I am happy to do the 1.0 release for OpenRun.
    • Recent findings suggest that openRun is an open source self-hosted GitOps platform for deploying web apps and internal tools declaratively.
    • Recent findings suggest that I started the OpenRun project (called Clace initially) in April 2023 - feels like an eternity ago.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    After over three years of development, over 2000 commits, 170 releases and with multiple customers running OpenRun in production, I am happy to do the 1.0 release for OpenRun.

    Recent findings suggest that openRun is an open source self-hosted GitOps platform for deploying web apps and internal tools declaratively. Deploy on a single node with Docker/Podman, or deploy apps onto a Kubernetes cluster. OpenRun adds the authentication, authorization and auditing features required by teams. Code based internal tools get the deployment and auth features which are usually available in low code platforms.

    Recent findings suggest that I started the OpenRun project (called Clace initially) in April 2023 - feels like an eternity ago. I have been working on OpenRun as a part time project, doing consulting on the side.

    OpenRun is built to make it easy for teams to declaratively deploy internal tools. OpenRun also aims to make it easy to set up OIDC/SAML based authentication, with RBAC policies to control which apps are available to which teams and roles.

    In a recent development, A sample OpenRun config looks like below. See intro for a comparison with Kubernetes.

    To declaratively create these two apps, run openrun apply apps.star. Setting a default auth and RBAC policies in the server config means they apply to all apps.

    Industry observers note that this reveals a recorded demo of a sample workload. See console tour for a walkthrough of the optional console UI or take a look at the console live demo.

    According to recent reports, go: OpenRun is implemented in Go. The fast compile cycle and excellent runtime performance of Go make developing in Go fun. The difficulty of adding dynamic behavior was the one challenge in Go, especially compared to something like the dynamic class loading available in the JVM. Out of process loading using go-plugin was the solution used to get dynamic loading behavior. There is an additional performance overhead of an RPC call but there are advantages in terms of ease of use and stability.

    In a recent development, starlark as the config language for declaring apps and defining app handler functions. The familiarity of Python which Starlark provides makes it very easy to get started with for end users.

    According to recent reports, hypermedia (using HTMX) based UI is used for the built-in actions UI and for the optional Console app. Hypermedia apps work well for the types of apps being built with OpenRun. Fewer frontend dependencies, no separate frontend build pipeline and avoiding the NPM ecosystem have been some benefits of building Hypermedia based apps.

    It has been revealed that SQLite and Postgres: For single node deployment, SQLite is used for metadata. For Kubernetes deployment, Postgres is used for metadata. No ORM is used. This was a bit more work to develop initially but allowed for complete control over the queries used for each database.

    It has been revealed that declarative deployments: Initially, the plan was to use the Kubernetes libraries for three way merge (between new config, previous config and current state), but implementing it in OpenRun itself turned out to be simpler and easier to maintain. The implementation is custom built for what OpenRun needs, so it does not have the complexity of a general purpose library.

    Sequencing: OpenRun is built for teams to deploy internal tools. The three types of apps which are supported (in the order in which support was added in OpenRun) are:.

    Starlark Apps: OpenRun did go somewhat overboard with Starlark support, with features like allowing database app development from Starlark. Containerized apps would have been better since they work with the complete language ecosystem. The Hypermedia support could have been limited to what is required for a backend for frontend pattern (although hypermedia apps do not need much of a frontend). Internal apps like the Console are built with Starlark, so the work done to support this was still useful.

    Sources indicate that container Management: Single node deployment with Docker/Podman and multi-node with Kubernetes are the two supported modes. A multi-node deployment, with each node having a Docker/Podman installation, was considered but not done since that would have introduced too many complexities in terms of container and volume management.

    There are many products which make deployments easier. OpenRun differs in that it provides a declarative solution and is targeted at teams deploying internal tools.

    With recent improvements in AI, internal tools which would have required weeks of development work can now be built much faster using AI agents. Higher level abstractions for deploying internal tools securely are necessary now, since the tools themselves are easier to build.

    Agents are at a point where they can handle the deployment workflow themselves. Letting agents directly do production deployments might be fine for testing and personal workflows, but that approach is not suited for team environments. A declarative approach is better if you want to set up multiple deployment environments and restore an environment from scratch.

    Agents are pretty good at writing the YAML boilerplate required for Kubernetes deployments. Internal tools generally require OIDC/SAML authentication, RBAC and audit logs. Kubernetes alone does not make enabling such access policies easy. OpenRun provides a higher level app deployment abstraction. This helps reduce the overhead of maintaining the deployment configuration. Using Kubernetes directly, multiple systems like CI builder, ArgoCD, auth proxy, Internal Developer Platform (IDP) etc. have to be configured to get the functionality OpenRun provides.

    The core config format, CLI commands and API are stable and will maintain backward compatibility across the 1.x releases. The plan is to ensure that existing deployments should work without issues when doing upgrades across 1.x, as new features are added and issues fixed.

    Recent findings suggest that date based versioning is being used for the 1.x releases. All fixes go on the main branch and releases use the 1.YYMM.D[D]V version format, where V is the version number on that day, zero-indexed. So v1.2611.130 means the first release on 13 Nov 2026.

    The OpenRun server and its built-in features, including SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and PostgreSQL/MySQL/Redis service bindings, are Apache 2.0 licensed.

    It has been revealed that service bindings for additional databases and data platforms (Snowflake, Databricks, SQL Server, Oracle, MongoDB, ClickHouse) are available as downloadable service providers. These are under the PolyForm Free Trial License 1.0.0, which allows limited duration evaluation use. Use beyond the evaluation period requires a commercial license.

    In a recent development, paid support is planned for OpenRun and the commercial service providers. The paid initiative will also include SemVer based long term support releases, with fixes backported from the main branch. All features and fixes will be available in releases from the main branch. A SOC 2 Type 2 report on the organization will be available to customers on the paid plan. Email contact@openrun.dev for support.

    To try out OpenRun, check out the Quick Start, which works on macOS, Windows and Linux.

    #57616. Accelerate ND-Parallel: A guide to Efficient Multi-GPU Training

    Accelerate ND-Parallel: A guide to Efficient Multi-GPU Training

    📅 08 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3264 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Training large models across multiple GPUs can be challenging due to the complexities of different parallelism strategies.
    • We've also included a more comprehensive end-to-end training script in the Accelerate repo which demonstrates how to setup your dataloader, optimizer, and training loop, and how to save your model after training.
    • To further streamline fine-tuning models at scale and compose parallelism strategies with a variety of fine-tuning techniques, we've also integrated this technique into Axolotl.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Training large models across multiple GPUs can be challenging due to the complexities of different parallelism strategies. In Accelerate, together with Axolotl, we have integrated a quick and easy way to use any combination of parallelism strategies in your training script!

    Here is how to add it to your training script:.

    We've also included a more comprehensive end-to-end training script in the Accelerate repo which demonstrates how to setup your dataloader, optimizer, and training loop, and how to save your model after training.

    To further streamline fine-tuning models at scale and compose parallelism strategies with a variety of fine-tuning techniques, we've also integrated this technique into Axolotl. To help you get started right away we've tested some example configs which you can modify to suit your needs - try one out with:.

    You can also check out the Axolotl ND-Parallelism docs for more details - adding ND parallel techniques to your existing configs is as simple as adding one or more of the following fields to your Axolotl config file:.

    We've made it easy to configure the degrees of different parallelism strategies and how they are combined through the ParallelismConfig class in Accelerate, or through config fields in Axolotl, but how do we know which configuration will work best for our use case? As we scale to training models with tens or even hundreds of billions of parameters, the primary challenge comes from understanding the different parallelism strategies and how they interact to minimise communication overhead across devices. In this post, we'll walk through how the different parallelism strategies work, and when and how you might want to compose them.

    Data parallelism (DP) is the most common technique for training models across multiple GPUs, and involves replicating the model, gradients and optimizer states across each device, whilst evenly distributing data batches between GPUs, and synchronising gradients across devices before updating parameters. This can significantly increase throughput compared to single-device training, but requires that your model is able to fit on a single device.

    We can control the number of replicas of the model with the dp_replicate_size parameter in Accelerate's ParallelismConfig or config field in Axolotl. It's worth noting that DP is a top-most-level parallelism strategy, meaning that if we use dp_replicate_size=2 and we compose it with other parallelism strategies, there would be 2 replicas of the model, each also influenced by the other parallelism strategies. For example, if we use dp_replicate_size=2 and tp_size=2, we would have 2 replicas of the model, each with 2 tensor parallel shards.

    We use the term shard to describe data on a single device which is a partition of a larger piece of data.

    Industry observers note that what if our model is too large to fit on a single device? Fully sharded data parallel (FSDP) addresses this issue by sharding (distributing evenly) the model’s weights, gradients, and optimizer states across GPUs (this is inspired by DeepSpeed’s ZeRO-3), whilst each device still receives its portion of the full batch of data. As you may notice from the diagram above, rather than requiring a full copy of the entire model on each device, we only gather the weights for a single layer at a time before the forward pass, after which the weights may be sharded again.

    According to recent reports, in this way, we trade memory usage for the communication overhead of gathering sharded parameters before each forward and backward pass, and reduce-scatter-ing local gradients. We can control this trade-off in FSDP by tuning the granularity at which parameters are gathered. On one extreme, we can gather and re-shard every layer of our model, which would result in the lowest peak memory usage, but incur the highest communication costs. In practice, a common approach is to gather the weights for an entire transformer decoder block at a time.

    Whilst we can make further memory-compute trade-offs and offload model parameters and gradients to the CPU to train larger models, this can be prohibitively slow. Instead, let’s consider how we can effectively utilise even more devices to train larger models whilst maintaining high data throughput.

    It has been revealed that we use the term node to refer to a single machine which hosts multiple GPUs (up to a maximum of 8), with fast intra-node communication channels using e.g. NVLink between GPUs. When using multiple nodes for training, we rely on relatively slower inter-node communication channels between machines using e.g. Infiniband. We also refer to the total number of devices in the process pool as the world size - e.g. a single node with 8 GPUs represents a world size of 8, and 4 nodes would represent a world size of 32.

    Recent findings suggest that when using FSDP across multiple nodes, we treat the entire set of devices across nodes as if we were training on a single node. For example, with 4 nodes containing 8 GPUs each, we perform our sharding across 32 devices, and perform our collective all-reduce and reduce-scatter operations using both inter-and-intra-node communication backends. In this manner, FSDP alone can scale to a substantial number of GPUs with a large global batch size to increase data throughput. However, there comes a point where several challenges arise that may require composing FSDP with other parallelism techniques. We usually try to avoid doing FSDP across more than a full node, as the communication overhead can become too high, we'll talk about how to address this in the section on Hybrid Sharded Data Parallelism.

    You can use the dp_shard_size parameter in Accelerate's ParallelismConfig together with a prepared FullyShardedDataParallelPlugin, or set the dp_shard_size config field in Axolotl to set the degree of FSDP applied to your model.

    Sources indicate that tensor Parallel (TP) is a kind of model parallelism technique, where shards of the model permanently live on separate devices, and in contrast to data parallel techniques, each device receives an identical batch of data. TP works by distributing the computation of linear layers across devices, so each device only computes a portion of the matrix multiplication. This technique works best when there are large linear layers, such as the feed-forward layers in transformer models, which can be split across devices. We can also use TP on each of the query, key, value, and output projections in the attention layers with almost no extra communication cost.

    To achieve the best performance, parameters of consecutive layers can be distributed in a specific fashion, minimizing the required communication. When working with pairs of linear layers, we can split the first layer column-wise, and the subsequent layer row-wise, allowing us to compute the output with only a single all-reduce operation to combine the sharded outputs.

    Industry observers note that unlike the dynamic sharding behaviour of FSDP, TP creates static memory partitions which result in a constant memory usage reduction scaling with the TP group size. This becomes crucial for massive models where even a single decoder layer is too large to fit into memory during the FSDP all-gather (recall that common practice in FSDP is to gather the weights of an entire decoder layer at a time). However, unlike FSDP which scales relatively linearly across nodes (up to a point - ~512 GPUs on a homogenous cluster, significantly less across lower-bandwidth connections), TP is only effective within the boundaries of a single node. TP requires frequent activation synchronization between devices during computation, as each device computes only a portion of the output, requiring the outputs from other devices to be communicated before continuing the forward pass. Thus, if we wish to utilise TP in a multi-node setup, we must consider composing TP with other parallelism techniques, while keeping TP only within a single node. Due to its large communications overhead, TP is not recommended for PCIe linked GPUs.

    In Accelerate, the TP size is configured through tp_size in ParallelismConfig, whilst in Axolotl you can use the tensor_parallel_size config field.

    Recently, reasoning capabilities in LLMs resulted in sequence lengths skyrocketing as models use more and more tokens to solve complex tasks. To achieve this behaviour through fine-tuning, we need a way to train models on very large sequence lengths - which can sometimes reach up to a million tokens!

    In a recent development, since the attention operation in transformers scales quadratically with context length, this becomes impossible on a single GPU. For example, when fine-tuning a relatively small model such as Mistral-7B (which uses 32 attention heads), if we use a sequence length of 128k a single attention matrix will utilise 128k * 128k * 2 bytes * num_heads=32 = ~32GB * 32 = ~1TB of activations memory! Whilst this example is not realistic when using optimised attention implementations such as FlashAttention, it helps illustrate the growth in memory requirements from increasing the context length.

    With context parallelism (CP), we can shard the inputs across the sequence dimension, resulting in each device only processing a chunk of the full context and computing a smaller portion of the full, prohibitively large, attention matrix. To see how this works, recall that the attention computation is described by the equation: Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKT)V \text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}(QK^T)V Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKT)V.

    According to recent reports, where Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V are the query, key, and value matrices respectively. Each query vector (row, or input embedding) of Q Q Q must compute the attention scores against every key vector of K K K in the entire sequence to correctly apply the softmax normalisation. These attention scores are then weighted with all value vectors in V V V.

    Sources indicate that the crucial detail here lies in the fact that each row in Q Q Q can compute its attention score independently of one another, but each query vector still requires the full K K K and V V V matrices. In other words, given an input with sequence length $n$, we can expand our above attention equation as:.

    Attention(Q,K,V)1=softmax(Q1KT)VAttention(Q,K,V)2=softmax(Q2KT)V⋮Attention(Q,K,V)n=softmax(QnKT)V \begin{align} \text{Attention}(Q, K, V)_1 &= \text{softmax}(Q_1 K^T) V \\ \text{Attention}(Q, K, V)_2 &= \text{softmax}(Q_2 K^T) V \\ &\vdots \\ \text{Attention}(Q, K, V)_n &= \text{softmax}(Q_n K^T) V \end{align} Attention(Q,K,V)1​Attention(Q,K,V)2​Attention(Q,K,V)n​​=softmax(Q1​KT)V=softmax(Q2​KT)V⋮=softmax(Qn​KT)V​​.

    Sources indicate that where we denote each row of the query matrix as Q1,Q2,...,Qn Q_1, Q_2, ..., Q_n Q1​,Q2​,...,Qn​. This can be generalized as: Attention(Q,K,V)i=softmax(QiKT)V∀i∈{1,2,...,n} \text{Attention}(Q, K, V)_i = \text{softmax}(Q_i K^T) V \quad \forall i \in \{1, 2, ..., n\} Attention(Q,K,V)i​=softmax(Qi​KT)V∀i∈{1,2,...,n}.

    When we shard the inputs across devices, the resulting Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V matrices (computed from these input shards) are also automatically sharded along the sequence dimension - each GPU computes queries, keys, and values only for its portion of the sequence. For example, with a world size of W W W GPUs and sequence length n n n:.

    How do we ensure the attention is computed correctly? As established above, each device only needs its own shard of Q Q Q, but requires the full K K K and V V V matrices to compute the attention correctly. We can achieve this by using a technique called RingAttention, which works as follows:.

    In a recent development, accelerate enables this with the accelerator.maybe_context_parallel decorator, which is also showcased in the Accelerate example script. You can also learn more about how it works and its limitations in our CP concept guide.

    Similar to TP, in Accelerate the CP size is configured through cp_size in ParallelismConfig, whilst in Axolotl you can use the context_parallel_size config field.

    In the multi-node setting, data parallel techniques such as FSDP treat the entire network topology as if it existed along a single dimension. You may find this approach limiting for a variety of reasons:.

    Recent findings suggest that to try and address some of these problems, we can think of multi-node clusters as having a two-dimensional topology: fast intra-node communication between devices along one axis, and relatively slower inter-node communication along another axis. Let’s consider how we can compose the parallelism techniques we’ve introduced so far to take advantage of this.

    In a recent development, hybrid Sharded Data Parallelism (HSDP) is a kind of 2D parallelism which performs FSDP within a node, and DP across nodes - that is to say the model is replicated across each node, and sharded using FSDP within each node. This allows the greater communication overhead of FSDP to utilize the faster intra-node links, whilst DP minimises the slower inter-node communication overhead to a single gradient synchronisation step. You might consider this approach if you were facing problem 1 and wished to speed up training at the cost of increased memory usage.

    It’s important to note that we can freely configure the shape of our 2D network topology, as we aren’t constrained to the dimensions being aligned with physical node boundaries - you might apply FSDP across 2 nodes whilst replicating across groups of 2 nodes, which would result in lower memory usage but slower throughput, but still reduce the intra-node FSDP communication overhead by a factor of two. This is a knob we encourage you to tune to your specific hardware setup and fine-tuning needs.

    You can enable HSDP by defining both dp_shard_size and dp_replicate_size in Accelerate's ParallelismConfig or through Axolotl's config fields.

    Recent findings suggest that as we mentioned earlier, TP should be applied within a node to utilize the high-bandwidth intra-node communications, thus, combining TP and FSDP involves sharding the model across nodes using FSDP, and within a node using TP. To a certain degree, this potentially offers a neat solution to all three of the problems above: the latency costs from FSDP could be reduced by a factor of 8, layers that are too large to fit on a single device are now evenly distributed across devices, and since each TP group receives an identical batch of data, we can also reduce our global batch size by a factor of 8. However, if this remains insufficient, we are unable to increase the TP size across nodes and must consider an alternative approach.

    In Accelerate you can combine TP and FSDP by defining both dp_shard_size and tp_size in ParallelismConfig, whilst in Axolotl you can add both of the dp_shard_size and tensor_parallel_size config fields.

    This is a 2D parallelism strategy that combines FSDP and CP, and while this is not very commonly used as CP already combines with FSDP (more on why in the accelerate concept guide), it can be useful in some cases i.e. when requiring a large sequence length, consequently requiring a large cp_size. If this still doesn't fit into your memory budget, you can apply FSDP on top of this, further reducing the memory usage.

    In Accelerate you can combine CP and FSDP by defining both dp_shard_size and cp_size in ParallelismConfig, whilst in Axolotl you can add both of the dp_shard_size and context_parallel_size config fields.

    In a recent development, with a sufficiently large world size (note: while the minimum world size for 3D parallelism is 8, it is most effective at much larger scales), we can consider combining HSDP with TP which creates a hierarchy where DP first replicates the model across groups of nodes, FSDP then shards the model within each group, and TP splits individual layers within each node. You might consider this approach when facing all of the scaling constraints we mentioned above, as it provides the most flexibility to adapt to your specific training setup by making trade-offs between memory usage and throughput.

    In Accelerate you can combine HSDP and TP by defining all of dp_shard_size, dp_replicate_size, and tp_size in ParallelismConfig. Similarly in Axolotl you can add all of the dp_shard_size, dp_replicate_size, and tensor_parallel_size config fields.

    There are additional ways to combine multiple parallelisms which we haven't covered, such as 4D parallel using HSDP + TP + CP, but they operate very similarly to the techniques we've already covered. Most of all, we encourage you to play with different techniques and configurations - this is the best way to gain an intuition for the different ways in which you can make memory/throughput trade-offs.

    Below are some additional tips you may find useful when working in distributed settings:.

    Industry observers note that when using FSDP and working with models that are too large to fit in a single device, enabling both CPU RAM efficient loading and sharded state dict checkpointing technique is crucial. You can enable this through the cpu_ram_efficient_loading and state_dict_type parameters in Accelerate's FullyShardedDataParallelPlugin,.

    or through the cpu_ram_efficient_loading and state_dict_type config fields inside the fsdp_config in Axolotl:.

    The total batch size used during training plays an important factor in training stability, memory usage, and data throughput. When using DP and/or FSDP the effective batch size is calculated as:.

    effective_batch_size = micro_batch_size * gradient_accumulation_steps * dp_world_size.

    where dp_world_size = (dp_shard_size * dp_replicate_size) / tp_size. You can increase your batch size by increasing your total micro batch size or gradient accumulation steps in your training loop, or setting the micro_batch_size and gradient_accumulation_steps config fields in Axolotl, or increasing the total dp_world_size by adding more GPUs. As we mentioned above, this imposes a minimum total batch size of dp_world_size - when using pure DP/FSDP, this will be your total world size, and if this is too high the only way to decrease the total batch size is by introducing tensor parallelism. Finally, with a fixed number of GPUs and in memory-constrained scenarios, we recommend increasing gradient_accumulation_steps instead of micro_batch_size to achieve larger effective batch sizes, and vice-versa.

    Industry observers note that correspondingly, when your effective batch size increases due to introducing data parallelism, you should scale your learning rate to maintain training stability. Common approaches include linear scaling scaled_lr = base_lr * (effective_batch_size / base_batch_size) or square root scaling scaled_lr = base_lr * sqrt(effective_batch_size / base_batch_size).

    Industry observers note that when memory constraints persist even with parallelism strategies, gradient checkpointing can provide additional memory savings by trading compute for memory. During the forward pass, only a subset of activations are kept in memory (typically at transformer block boundaries), and intermediate activations are recomputed during the backward pass. This technique works seamlessly with all parallelism strategies covered above. In Accelerate, you can enable it by setting activation_checkpointing=true in FullyShardedDataParallelPlugin:.

    Note that gradient checkpointing typically increases training time by ~20-30% due to activation recomputation, but can reduce activation memory by 60-80%, making it particularly valuable when training very large models or using long sequence lengths.

    May I ask why is dp_world_size realted to tp_size?

    In a recent development, based on my understanding, it should be just dp_world_size = dp_shard_size * dp_replicate_size. Or am I missing some points here?

    May I ask why is dp_world_size realted to tp_size?

    Based on my understanding, it should be just dp_world_size = dp_shard_size * dp_replicate_size. Or am I missing some points here?

    According to recent reports, correct, I think we had a previous version where it was dp_world_size = world_size / tp_size, which we then changed to this version and forgot to remove the denominator. Will push a fix 🤗.

    How to use accelerate config with this feature？.

    Does this pipeline work for a custom model?

    Breaking: pgEdge Adds Jev to Triage PostgreSQL Alerts in AI DBA Workbench

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (911 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, pgEdge remarked on November 19 that its open-source AI DBA Workbench can use TypeSafe AI’s Jev to decide which PostgreSQL monitoring anomalies warrant an alert.
    • The change addresses a recurring problem for database teams: a metric can stray from its usual range without signaling an incident.
    • It has been revealed that the Workbench uses multiple stages to detect and assess anomalies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, pgEdge remarked on November 19 that its open-source AI DBA Workbench can use TypeSafe AI’s Jev to decide which PostgreSQL monitoring anomalies warrant an alert. Instead of asking a large language model to write its way through each candidate, the software can ask a decision model for a probability, then generate an explanation separately if an administrator requests one. Support is optional and is included in the publicly available Workbench 2.0 beta.

    The change addresses a recurring problem for database teams: a metric can stray from its usual range without signaling an incident. Treating every deviation as urgent creates noise, but dismissing too many leaves operators blind to real problems. pgEdge’s approach separates the frequent, narrow act of sorting signals from the less frequent work of explaining what operators should investigate.

    It has been revealed that the Workbench uses multiple stages to detect and assess anomalies. Its earlier stages examine monitoring data and identify departures from normal behavior. Only candidates that make it to the final classification stage go to the optional decision model. Jev returns a probability that the candidate reflects a real glitch rather than producing a written analysis. The software uses a configurable threshold to determine whether to surface or suppress the alert.

    Recent findings suggest that if a decision model cannot return a usable result, the Workbench falls back to a configured reasoning model. If no reasoning model is configured, or the fallback also fails, it raises the alert instead of quietly dismissing it. That behavior reduces the risk that a provider outage is mistaken for a healthy database. It does not remove the possibility of a model making a wrong classification when the provider is available.

    Industry observers note that the Workbench can also ask a separate reasoning model to explain a flagged anomaly on demand. The resulting explanation is generated from the stored monitoring data. It is not a transcript of how Jev reached its score, and it is not an independent confirmation of the cause. Database administrators still decide how to investigate and what to change.

    In pgEdge’s October test, Jev took about 200 milliseconds per classification at the median, compared with roughly three seconds for Claude Haiku 4.5. Using October 2026 prices, pgEdge estimated the cost of 1,000 classifications at about four cents for Jev and $1.93 for Haiku. That is a roughly 15-fold difference in median classification latency and about a 48-fold difference in estimated model cost. Neither comparison measures the total time or cost of monitoring a database, which also includes data collection, earlier detection stages and any follow-up explanations.

    Sources indicate that the test used 150 anomalies selected from 30 days of monitoring, split evenly between ones previously raised and ones previously suppressed. Jev matched 89% of the stored decisions, and a fresh Haiku run matched 91%. The two models agreed directly on 88% of candidates. Jev did not suppress any candidate that had been stored as an alert in that sample; where it disagreed with the stored decisions, it raised alerts that had previously been suppressed.

    It has been revealed that there were no human labels in that test, so the results show agreement with earlier model decisions, not whether the models were right. The balanced sample also does not establish how often an operator would see a false alarm in production. The extra alerts Jev raised could be useful signals or additional noise. Answering that question would require incident outcomes and human review.

    Teams monitoring many PostgreSQL instances have a reason to evaluate this design even if the exact savings vary. A probability score is enough to route some signals to an on-call queue, while a more expensive explanation is most valuable when a person needs to make a decision. Measuring how many alerts lead to action, how many real incidents are missed and how often operators request explanations would give teams a better basis for judging the trade-off than classification speed alone.

    The Workbench 2.0 beta also supports an OpenAI decision-model option, and pgEdge says it works with standard PostgreSQL 15 and later. The broader test for decision models is whether they can keep alert volumes manageable without hiding the incidents operators need to see. Lower latency and lower model costs are useful, but neither tells a database team whether it can trust the next alert.

    Breaking: Daily disruptive outages that ground planes and halt work – welcome to the new normal

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • NSA, Apple add to a week of high-profile network outages, largely attributed to 'routine maintenance'.
    • Another day, another disruptive network outage (or two) as government officials and organization execs scramble to assure an anxious populace that these are not coordinated cyberattacks – and security experts call this the latest normal.
    • A classified network that the US National Security Agency uses for internal communications, called NSANet, went offline on Tuesday in what the agency described as a “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.”.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    NSA, Apple add to a week of high-profile network outages, largely attributed to 'routine maintenance'.

    Another day, another disruptive network outage (or two) as government officials and organization execs scramble to assure an anxious populace that these are not coordinated cyberattacks – and security experts call this the latest normal.

    A classified network that the US National Security Agency uses for internal communications, called NSANet, went offline on Tuesday in what the agency described as a “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.”.

    In a recent development, “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues,” the NSA remarked in a statement following media reports about the outage. “NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.”.

    Around the same time, Apple owners began reporting problems across multiple services – including Apple Support, iCloud, the App Store, Apple Pay, and more – with Apple retail stores worldwide also reportedly experiencing disruptions that halted sales and in-person support.

    A day earlier, customers at major US banks including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, and US Bank reported service outages that Chase attributed to “a software bug in on-premise hardware systems - there is no evidence this is cyber-related.”.

    All of these high-profile outages followed last week’s US Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) order grounding all planes on Friday due to problems with copper wiring during an L3Harris network upgrade, and a Microsoft 365 outage on Thursday.

    Redmond later blamed the massive service disruption on a faulty software enhancement it pushed back in July.

    Despite the weekend respite from network outages, your humble vulture still had to field is-this-the-beginning-of-the-end questions from friends and family all day Saturday and Sunday, most of whom suspected Russia or China – maybe even Iran – caused the spate of downed systems and services.

    It has been revealed that A highly sophisticated, coordinated nation-state hack would be a much more exciting cause for the disruptions. The real culprit, however, appears to be aging, under-funded infrastructure, riddled with decades-old bugs and held together by digital sticks and glue.

    “As someone who started out as a hacker, I know how tempting it is to connect the dots when major systems fail one after another,” Remedio CEO Tal Kollender told The Register, adding that there’s “no credible public evidence that these outages were part of a coordinated cyberattack,” and most have been attributed to technical failures.

    Industry observers note that “What concerns me more is what these incidents reveal about the fragility of our digital infrastructure. We've built an interconnected world on layers of aging systems, complex configurations, and dependencies that organizations don't always fully understand. A single misconfiguration, failed enhancement, or broken dependency can create disruption on a massive scale, even without an attacker,” Kollender stated. “The uncomfortable reality I think we're grappling with is that attackers don't always have to break our systems. Sometimes, our systems are already capable of breaking on their own.”.

    For people who couldn’t withdraw money from their bank, board a flight, or use email at work on Friday, “the disruption was real regardless of the cause,” she said.

    “Cybersecurity has spent decades investing in detecting threats, identifying vulnerabilities, and generating reports,” according to Kollender. “Yet we still allow for these preventable weaknesses and configurations that can bring entire systems down.”.

    Cynthia Kaiser, senior VP of Halcyon’s Ransomware Research Center and former deputy director of the FBI’s Cyber Division, told The Reg that the recent disruptions show “how deeply interconnected our digital infrastructure has become, and how a single technical failure or software enhancement can cascade with outsized effects across critical systems.”.

    Then we go and add AI to this already delicate balance, and everything essentially blows up.

    AI-assisted bug hunting and exploit development has surfaced more than 100,000 CVEs so far this year, with Microsoft’s Patch Tuesday disclosing more than 1,000 vulnerabilities in each of the past two months. AI has also shrunk the elapsed time between the public release of a security patch and attackers developing working exploits.

    Recent findings suggest that “We are in an era where AI is accelerating the discovery of legacy software flaws, forcing organizations to race to patch vulnerabilities before adversaries can exploit them, which inevitably creates friction and disruptions,” Kaiser stated. “Even when an outage isn’t caused by a cyberattack, these moments of operational distraction leave dangerous gaps open for threat actors and opportunists to take advantage of, making it crucial for both institutions and everyday individuals to remain on high alert against social engineering and unsolicited outreach.”.

    Even when attackers aren’t using AI to facilitate intrusions, the technology itself has become a source of risk to organizations.

    It has been revealed that “Autonomous agents can execute actions, change configurations, access sensitive information, and interact with critical systems at machine speed,” Kollender remarked. “When those systems lack proper governance and safeguards, a mistake can develop just as rapidly as an attack.

    According to recent reports, former US Department of Defense network exploitation and vulnerability analyst Mike Wiacek, when asked if these regular system outages are the fresh normal, told us: “The brutal truth is yes. Especially in the AI world that we live in.”.

    After the DoD, Wiacek founded Google’s Threat Analysis Group. He's since founded Stairwell, a threat-intel firm he serves as chief technology officer.

    “The idea that we are going to patch ourselves to security is, dare I say, an antiquated concept,” he told The Register.

    One of Stairwell’s engineers was doing regular, daily software development tasks on an open source library with Anthropic’s Claude Mythos, and the model told the engineer about a buffer-overflow vulnerability in the code.

    According to recent reports, “We weren't even looking for it,” Wiacek said. “It found a vulnerability in open source software by accident. You used to need specialized bug hunters and really, really technical security folks to discover and develop vulnerabilities and exploits. Now, it’s almost too easy to do it.”.

    This newly introduced reality, he stated, necessitates a total rethink of how we build and maintain digital infrastructure.

    Sources indicate that “How do we get to a world where we assume compromised by default, and continuously recompromised, and then develop the architectures and the systems necessary to make what was the expense of incident-response investigation really fast and cheap? Because we will not be able to patch our way out of it.”.

    Recent findings suggest that it requires vulnerability managers and system administrators to patch as soon as software updates become available. But from an engineering perspective, it also means building in “as many fail-safes as possible,” Wiacek stated.

    It has been revealed that “An elevator doesn't have just one cable hoisting it,” he continued. “There's a lot of redundancy in those systems. Enterprises and organizations and governments haven't really had to operate like that. But that's going to be the newly introduced norm, whether we want it to be or not. Pandora's box is opened, and it's not going to go back inside.” ®.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that seven vulnerabilities have been discovered in Ruby’s regular expression engine and in the case conversion of strings. We are aware of PoCs that prove some of them can be used to trigger remote code execution. We have released Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 to fix them. We strongly recommend upgrading.

    CVE identifiers have been requested for these vulnerabilities but have not been assigned yet, so this advisory refers to them by their GitHub Security Advisory (GHSA) identifiers.

    Sources indicate that ruby has a one-byte heap-based buffer overflow in the case conversion of strings. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios.

    Recent findings suggest that ruby has a double free in its regular expression engine. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios.

    Recent findings suggest that ruby has an integer overflow in the case conversion of strings, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios.

    Sources indicate that ruby has an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine. Matching against a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that use attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can lead to memory corruption in an attacker-controlled way.

    Ruby has an integer overflow in its regular expression engine, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios.

    Ruby has a heap-based buffer overflow in Regexp#to_s. Converting a crafted regular expression to a string may allow information disclosure or remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios.

    Ruby has an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine. Matching a crafted string may disclose memory contents or crash the process.

    We strongly recommend upgrading to Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 or 3.3.14.

    It has been revealed that ruby 3.3 is in the security maintenance phase. Ruby 3.2 and earlier have reached their end of life and will not receive these fixes.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Emerson revealed a collaboration with Databricks on November 19, 2026 to make contextualized industrial operating data available inside the Databricks Data + AI Platform, giving industrial companies a route to use plant information in analytics, AI applications and agents.
    • Recent findings suggest that native access to AspenTech Inmation OT Data Fabric is the mechanism.
    • The collaboration targets a specific industrial AI problem: plant, asset and operational data must retain its context when used with enterprise systems.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Emerson revealed a collaboration with Databricks on November 19, 2026 to make contextualized industrial operating data available inside the Databricks Data + AI Platform, giving industrial companies a route to use plant information in analytics, AI applications and agents.

    Recent findings suggest that native access to AspenTech Inmation OT Data Fabric is the mechanism. Customers will be able to combine business data with real-time, historical and contextualized industrial data managed by Inmation, and to access the AspenTech AVA AI platform within Databricks. The customer access described in the announcement is forthcoming.

    The collaboration targets a specific industrial AI problem: plant, asset and operational data must retain its context when used with enterprise systems. Emerson identifies that requirement as a barrier to closing the IT/OT gap, the divide between information technology and operational technology, and as a constraint on applying AI to real operating conditions.

    “By bringing contextualized OT data into Databricks, we are helping customers turn trusted industrial data into a governed foundation for AI applications that can improve performance across operations and the business,” noted Claudio Fayad, chief technology officer at Emerson’s Aspen Technology business.

    It has been revealed that aspenTech’s Inmation capability overview describes a fabric that unifies OT data into a persistent, enterprise-wide structure and continuously adds context to produce AI-ready information. It connects plants, assets and applications across edge, cloud and on-premises environments to create a real-time, query-ready operational picture that can scale from one site to a global enterprise. Centralized governance, role-based access and auditability are designed to support secure decision-making and regulatory compliance in sectors including chemicals, energy and life sciences.

    The reuse of that contextualized layer is central to the collaboration’s potential value. Emerson states Inmation reduces the need to integrate, contextualize and prepare OT data separately for each use case, potentially shortening time-to-value for predictive maintenance and performance optimization. For industrial AI teams, the same operational context could support multiple workflows instead of requiring a fresh data-preparation exercise for every model or agent.

    General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Theregister ↗ Open Full Page

    Oracle reveals fix-this-ASAP-grade Java4Shell bug that allows attacks on many third-party apps

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (702 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Attackers can crash the JVM or achieve unauthenticated RCE.
    • The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged Java users to immediately patch a high-severity flaw in the software, which attackers can use to crash the Java virtual machine or achieve unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE).
    • Oracle revealed the flaw in its monthly patch dump for November, which offers 655 patches, 62 of them rated critical, affecting 62 products.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Attackers can crash the JVM or achieve unauthenticated RCE.

    The United States Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged Java users to immediately patch a high-severity flaw in the software, which attackers can use to crash the Java virtual machine or achieve unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE).

    Oracle revealed the flaw in its monthly patch dump for November, which offers 655 patches, 62 of them rated critical, affecting 62 products.

    Several of the flaws are rated more dangerous than the Java problem, CVE-2026-114938, which Big Red didn’t single out as worthy of special attention despite CISA’s warning.

    The cyber-agency’s decision seems apt because vulnerability research and red teaming outfit Calif.io, which discovered the flaw, used its X account to claim news of the problem had leaked before public disclosure and the release of Oracle's fixes.

    By then, Calif had already tested the flaw, which it named “Java4Shell,” and found applications including Keycloak, Atlassian’s Jira and Confluence, Jenkins, Apache Kafka Broker, and Elasticsearch are susceptible to RCE.

    Calif, which also helped to find the PHP2Shell flaw, says the flaw is a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder.

    In a recent development, “Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages,” the manufacturer explained. “To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once.”.

    “We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:”.

    Calif applied the CVSS 4.0 bug-rating scheme and gave the flaw a critical-rated score of 9.2/10.

    Infosec outfit SentinelOne’s analysis suggests the flaw “sits in the Java standard library, so exploit traffic is specific to each application.”.

    Sources indicate that “Any Base64 value an application passes to java.util.Base64.Decoder can carry the payload, including HTTP Basic credentials, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, and MIME encoded words. In default configurations of the affected applications listed above, attackers can reach this code path prior to authentication.”.

    Cisco’s Talos security team pointed out that the flaw is present in OpenJDK Java versions 17.0.6 and later running on x86-64 CPUs with AVX-512 VBMI (Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions) support enabled.

    “These vulnerabilities have already been tested against a suite of Java applications with success, but the attack surface is likely much larger as additional targets are tested and confirmed,” Talos advised.

    Cisco’s infosec experts urged adoption of the fixed versions of Java Oracle posted on Tuesday but noted it is possible to mitigate the flaw on x86-64 machines by starting the JVM with support for AVX-512 disabled.

    Akamai’s Chief Information Security Architect Jan Schaumann, writing on the Openwall project’s mailing list, expressed a little discomfort with Calif’s work.

    “Calif.io set their priorities on publicity-maxxing, it seems,” he wrote, pointing out that the flaw-finding firm’s announcement of Java4Shell opens by stating “After we disclosed PHP2Shell, we realized many people didn't know what PHP was. So we decided to go after something a little more familiar: Java.”.

    Talos’s analysis of Java4Shell includes the interesting observation that it “has not observed in-the-wild exploitation of this vulnerability yet. However, we anticipate probing attempts may pick up soon after public disclosure.”.

    That second sentence perhaps supports Calif’s assertion that news of the flaw leaked before disclosure.

    Java4Shell deserves a place high up on patch priority lists.

    So do the six 10.10 flaws Oracle reported, three in its Access Manager product, one in the Oracle Platform Security for Java, another in the WebLogic Server, and one in Business Intelligence Enterprise Edition.

    Substantial Red also repaired five 9.9-rated bugs, in Oracle Text, Hyperion, RDBMS, and Autovue.

    The November patch dump also includes 28 flaws rated 9.8/10.

    By Tenable Security’s count, 249 of the patches are for high severity bugs. Oracle’s Hyperion enterprise performance management accounts for 267 of the bugs.

    Such is life in the age of AI-powered flaw finders – which Calif says burned through just $200 worth of tokens to find Java4Shell. ®.

    🇵🇭 FilBench - Can LLMs Understand and Generate Filipino?

    📅 12 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into our lives, it becomes crucial to assess whether they reflect the nuances and capabilities of specific language communities.
    • That’s why we developed FilBench: a comprehensive evaluation suite to assess the capabilities of LLMs for Tagalog, Filipino (the standardized form of Tagalog), and Cebuano, on fluency, linguistic and translation abilities, as well as specific cultural knowledge.
    • We used it to evaluate 20+ state-of-the-art LLMs on FilBench, providing a comprehensive assessment of their performance in Philippine languages:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into our lives, it becomes crucial to assess whether they reflect the nuances and capabilities of specific language communities. For example, Filipinos are among the most active ChatGPT owners globally, ranking fourth in ChatGPT traffic (behind the United States, India, and Brazil [1] [2]), but despite this strong usage, we lack a clear understanding of how LLMs perform for their languages, such as Tagalog and Cebuano. Most of the existing evidence is anecdotal, such as screenshots of ChatGPT responding in Filipino as proof that it is fluent. What we need instead is a systematic evaluation of LLM capabilities in Philippine languages.

    That’s why we developed FilBench: a comprehensive evaluation suite to assess the capabilities of LLMs for Tagalog, Filipino (the standardized form of Tagalog), and Cebuano, on fluency, linguistic and translation abilities, as well as specific cultural knowledge.

    We used it to evaluate 20+ state-of-the-art LLMs on FilBench, providing a comprehensive assessment of their performance in Philippine languages:.

    In a recent development, the FilBench evaluation suite contains four major categories–Cultural Knowledge, Classical NLP, Reading Comprehension, and Generation–divided into 12 tasks. For example, the Classical NLP category includes tasks such as sentiment analysis, whereas Generation tasks include different aspects of translation. In order to ensure that these categories reflect the priorities and trends in NLP research and usage, we curate them based on a historical survey of NLP research on Philippine languages from 2006 to early 2024. (Most of these categories exclusively contain non-translated content to ensure faithfulness to the natural use of Philippine languages.).

    Sources indicate that each of these categories provides an aggregated metric. To create a single representative score, we compute the weighted average based on the number of examples in each category, which we call the FilBench Score.

    According to recent reports, to simplify usage and set up, we built FilBench on top of Lighteval, an all-in-one framework for LLM evaluation. For language-specific evaluation, we first defined translation pairs from English to Tagalog (or Cebuano) for common terms used in evaluation such as "yes" (oo), "no" (hindi), and "true" (totoo) among others. Then, we used the provided templates to implement custom tasks for the capabilities we care about.

    FilBench is now available as a set of community tasks in the official Lighteval repository!

    By evaluating several LLMs on FilBench, we uncovered several insights into how they perform in Filipino.

    Recent findings suggest that in the past few years, we have seen an increase in region-specific LLMs that target Southeast Asian languages (SEA-specific), such as SEA-LION and SeaLLM. These are open-weight LLMs that you can freely download from HuggingFace. We find that SEA-specific LLMs are often the most parameter-efficient for our languages, achieving the highest FilBench scores compared to other models of their size. However, the best SEA-specific model is still outperformed by closed-source LLMs like GPT-4o.

    It has been revealed that building region-specific LLMs still makes sense, as we observe performance gains of 2-3% when continuously fine-tuning a base LLM with SEA-specific instruction-tuning data. This suggests that efforts to curate Filipino/SEA-specific training data for fine-tuning remain relevant, as they can lead to better performance on FilBench.

    We also observe that across the four categories on FilBench, most models struggle with Generation capabilities. Upon inspecting failure modes in Generation, we find that these include cases where the model fails to follow translation instructions, generates overly verbose texts, or hallucinates another language instead of Tagalog or Cebuano.

    Recent findings suggest that the Philippines tends to have limited internet infrastructure and lower average incomes [3], necessitating accessible LLMs that are cost- and compute-efficient. Through FilBench, we were able to identify LLMs that are on the Pareto frontier of efficiency.

    In general, we find that open-weight LLMs, i.e., models that you can freely download from HuggingFace, are way cheaper than commercial models without sacrificing their performance. If you want an alternative to GPT-4o for your Filipino language tasks, then try Llama 4 Maverick!

    We also make this information available in the HuggingFace space of the FilBench leaderboard.

    Recent findings suggest that we hope that FilBench provides deeper insights into LLM capabilities for Philippine languages and serves as a catalyst for advancing Filipino NLP research and development. The FilBench evaluation suite is built on top of Hugging Face's lighteval, allowing LLM developers to easily evaluate their models on our benchmark. For more information, please visit the links below:.

    The authors would like to thank Cohere Labs for providing credits through the Cohere Research Grant to run the Aya model series, and Together AI for additional computational credits for running several open models. We also acknowledge the Hugging Face team, particularly the OpenEvals team (Clémentine Fourrier and Nathan Habib) and Daniel van Strien, for their support in publishing this blog post.

    If you are evaluating on FilBench, please cite our work:.

    #57608. Windows 11 collects data on which coding agents and dev tools you use

    📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1242 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Xusheng ↗ Open Full Page

    Windows 11 collects data on which coding agents and dev tools you use

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1242 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Xusheng

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that I recently asked AI to help me look through the latest Windows binaries for undocumented features and functionality.
    • Why would a Windows system DLL need a list of coding agents and developer tools?
    • The names were in MissionControlAggregator.dll.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that I recently asked AI to help me look through the latest Windows binaries for undocumented features and functionality. Among the leads it turned up, one list immediately caught my attention: coding agents such as codex.exe, claude.exe, copilot.exe, and cursor.exe, alongside familiar developer tools such as python.exe, dotnet.exe, gcc.exe, and code.exe.

    Why would a Windows system DLL need a list of coding agents and developer tools?

    The names were in MissionControlAggregator.dll. I asked the agent to follow the references and dig into what the DLL actually does. That led from a handful of string comparisons to a running Windows component that records which coding agents and developer tools have been used, saves that information locally, and reports it to Windows Diagnostics. And unless you have opted out of the “optional” diagnostic data (which is enabled by default), the data is uploaded to Microsoft.

    Industry observers note that I shared the initial finding on X. This post includes more details about the investigation behind it.

    Opening the DLL in Binary Ninja made the first lead easy to see. These were explicit executable names embedded in a Windows component:.

    Following the references highlighted that the names were used in comparisons. There are four CLI-agent slots checking copilot.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe, and agy.exe, with extensionless equivalents on the WSL route. Five desktop-agent slots check github.exe, claude.exe, codex.exe, cursor.exe, and antigravity.exe.

    Here is one of the comparisons against codex.exe:.

    Recent findings suggest that the compiler-generated C++ names are unwieldy, so I will call these functions executable-name matchers. For reference, one related matcher is std::_Func_impl_no_alloc<, bool, std::basic_string_view> const&, Microsoft::Diagnostics::MissionControlAggregator::Utils::AppType>::_Do_call. The screenshot reveals another lambda instantiation performing the same kind of name comparison.

    The feature guarding the new agent checks has a particularly direct name: CLICodingAgentUsage, feature ID 62580080.

    Industry observers note that and the list extends beyond AI agents. The same component checks for node.exe, python.exe, dotnet.exe, gcc.exe, clang.exe, gdb.exe, javac.exe, devenv.exe, and code.exe, among others. Those checks feed broader developer-tool categories. Some of these checks also verify the publisher: the Node.js slot expects Node.js Foundation, Python expects Python Software Foundation, and the .NET and Visual Studio slots expect Microsoft Corporation. The compiler/debugger group containing GCC and Clang has no additional publisher check in this path.

    For Windows programs, it consumes KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary and Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary. These provide application identities that its handlers parse and pass to the matchers. For WSL, it consumes Microsoft.Windows.Lxss.Manager.Exec and ExecCritical, using the imageName field. A regular Windows codex.exe can therefore reach the CLI-agent checks through the app-state summary route; this is not limited to Linux programs running inside WSL.

    The relevant flow looks like this:.

    A successful match sets a slot in the aggregator’s state. Later, ReportCohorts<12,4,5> turns those slots into bitsets and emits a report named Segments.SubCohorts. The numbers correspond to twelve broader tool categories, four CLI agents, and five desktop agents.

    Sources indicate that ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) is the mechanism carrying that report. In this case, it is a self-describing TraceLogging event. Rather than writing the executable names into every report, the component assigns each category a bit. A set Codex bit means the matching tool was observed during the reporting window.

    The source events also include runtime, time in focus, interaction counters, and resource usage. This component appears to discard those details and record only a bitmap of which agents were observed. The report’s timestamps describe the collection window, not how long each agent was used.

    Although I found no prompt text or source code in this report, collecting which agents and developer tools someone uses already has significant privacy implications.

    Sources indicate that strings and code are a useful lead, but I wanted to see the component running. I checked my Parallels Windows 11 ARM64 VM, build 26200.9974. Its MissionControlAggregator.dll was version 10.0.26100.9818, and CLICodingAgentUsage was already enabled as a service experiment. I had not manually enabled the feature.

    Recent findings suggest that diagTrack, the Connected User Experiences and Telemetry service, was also already running with its startup type set to Automatic. It starts a separate AggregatorHost.exe process, and that process loads the DLL. The following administrative PowerShell commands show the service, its child process, and the loaded module:.

    The process IDs connect the pieces: DiagTrack runs in process 10148, which is the parent of AggregatorHost.exe, process 1500; the module listing places MissionControlAggregator.dll inside that child.

    To test the finding in practice, I copied cmd.exe to a file named codex.exe and ran it in the interactive Windows session. The name alone was enough for the component to recognize it as Codex.

    I captured an AppStateChangeSummary for the running process from the KernelProcess provider ({2839ff94-8f12-4e1b-82e3-af7af77a450f}), with LaunchCount=1 and TerminateCount=0. The aggregator’s saved state contained the value 2 in CLI slot 2, the Codex slot. A separate run without an additional ETW trace also set that slot, confirming that detection worked through Windows’ existing diagnostic collection.

    Recent findings suggest that the report normally follows a roughly daily boundary. To capture it immediately, I temporarily moved the saved reporting-window start 25 hours into the past and restarted DiagTrack with a trace listening for the aggregator. The resulting Segments.SubCohorts event contained:.

    The value 4 is 1 << 2: the Codex CLI bit. The name had made it through the input summary, the matcher, the persisted state, and the emitted report.

    Recent findings suggest that I also tested the developer-tool path separately, using a copy of cmd.exe named gcc.exe. It set developer-tool slot 3. With optional diagnostic data allowed, I found the resulting Segments.SubCohorts event in DiagTrack’s upload queue with SubCohorts: [8] (1 << 3). This is the compiler/debugger category shared by GCC, Clang, and related tools, rather than a separate bit for each executable.

    An ETW event by itself would not establish that anything leaves the machine. ETW is used for plenty of local diagnostics. The more revealing question was who was listening to this particular report.

    The first subscription, for KernelProcess, had MatchAnyKeyword=0x400000000002, which includes the summary’s 0x400000000000 keyword. The second, for Microsoft.Windows.MissionControlAggregator, had MatchAnyKeyword=0xe00000000000, which includes the report’s 0x800000000000 keyword. Both had level 255.

    It has been revealed that the subscription demonstrated where the report could go. To check whether Windows actually queued it for transmission, I inspected DiagTrack’s EventStore.db and decompressed the JSON batches in its AsimovEvents table. This revealed an important condition: the agent-usage report is treated as optional diagnostic data.

    When optional diagnostic data is allowed (enabled by default in the US setup I tested), Windows queues the coding-agent usage report for upload to Microsoft. I verified this by finding the agent event itself in DiagTrack’s upload queue:.

    It has been revealed that I checked this with a clean installation of Windows 11 Home ARM64 using the latest official ISO, with the region set to the United States. Before changing any privacy settings, the Diagnostic data toggle was already enabled and labeled Include Optional. After completing setup with those defaults, AllowTelemetry was 3, confirming that optional diagnostic data was enabled.

    Optional diagnostic data is therefore enabled by default, at least in the US setup I tested. If you did not opt out of it during installation or disable optional diagnostic data later, it is still enabled and your coding agent usage data is being uploaded. You can decline optional diagnostics during setup or turn off Send optional diagnostic data later under Settings → Privacy & security → Diagnostics & feedback. Microsoft’s diagnostics and privacy guide explains how to change it.

    Latest Update: Reply.io Releases an Open-Source AI Agent Harness for Sales Outreach

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (788 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that reply.io has announced Jason Harness, an open-source tool that turns general-purpose AI agents into a workspace for sales outreach.
    • It has been revealed that jason Harness is separate from Reply’s managed Jason AI sales development representative.
    • Recent findings suggest that reply describes nine roles covering campaign management, planning, research, writing, personalization, critique, response handling, analytics and deliverability.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that reply.io has announced Jason Harness, an open-source tool that turns general-purpose AI agents into a workspace for sales outreach. Announced publicly on November 17, the alpha release gives tools such as Claude Code or OpenAI Codex distinct roles for researching prospects, planning follow-ups and drafting messages. The tool keeps campaign state on the operator’s computer and leaves delivery to an external sending service. Reply claims a person must approve messages before they go out.

    It has been revealed that jason Harness is separate from Reply’s managed Jason AI sales development representative. It does not ship with its own model. Instead, it packages the instructions, campaign records and approval steps that an existing agent needs to pick up a campaign across sessions. Reply’s changelog dates the opening of the complete runtime source to November 1, ahead of the broader public launch.

    Recent findings suggest that reply describes nine roles covering campaign management, planning, research, writing, personalization, critique, response handling, analytics and deliverability. That designation does not necessarily mean nine different models are running. The roles define distinct jobs for the host agent. A planner can propose a sequence, a researcher can gather context, and a critic can flag an unsupported claim before a draft goes to a human reviewer.

    Sources indicate that keeping campaign state outside the chat addresses a practical limitation of general-purpose assistants. A seller who starts a fresh conversation still needs to know which pitch a prospect saw, what the prospect said in response and whether a colleague already approved a follow-up. Reply describes storing campaigns, contacts and history in a local database, with rules and memory in local files. The code for the runtime and its extension system is available under the MIT license, according to Reply’s open-source documentation.

    Local storage does not mean everything runs offline. The underlying agent processes requests according to its own provider and strategy. Sending takes place through Reply or another provider connected through an extension, and connected services may receive the data they need to perform a task. Any organization evaluating the alpha would need to trace what goes to each service rather than treating a locally stored database as a blanket privacy guarantee.

    Recent findings suggest that moving drafting and research into the same workspace may reduce context switching. It does not remove the cost of reviewing what the AI produces. A message can sound specific while relying on an outdated job title or an unsupported claim about the recipient’s tech giant. The reviewer also needs to know whether someone opted out, whether the proposed follow-up repeats an earlier touch and whether the send still fits the original campaign brief. An approval step is more useful when it makes those facts visible alongside the draft.

    The open-source release makes it possible to inspect and adapt the tool, but free access to the code is not the same as free outreach. AI subscriptions may have usage limits, and sending accounts or prospect data can carry separate costs. Reply has described the product as an alpha; its launch material does not provide independently validated results for deliverability, qualified replies or meetings compared with a conventional workflow.

    The clearest test is whether the harness can reduce time spent reconstructing campaign context without increasing the time needed to correct it. Teams comparing the tool with an existing workflow could look at review time per message, how often drafts are rejected for inaccurate claims and whether replies are passed back to the right person. Those measures would say more about the tool’s value than the number of roles it can assign.
