    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Prepares to unleash full wrath of Digital Services Act over Chinese e-tailer's alleged sales of illegal products.
    • Chinese e-tailer Temu has a reputation for selling low-quality knockoff products at low prices made possible through use of forced labor.
    • The Commission issued that finding yesterday, accusing Temu of breaching its Digital Services Act (DSA) obligation to operate serious measures that mitigate the risk of illegal products being offered on its platform.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Prepares to unleash full wrath of Digital Services Act over Chinese e-tailer's alleged sales of illegal products.

    Chinese e-tailer Temu has a reputation for selling low-quality knockoff products at low prices made possible through use of forced labor. Now, the European Commission has made a preliminary finding that the firm also runs a low-quality compliance regime that means it’s not meeting its regulatory obligations.

    The Commission issued that finding yesterday, accusing Temu of breaching its Digital Services Act (DSA) obligation to operate serious measures that mitigate the risk of illegal products being offered on its platform.

    Temu is a marketplace that allows third parties to sell on its platform, a model that doesn’t relieve it of responsibility for the goods available on its site and apps.

    Eurocrats therefore have beef with Temu over several matters, including:.

    Requiring sellers who use the platform to test the quality of “only a very small share of products,” and then often not bothering to check the reports;.

    Not doing enough to prioritize checks of products in known high risk categories, like toys and cosmetics, then not following up on those checks;.

    Running a moderation system that mostly considers whether products comply with Temu’s terms and conditions, rather than product safety;.

    Not hiring enough human moderators to keep pace with growth in listings on Temu;.

    When it finds stores selling non-compliant goods, Temu acts against that store – but not the trader who may sell the same products in multiple stores;.

    Allowing stores to commit many serious infringements, including selling products that fail safety checks, before suspending their stores.

    A Temu spokesperson told The Register the manufacturer respectfully disagrees with the EC's findings.

    Recent findings suggest that "Temu invests significantly in compliance infrastructure and human expertise and implements a suite of control measures that effectively mitigate illegal product risks with a consistently low incidence of problematic products," the spokesperson mentioned. "We will review and respond to the preliminary findings carefully and will continue to engage constructively with the Commission. We are confident that we will reach an amicable resolution of the matter that fully addresses the Commission's remaining concerns.".

    Industry observers note that the EC has already tangled with Temu. In 2024 Eurocrats investigated its risk assessment processes. In May 2026, Eurocrats found Temu’s processes inadequate and levied a €200 million fine.

    Brussels also sent a €550 million fine to another Chinese e-tailer, Alibaba, for not doing enough to stop the sale of dangerous goods.

    This announcement of fresh action against Temu invoked Article 35 of the Digital Services Act, the sweeping regulation of online businesses under which the EU could fine Temu up to six percent of its global revenue and order corrective actions.

    Industry observers note that europe is concerned that the low prices Chinese e-tailers charge are enabled by forced labor and ignoring dangerous products. EC officials believe those practices mean the likes of Temu don’t compete on a level playing field with continental retailers. The bloc has tried to make life harder for Chinese e-commerce outfits by charging a temporary €3 customs duty for every shipment sent from outside the EU and valued at under €150. Google recently revealed that newly introduced charge saw its advertising revenue from Asian customers fall.

    Beijing sees its e-tail giants Temu, Shein, and Alibaba as crucial actors in its strategy to grow China’s exports and overall economy, which hasn’t performed strongly in recent years. Indeed, Chinese consumers have slowed their discretionary spending to the extent that Beijing last year subsidized purchases of consumer electronics – including Apple products –  to keep cash registers ticking over. ®.

    Industry News: Postel Awardee Dave Täht Made Every Millisecond Count

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that dave Täht understood the Internet.
    • It has been revealed that this drive stemmed from his visceral understanding that for change to be possible, people need to both understand and care about the stakes of inaction.
    • According to recent reports, täht saw every dropped video call, every slow loading page, and every frozen progress-bar—all symptoms of what’s known as bufferbloat—as a barrier to Internet connectivity.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that dave Täht understood the Internet. And it was key to him that everyone else understand it, too. Which is why he spent decades going to ambitious and creative lengths to explain it. To regulators, to standard setting bodies, to the most influential tech companies in the world, to the next generation of Internet leaders, and to absolutely anyone who would ask him about it.

    It has been revealed that this drive stemmed from his visceral understanding that for change to be possible, people need to both understand and care about the stakes of inaction. And what he desperately wanted to change was the Internet. Specifically, people’s ability to use it meaningfully.

    According to recent reports, täht saw every dropped video call, every slow loading page, and every frozen progress-bar—all symptoms of what’s known as bufferbloat—as a barrier to Internet connectivity. Bufferbloat is the time that data spends stuck in the hardware responsible for forwarding traffic. Täht went about identifying and advocating for solutions to that congestion, with the goal of delivering the full promise of the Internet to people. And also, he joked, so that he could jam remotely with his drummer who kept missing band practice.

    Getting people to care about bufferbloat wasn’t always an easy pitch. Latency is the time it takes for data to travel across a network from one point to another. The lower the latency, the more seamless the experience, while high latency renders the network effectively unusable. Täht was adamant that latency, far more so than bandwidth, determined how much time people spent waiting for a page to load.

    Recent findings suggest that dave’s communication style is the stuff of Internet lore. “He did not seek to monetize his performance work but simply applied himself passionately and articulately to solving problems,” remembers Internet pioneer and one of the Internet Society’s founders, Vint Cerf. Täht famously galvanized a conference roomful of people to enact traffic moving through the network, wrote songs about open-source software, and relentlessly pushed regulators and companies to take action.

    Industry observers note that just as Jon Postel did, Täht unfortunately passed away prematurely. And, like Postel, Täht died having left the kind of mark on the world that is rare for any one person to accomplish.

    Täht’s legacy can be found in community hubs in Nicaragua, where he worked to expand connectivity, and first discovered the urgency of solving bufferbloat. It can be found in every lag-free video call with a loved one. It can be found in outer space—Täht helped Starlink solve its latency challenges. And it can be found in the countless people he mentored and befriended over the years, who will not stop until bufferbloat stops getting in the way of band practice. “We are in milliseconds territory now,” remarked Borsik. “But for the future we will need microseconds.”.

    As much as Täht loved the Internet, and as crucial as it was for him that all of us understand and can access it, he didn’t just sing about open-source, he sang about how we all need to log off and go outside, too.

    Sources indicate that täht is remembered as a brilliant, passionate engineer. A generous friend. And an Internet troubadour.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, AI agents are becoming common in the teams that keep enterprise software running, but the tools to monitor what those agents decide and do lag behind.
    • Sources indicate that the results are based on an online survey Dynatrace commissioned in August 2026 of 1,202 enterprise technology leaders in 12 countries.
    • The survey’s adoption figure describes a particular part of enterprise technology: monitoring software and running IT systems.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, AI agents are becoming common in the teams that keep enterprise software running, but the tools to monitor what those agents decide and do lag behind. In its State of Observability 2026 findings, published November 10, Dynatrace noted 87% of surveyed technology leaders reported moderate or extensive use of AI agents for observability and IT operations. Only 27% say they presently address visibility into agent decisions and actions.

    Sources indicate that the results are based on an online survey Dynatrace commissioned in August 2026 of 1,202 enterprise technology leaders in 12 countries. They describe what respondents report about their own organizations, not what researchers independently verified in production. Dynatrace sells observability software, so the report is best read as a snapshot of the challenges its survey respondents describe, not a census of enterprise AI use.

    The survey’s adoption figure describes a particular part of enterprise technology: monitoring software and running IT systems. It does not mean 87% of companies have agents authorized to make consequential decisions on their own. One organization might use an agent to summarize an incident and propose a response for an engineer to review. Another might allow an agent to carry out a predefined action inside a narrow part of its infrastructure. Both can report using agents, even though the agents have very different responsibilities.

    Respondents estimated that people still verify an average of 66% of AI-powered decisions. Separately, 12% reported fully autonomous operations, while 44% said they were targeting that level within five years. That makes the latter figure a measure of ambition, not a forecast. The survey also found that integration complexity was the most frequently cited barrier to autonomy, at 31%, alongside challenges such as skills, oversight and data quality.

    Recent findings suggest that standard system monitoring can tell an engineer that a service responded and how long it took. That does not reveal whether an agent selected an appropriate action or whether the action resolved the underlying incident. For instance, if an agent recommends restarting a service, a useful record would show which alerts informed the recommendation, whether a person approved it, and what happened to the service afterward. Engineers could then check whether the restart helped or merely coincided with recovery.

    Dynatrace found that 43% considered visibility into agent decisions an notable observability requirement, compared with 27% that reported addressing it. That gap is not evidence that everyone else has no logs. It is a comparison between what respondents regarded as important and what they mentioned their organizations were addressing.

    In a recent development, costs add another dimension. Some 81% reported higher compute and infrastructure spending from AI workloads, and 77% said they needed better visibility into how costs are allocated. A tool that measures how long operators spend on an incident without capturing the extra resources an agent consumes can make the automation look cheaper than it is. Connecting the two measures allows teams to compare the cost of different approaches to the same work.

    In a recent development, in a November 17 follow-up, Dynatrace outlined a progression from gathering evidence to recommending actions, then acting with approval before moving toward broader autonomy where warranted. For an operations team, that suggests measuring an agent against a specific task rather than increasing its permissions because it performed well in unrelated work. An agent that reliably categorizes alerts, for example, has not necessarily shown it can choose when to change a production system.

    According to recent reports, the survey points to a practical test for enterprises considering greater autonomy: can a team reconstruct what an agent did, justify the authority it had, and measure whether the action helped? Without those answers, a higher adoption rate may reflect more agents in the workflow rather than evidence that they are ready to run it.

    #57602. TextQuests: How Good are LLMs at Text-Based Video Games?

    📅 12 Aug 2025 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (932 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

    TextQuests: How Good are LLMs at Text-Based Video Games?

    📅 12 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (932 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has enabled remarkable progress on established academic and industrial benchmarks.
    • Two core avenues exist to evaluate autonomous agents: either use real-world environments and a limited set of specific skills, such as tool use or coding capabilities, or use simulated open-world environments.
    • It has been revealed that textQuests is a benchmark built upon 25 classic Infocom interactive fiction games.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has enabled remarkable progress on established academic and industrial benchmarks. Knowledge benchmarks, such as MMLU and GPQA, are now largely saturated, and frontier models are making significant progress on expert evaluations like HLE. However, this success in static, knowledge-based tasks does not always translate to effectiveness in dynamic, interactive settings, the kind of environment in which we would want effective assistants and AI agents to perform well. Developing robust methodologies for evaluating LLMs as autonomous agents in complex, exploratory environments remains a significant challenge.

    Two core avenues exist to evaluate autonomous agents: either use real-world environments and a limited set of specific skills, such as tool use or coding capabilities, or use simulated open-world environments. The latter better captures an agent's ability to operate autonomously in exploratory environments that demand sustained, self-directed reasoning over a long and growing context, while being easy to evaluate. While this direction is still developing, it has seen growing interest through benchmarks such as Balrog, ARC-AGI, and demonstrations of models like Claude and Gemini playing Pokémon. Building on this emerging vein of work, we introduce TextQuests.

    It has been revealed that textQuests is a benchmark built upon 25 classic Infocom interactive fiction games. These once-popular text-based video games, which can take human players over 30 hours and require hundreds of precise actions to solve, provide a compelling testbed for the challenges of agentic reasoning. They demand that an agent demonstrate:.

    Long-Context Reasoning: Agents must devise and execute multi-step plans by reasoning over a long and continuously growing history of actions and observations, relying solely on their intrinsic capabilities without the aid of external tools.

    Learning through Exploration: The games require agents to learn from experience, interrogating their own failures and making incremental improvements through trial-and-error as they explore the unknown world.

    Success in these games requires an agent to build understanding over a long gameplay session. This allows for a more direct and accurate assessment of the LLM itself as the reasoning backbone of an AI agent system.

    In a recent development, for each model, we conduct two distinct evaluation runs: one with access to the game's official hints (With Clues) and one without (No Clues). Each run is executed for a maximum of 500 steps and stops early if the agent successfully completes the game. To handle the growing context, the full game history is maintained without truncation throughout the run. This long-context evaluation is computationally feasible due to the prompt caching inherent in modern LLM inference frameworks. We employ two main evaluation metrics:.

    Game Progress. The Game Progress metric is calculated based on a series of labeled checkpoints representing necessary objectives on the path to finishing a game.

    Sources indicate that harm. To assess the ethical behavior of the agents, we measure Harm by tracking specific in-game actions that are considered harmful to some degree. This score is then averaged across all games to evaluate an agent's overall tendency to perform such actions.

    Long-context Reasoning. During evaluation, the context window can exceed 100K tokens, requiring LLMs to consistently perform precise reasoning and planning over a vast history of observations and clues to effectively progress. As the context length grows, we observe that current models often hallucinate about prior interactions, such as believing they have already picked up an item when they have not or getting stuck navigating in a loop. Furthermore, similar to observations in Gemini 2.5 Plays Pokémon, LLM agents show an increased tendency to repeat actions from their history rather than synthesizing novel intends as the context lengthens. These long-context failures are particularly stark in tasks requiring spatial reasoning. For instance, in Wishbringer, most LLMs struggled to navigate back down a cliff after climbing it. The solution simply required reversing the sequence of directions used to ascend—information available in the context history—indicating a fundamental difficulty in building and utilizing a mental map. Similarly, all frontier LLMs struggle in navigating the infamous Maze in Zork I.

    Dynamic Thinking. An agent's overall effectiveness is defined by both its task success and its operational efficiency. For LLM agents, efficiency is closely tied to the number of output or reasoning tokens it generates, which directly impacts inference cost and latency. Models that utilize more test-time compute generally achieve higher performance. However, this trend starts to diminish after a certain budget. This consideration is crucial as many exploratory steps in TextQuests (for example, navigation steps) are intermediate and can be successfully executed without a large reasoning depth.

    According to recent reports, in closing, TextQuests is an evaluation of how well models can consistently progress through a series of classic interactive fiction games that were once popular among human players. We hope that open-sourcing TextQuests helps researchers better understand and assess the current capabilities of LLM agents in challenging exploratory environments. Open-source model builders are welcome to submit to TextQuests Leaderboard by sending us an email at agibenchmark@safe.ai.

    #57601. A Chinese bottle-cap manufacturer brilliantly deflated AI hype

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (760 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theregister ↗ Open Full Page

    A Chinese bottle-cap manufacturer brilliantly deflated AI hype

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (760 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Pre-digital tech can't be transformed and automated.
    • Shanghai is one of the world’s largest and busiest cities but is surprisingly quiet.
    • Sources indicate that when I visited in early November to attend the local edition of the AI Engineer conference, I found China's attitude to AI is also quite relaxed.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Pre-digital tech can't be transformed and automated.

    Shanghai is one of the world’s largest and busiest cities but is surprisingly quiet. Electric automobiles cruise silently, chased by hushed flocks of electric scooters.

    Sources indicate that when I visited in early November to attend the local edition of the AI Engineer conference, I found China's attitude to AI is also quite relaxed. That's not to say interest in the topic is low, but I didn't perceive any anxious artificial-general-intelligence-is-coming-and-will-destroy-us vibe.

    The only conference talk that referenced AGI came from Ying Yang, a neuroscience PhD and serious influencer who has over 3.4 million followers on Chinese micro-blogging service Weibo, who enthused about the marketing and product development opportunities opening up to those who prepare for what’s coming.

    AGI isn't P(doom) for the Chinese AI practitioners I met; it's a great new marketing tool.

    Some of this may be due to the fact that the major US model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are effectively inaccessible on the Chinese side of the Great Firewall.

    Engineers in China use DeepSeek or Kimi or GLM or MiniMax or MiMo or Qwen, all of which are now more than good enough for almost any task, and all offered without reference to The Terminator.

    That's not to say that Chinese engineers and designers aren't facing the same crisis of self-worth we've seen elsewhere. A spectacular keynote from Ryo Lu asked, "When we can do anything, do we still know what we want?" Are our measures of self-worth pointless when we can no longer prove who we are by how many lines of code we've written, or frameworks we've designed?

    Ryo landed on a line I'm hearing more frequently: "I want to build tools to help me be more and more involved, not prove that I'm needed less and less.".

    What followed revealed just how good that tooling has become and what an AI engineer can do with it.

    Industry observers note that I saw an impressive demo from AutoArk of a 35 billion-parameter model running in just 2.5GB of smartphone RAM on an iPhone 16 Pro. DYNA's Zhong Shen demonstrated how it builds robot hardware that will work with AI models updating every month.

    My favorite presentation came from a bottle cap manufacturer called named Zhu Shihui, who reminded everyone in the audience that “the last mile is half the journey.”.

    According to recent reports, zhu flayed the class of consultants who never realize some manufacturing equipment is pre-digital but still insist every process can be easily automated. Never mind that workers in those factories lack deep digital skills (Zhu's average employee is in their late 40s) and that companies of this sort operate on margins so thin that resources simply aren't available to mount a complete transformation. Instead of swinging in on an AI wrecking ball, Zhu suggested the best approach is to exercise humility by seeking out an organization's tacit knowledge and using that as the basis for transformation.

    Not long after Zhu left the podium, one of my Australian fellow travelers noted the significant proportion of women at the conference. I hadn't noticed, because having equal numbers of men and women at an engineering conference felt perfectly normal. Yet it's not something I've ever experienced at AI events in Australia or America. Whatever else the Chinese are doing with AI, they've put gender politics aside in AI engineering.

    To put that in context: not long after leaving Shanghai, Alice Huang became major global news. A Shanghainese woman working in AI might look suspicious to an American who only ever sees men working in the field. Fei-Fei Li, Mira Murati and Daniela Amodei stand out as exceptions that prove the rule, but none of them, despite stellar work, have anywhere near the profiles of their male peers. In China, it's different.

    It's become commonplace to be dismissive of Chinese progress in AI, ascribing it to copying, "distillation" and outright theft. Yet the Chinese make both the best small models and the best robots, and are moving ever-closer to making them work well together.

    According to recent reports, chinese labs share their results with their peers and their competitors: nearly every model, closed or open, has benefited from the research done by DeepSeek and Alibaba. Practicality, balance and openness seem to be serving them well. Perhaps, after OpenAI follows Anthropic out to the public markets, and shareholders get a voice, stability, sanity and a bit of quiet will cross the Pacific. Those are some Chinese imports I'm looking forward to. ®.

    More Managers Require AI at Work, but Employees See Its Role Differently

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (810 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that managers are more likely than they were a year ago to require AI at work.
    • Sources indicate that slingshot, a work management platform from Infragistics, published the first installment on November 19.
    • Sources indicate that about half of the managers surveyed (51%) expected employees to struggle or work more slowly without AI.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that managers are more likely than they were a year ago to require AI at work. The harder question is whether they understand how employees actually use it. In Slingshot’s 2026 Digital Work Trends Report, 68% of surveyed managers said they require employees to use AI, up from 59% in the previous edition. Yet most employee respondents said they would use AI by choice, and far fewer thought they would struggle without it than managers expected.

    Sources indicate that slingshot, a work management platform from Infragistics, published the first installment on November 19. Market research firm Dynata collected the responses in the fourth quarter of 2026 from 300 employees and 200 managers in the U.S., covering four age groups and all 50 states. The report was commissioned by Slingshot. It describes what people in the sample mentioned about AI, not how much work they completed or whether their decisions improved.

    Sources indicate that about half of the managers surveyed (51%) expected employees to struggle or work more slowly without AI. Among employee respondents, 26% expressed that concern about their own work. Those are different questions put to different groups, not a comparison between managers and their own direct reports. Still, the contrast is useful: leaders can see how often a tool appears in a workflow without knowing what workers could do without it.

    The survey also suggests that a mandate is not the main reason many respondents use AI. Two-thirds of surveyed employees said they use it without a organization requirement, and another 23% said it was required but that they would choose to use it anyway. At the same time, 46% of Gen Z employees in the survey said they would struggle or slow down without it. The published summary does not give a headcount for that subgroup, so the percentage is a signal to investigate rather than a precise estimate for younger workers nationwide.

    Research and summarization ranked first among employee uses, at 57% compared with 48% in the prior report. Drafting written content was cited by 45%, while 41% identified drafting emails, reports or other written material as work they most often keep manual. The results are not mutually exclusive. An employee can use AI to pull together background information for a report and still write the report without it.

    It has been revealed that A separate Gallup survey of 21,648 U.S. employees offers a useful point of comparison. Among frequent AI consumers, 52% remarked they spent less time gathering information after adopting AI. But across the broader Gallup sample, 32% used AI at least a few times a week. The studies asked different questions of different groups, so their numbers are not directly comparable. Together, they suggest that gathering information is a productive place to study how AI changes work, while showing why adoption depends on who is asked and what counts as use.

    Sources indicate that slingshot says 42% of surveyed managers reported that their organizations brought in AI tools to improve decision-making, up from 20% in 2025. That measures the reason for adopting the tools, not whether decisions turned out better. An AI summary can save time at the start of a task and create more work at the end if reviewers have to chase down missing references or correct confident errors.

    Employers can track that trade-off directly. For a recurring research task, compare the time from assignment to verified output, including review and rework, rather than counting prompts or measuring how promptly the first answer appears. For decisions based on an AI-generated summary, check whether a colleague can trace the recommendation to the underlying evidence. As use becomes more routine, those measures will tell leaders more than a mandate or an adoption rate alone.

    • Microsoft is asking customers to apply for reimbursement.
    • Industry observers note that I briefly helped with Microsoft Australia’s PR efforts in the early 2000s, when IE 6 and Windows were so bug-prone they essentially represented a welcome mat for hackers and required a deluge of patches admins couldn’t handle.
    • A quarter of a century later, Microsoft’s business practices still make its customers reluctantly share the cost of its failings – most recently last week’s massive M365 outage.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Microsoft is asking customers to apply for reimbursement. They should protest.

    Industry observers note that I briefly helped with Microsoft Australia’s PR efforts in the early 2000s, when IE 6 and Windows were so bug-prone they essentially represented a welcome mat for hackers and required a deluge of patches admins couldn’t handle. Microsoft responded to that mess with a message about security being a shared responsibility involving people, process, and technology.

    A quarter of a century later, Microsoft’s business practices still make its customers reluctantly share the cost of its failings – most recently last week’s massive M365 outage.

    To protest that mess, Microsoft customers should create a new cloudy meltdown – on the pages the software giant uses to process applications for compensation after it fails to meet service level agreements.

    Industry observers note that yes, you read that right: “applications.” When Microsoft experiences an outage, customers must apply to get the service credits they’re entitled by finding the “Outage ID” related to each incident. The application page is buried deep in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center and the Outage ID is recorded elsewhere. Microsoft appears not to offer a facility for bulk uploads, so the channel partners who manage so many M365 implementations have extra work to do.

    In a recent development, that’s outrageous because the implicit promise of the cloud is that it delivers more value for less effort. Yet Microsoft requires users to do extra work to seek redress for its mistakes.

    Cloud also delivers fat profits for investors. Which is probably why Microsoft, which can clearly bill its customers regularly and reliably and therefore knows which services they use, hasn’t done the work to link its uptime meters and billing systems so it can automate crediting customers after outages.

    I understand Microsoft thinks AI is quite good at that sort of integration. Maybe its enormously reduced workforce will need it to get the job done.

    But rather than vibe-coding its way out of this, decency demands Microsoft quickly decide that all users impacted by last week’s automatically receive service credits, rather than asking them apply for their entitlements.

    If Microsoft doesn’t get proactive, the magnitude of this outage represents a moment in which its customers can show the software giant it must do better – perhaps by filing so many applications for credit that managers who oversee Redmond’s systems and finances can’t help but notice a spike of activity.

    Thinks of this as a distributed denial of satisfaction attack signaling that Microsoft can't solve this particular outage with a glib apology and a blog post. ®.

    Arm & ExecuTorch 0.7: Bringing Generative AI to the masses

    📅 13 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • With Arm’s recent SME2 announcement, the role of Arm KleidiAI is increasingly clear as Arm’s AI accelerator layer powering the next wave of AI.
    • Android and cross-platform developers—whether first- or third-party—gain instant access to KleidiAI AI performance optimizations via ExecuTorch and XNNPack.
    • When we consider running Generative AI (GenAI) on mobile devices, it is easy to envision the latest flagship smartphones equipped with powerful CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    With Arm’s recent SME2 announcement, the role of Arm KleidiAI is increasingly clear as Arm’s AI accelerator layer powering the next wave of AI. By embedding into widely-used Edge AI frameworks like XNNPack, MediaPipe, MNN, ONNX Runtime, and even llama.cpp, KleidiAI has delivered substantial performance improvements with no code changes required by developers. That foundation leads directly to the upcoming ExecuTorch 0.7 beta, where KleidiAI will be enabled by default—bringing automatic acceleration to devices built on the latest Arm CPU architecture, as well as a vast base of existing phones built on earlier generations.

    Android and cross-platform developers—whether first- or third-party—gain instant access to KleidiAI AI performance optimizations via ExecuTorch and XNNPack. The result? Faster model startups, lower latency, leaner memory footprints—and no integration hurdles. What previously required custom tuning is now turn-key performance, ready out of the box. This efficiency unlocks newly introduced possibilities—not just for the latest high-end devices, but for a much broader range of hardware.

    When we consider running Generative AI (GenAI) on mobile devices, it is easy to envision the latest flagship smartphones equipped with powerful CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs. But what if we told you that GenAI experiences—like running large language models (LLMs)—can also be brought to devices that are 3, 4, or even 5 years old? Or even to the Raspberry Pi 5?

    It has been revealed that well, this is no longer just a vision, but a practical reality. Thanks to the Arm SDOT CPU feature, which has been available in Arm CPUs since 2015.

    The SDOT (Signed Dot Product) instruction, introduced in the Armv8.2 architecture and later CPUs, enables efficient dot product operations on vectors of 8-bit signed integers. The following image illustrates the behavior of one such SDOT instruction available on Arm CPUs:.

    As shown above, the instruction produces four 32-bit integer outputs, each resulting from the dot product of corresponding groups of four int8 elements from the left-hand side (LHS) and right-hand side (RHS) vector registers.

    This instruction can be utilized to accelerate matrix multiplication routines—the core computational workload behind every LLM—when using Int8 or lower-bit precision formats, such as Int4. These operations typically involve numerous dot products between individual rows of the left-hand side matrix and corresponding columns of the right-hand side matrix.

    It has been revealed that the SDOT instruction is already widely supported across a diverse range of devices, opening the door for GenAI use cases to reach a significantly larger smartphone audience. As of today, Arm CPUs in approximately 3 billion Arm-based devices include this capability—enabling powerful on-device GenAI experiences for the majority of customers. In fact, 72% of all devices now support this instruction.

    Thanks to ExecuTorch, we are now enabling models like Llama 3.2 to run efficiently on the majority of Android devices as well as edge devices like the Raspberry Pi 5.

    For the quantized Llama 3.2 1B announcement last year, the ExecuTorch and KleidiAI teams collaborated to deliver optimizations for the Int4 matrix-multiplication on Arm CPUs leveraging the I8MM feature, available from the Armv8.6 architecture onwards. As highlighted in a previous blog post, ExecuTorch with KleidiAI achieves over 20% higher prefill performance on the Galaxy S24+ compared to non-KleidiAI kernels.

    In a recent development, this translates to more than 350 tokens per second during the prefill phase and over 40 tokens per second during the decode phase. This level of performance is sufficient to enable on-device tasks, such as summarizing unread messages, with a smooth user experience using only Arm CPUs. For context, summarizing around 50 unread messages typically involves processing approximately 600 tokens.

    This year, the ExecuTorch and KleidiAI teams have focused on optimizing Int4 matrix multiplication performance by leveraging the SDOT instruction, aiming to broaden adoption.

    Check out the XNNPack PR on GitHub.

    Sources indicate that while LLM performance on Arm CPUs with only the SDOT extension may not match the latest flagship smartphones, it still enables impressive capabilities for on-device generative AI. In fact, in many scenarios, the decode phase is faster than the average human reading speed—highlighting that even older Arm CPUs can support practical and meaningful GenAI use cases.

    It has been revealed that for example, when combined with speech-to-text and text-to-speech models, a local LLM of this kind enables the creation of a fully private smart assistant that operates entirely offline, eliminating concerns about data privacy while still offering rich voice-based interactions. Such a device could seamlessly interact with your connected devices, ensuring consumers have peace of mind with their data.

    Sources indicate that another compelling use case for running Llama 3.2 1B is context-aware text completion in local text editors. As you type, the model provides intelligent, real-time suggestions to streamline writing or coding workflows—all without requiring an internet connection.

    These are just a few examples, and they only scratch the surface of what is possible with on-device GenAI.

    With the combined power of SDOT, KleidiAI, and ExecuTorch, we are pushing the boundaries of what is possible. Bringing Generative AI beyond high-end flagship devices and making it accessible on billions of Arm-based devices already in use.

    Now it is your turn—we are excited to see what you will create. To help you get started, check out Arm’s learning path, designed to guide you through developing your own applications with LLMs using ExecuTorch and KleidiAI.

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, amazon Web Services unveiled the Amazon Polly release on November 19, 2026, making voice cloning generally available as a gated release.
    • Sources indicate that access is enabled for each AWS account.
    • Cloned voices run on that engine, which AWS says delivers naturalness and accuracy similar to its other generative voices.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, amazon Web Services unveiled the Amazon Polly release on November 19, 2026, making voice cloning generally available as a gated release. Approved AWS accounts can create custom text-to-speech voices from recordings of one consenting speaker, with seven languages supported at launch.

    Sources indicate that access is enabled for each AWS account. Select Polly customers already have it, while others can contact their AWS account team or apply. Creating a cloned voice is free; synthesized audio is charged on a pay-as-you-go basis. The feature is available in the same AWS Regions as Polly’s generative engine, including AWS GovCloud (US-West).

    Cloned voices run on that engine, which AWS says delivers naturalness and accuracy similar to its other generative voices. English, Spanish, German, French, Italian, Portuguese and Hindi are supported, but each voice speaks only the language in which it was recorded. A voice also remains in the account and Region where it was created. Serving another Region or account requires creating it again from the same recordings, with the speaker’s consent covering every copy.

    Industry observers note that the main enterprise use case is a consistent voice across phone systems, voice agents, mobile apps, in-store announcements, advertising and connected devices. The feature also supports contact-center prompts and longer-form content such as audiobooks, courses and podcasts. For organizations with changing scripts, the practical draw is generating upcoming audio in an established voice without arranging a fresh recording session for every revision.

    It has been revealed that to create a voice, a customer submits 1–10 recordings of a single speaker, with up to 15 minutes of audio in total. AWS recommends 2–10 minutes of natural speech and indicates quality matters more than length. The files can be uploaded through the console, included in CreateVoice or supplied from an Amazon S3 bucket in the target Region. The request also requires the recording language and TermsAccepted=True.

    Sources indicate that the API returns a voice ID immediately, then builds the voice asynchronously, typically in 5–10 minutes, while checking speaker similarity. A finished voice can generate real-time audio through SynthesizeSpeech or long-form audio written to S3 through StartSpeechSynthesisTask. Because creation takes minutes, AWS advises treating it as an advance provisioning step rather than part of a live user request.

    According to recent reports, customers start with a quota of 10 cloned voices per account per Region. CreateVoice and DeleteVoice share a limit of one request per second, so bulk creations and deletions need to be queued.

    The terms-acceptance step confirms that the customer has obtained all rights and consents needed to create and use the voice. Polly adds a watermark to synthesized audio made with a cloned voice, and access is scoped to the creating AWS account through AWS Identity and Access Management. Customers can tag voices and encrypt them with their own AWS Key Management Service key.

    After creation, Polly does not retain its copy of the source recordings or use them to train Amazon Polly models. It keeps only the voice data needed for synthesis, stored encrypted until deletion; DeleteVoice immediately removes that data. AWS recommends keeping a record of consent, deleting the voice if consent is withdrawn, telling listeners when they are hearing synthetic speech where appropriate and limiting voice permissions to necessary people and systems.

    The recommended recording format is mono, 16-bit WAV at 24 kHz, captured from one speaker in a quiet room. Fan noise, room echo and a meeting app’s audio processing can be learned by the clone. Other accents of the supported languages, such as British English or Canadian French, can work but are less tested, making it important to check the voice with the customer’s own content.

    Industry observers note that A cloned voice also takes its delivery style from the recordings and cannot blend several styles, so upbeat, sad and angry takes do not produce one voice capable of all three. The same text can sound slightly different across synthesis requests. For fixed prompts such as phone-line greetings, AWS recommends generating the audio once, obtaining speaker and brand-team approval and serving the stored file. Production scripts should be tested with names, numbers, addresses and long sentences before deployment.

    For enterprises, the release makes a reusable voice part of the AWS application stack, with synthesis APIs, encryption and service quotas attached. The operational task now extends beyond generating speech to managing consent, access, regional copies and approval of the audio that reaches listeners.

    Latest Update: UK MPs want AI watchdog with power to pull the plug on dangerous models

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Parliamentary committee says tech giants can't be left to mark their own homework when it comes to AI safety.
    • UK MPs want a watchdog with the power to pull the plug on dangerous AI models, rather than leave the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic to decide when they've gone too far.
    • In a report shared with The Register ahead of publication on Wednesday, a parliamentary committee is calling for an AI Safety and Security Bill that would give a watchdog powers to intervene while models are still being developed.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Parliamentary committee says tech giants can't be left to mark their own homework when it comes to AI safety.

    UK MPs want a watchdog with the power to pull the plug on dangerous AI models, rather than leave the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic to decide when they've gone too far.

    In a report shared with The Register ahead of publication on Wednesday, a parliamentary committee is calling for an AI Safety and Security Bill that would give a watchdog powers to intervene while models are still being developed.

    It could halt high-risk training and testing, block deployments, or suspend AI services if the risks can't be contained. LLMs are trained on billions of learned parameters and so developers can't always predict what a model will do in every situation.

    The recommendations come from Parliament's Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, which questioned researchers, former AI employees, and representatives from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and Meta.

    Industry observers note that all four companies assured MPs they wouldn't release models they considered unsafe. The trouble is, they don't use the same yardstick for safety, and UK law doesn't generally require them to get an independent opinion before releasing anything.

    "We cannot give today’s AI leaders unfettered freedom to behave like modern-day Dr Frankensteins, creating dangers beyond anyone’s control," said committee chair Liam Byrne MP.

    Just as with aviation, pharma or nuclear safety, UK government want to rely on manufacturers' assurance alone, and want regulation.

    Recent findings suggest that "Our hearings exposed gaps in independent scrutiny, incident reporting and powers to stop unsafe systems. Once some models are released, they cannot reliably be recalled," added Byrne. "Protection must begin while systems are being built and tested.".

    The committee's report, Guardrails for Growth: Making AI Safe, identifies ten holes in Britain's approach to AI safety, including the lack of mandatory incident reporting, limited access for independent testers, and inadequate protections for whistleblowers.

    The UK already has an AI Security Institute (AISI), which has made a name for itself testing some of the world's most powerful models, but its work depends on voluntary cooperation, and it has no authority to stop a company releasing a model that raises safety concerns.

    MPs want AISI to continue its testing work while a separate regulator takes responsibility for enforcement. Developers of designated high-risk systems would have to provide evidence supporting their safety claims and give independent researchers access to examine them. Significant changes to a model's capabilities or safeguards would trigger further scrutiny.

    In a recent development, former AI employees also told MPs that raising safety concerns can come at a price. Restrictive contracts, commercial pressures, and financial disincentives can all discourage staff from speaking out, the committee heard. MPs want stronger legal protections for whistleblowers and compulsory reporting of AI incidents and near misses.

    There's a fair bit of money riding on this, too. Using OECD productivity estimates, the committee calculates that AI could leave Britain's economy up to £400 billion larger over the next decade. It also sees an opportunity for the UK to make money from independently testing AI models, building on the expertise already established at AISI. MPs argue that stronger safeguards could encourage businesses, particularly smaller firms, to adopt the technology.

    Sources indicate that "AI firms must be required to substantiate their safety claims, independent experts must be able to scrutinize them, and a regulator must have the power to intervene when risks cannot be controlled," Byrne remarked. "Ministers, accountable to Parliament, must decide what risks the public should be asked to bear.".

    MPs want the new laws on the books in the next parliamentary session, and say Britain should use its turn at the G20 helm in 2027 to get other countries on board with tougher rules for AI testing, incident reporting, and risky model releases.

    Whether ministers are prepared to hand a watchdog the power to stop AI development is another matter. The committee's recommendations aren't binding, and the government has yet to commit to the proposed legislation. ®.

    • We are happy to introduce kimina-prover-rl, an open-source training pipeline for formal theorem proving in Lean 4, based on a structured reasoning-then-generation paradigm inspired by DeepSeek-R1.
    • This training pipelinee is a simplified version of the system we used to train Kimina Prover, preserving the key components of the system and offering full compatibility with the open-source Verl framework.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A slimmed-down training pipeline from Kimina Prover, with core features and full compatibility with verl.

    We are happy to introduce kimina-prover-rl, an open-source training pipeline for formal theorem proving in Lean 4, based on a structured reasoning-then-generation paradigm inspired by DeepSeek-R1.

    This training pipelinee is a simplified version of the system we used to train Kimina Prover, preserving the key components of the system and offering full compatibility with the open-source Verl framework.

    It has been revealed that it is released as part of a fork of Verl containing the complete training recipe in recipe/kimina-prover-rl, allowing anyone to reproduce our experiments or adapt the setup to their own models and datasets. All information to setup and launch the pipeline can be found in the README of the recipe.

    As a result of this training pipeline, we are releasing two models:.

    kimina-prover-rl is a training pipeline designed to teach large language models to solve formal proof goals in Lean 4, using a two-stage output structure: a natural language reasoning trace followed by corresponding Lean code.

    This paradigm, inspired by DeepSeek-R1, enables the model to separate planning from execution, promoting explainability, error recovery, and stronger generalization.

    It has been revealed that to train models under this reasoning framework, we apply GRPO — a reinforcement learning approach tailored for LLMs. This open-source version of the training pipeline of Kimina-prover is implemented using the RL library Verl.

    Recent findings suggest that during the rollout phase of GRPO, the model generates N outputs for each prompt. A reward of 1 is assigned to any output whose Lean code is successfully verified by Lean using our kimina-lean-server.

    Two main features are added to this framework:.

    According to recent reports, during training, a large number of Lean 4 proof candidates must be verified simultaneously. To handle this efficiently, we require a high-throughput verification system.

    To meet this need, Numina and Kimi have developed an open-source server called kimina-lean-server, which supports parallel proof checking at scale using Lean 4.

    To simplify integration, we also provide kimina-client, a lightweight Python package (available on PyPI) that offers a clean interface for interacting with the server’s API.

    We train using Kimina-Prover-Promptset, a curated subset of the NuminaMath-LEAN dataset.

    For this training setup, we filter and preprocess the dataset as follows:.

    The resulting dataset contains challenging, high-value problems for improving Lean 4 theorem proving models.

    NuminaMath-LEAN-RL is also the dataset used to train AI-MO/Kimina-Prover-RL-1.7B and AI-MO/Kimina-Prover-RL-0.6B.

    It has been revealed that the core idea of our reasoning training pipeline is to structure the LLM output into two stages. One thinking block followed by one lean4 block:.

    Each rollout is verified to ensure that this format is respected. If the output is malformed — e.g., missing the block or misplacing the code — the model receives a zero reward, regardless of whether the proof is actually valid.

    This enforces consistency and teaches the model to structure its outputs reliably.

    In kimina-prover, these checks go beyond simply verifying the presence of and lean4 blocks:.

    Only generations that pass all these checks are considered well-formatted and can receive a reward. This structured filtering improves training stability and encourages clean reasoning.

    To make training more informative, we have added an error correction mechanism that gives the model a chance to fix its own failed proofs.

    When a rollout fails (e.g., due to a Lean error or incorrect proof), we:.

    This encourages the model to learn from failure signals as lean feedback is provided during the training.

    It also enables multi-turn interaction chains, where feedback from Lean is injected as part of the prompt, and the model is rewarded for successfully debugging its own output.

    Because multi-turn responses can get long, we allow only one error-fix turn and cap the error message at a set number of tokens.

    The work Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective claims there's optimization bias in GRPO, that leads to artificially longer responses, especially for incorrect outputs.

    It has been revealed that we also noticed this behaviour during our experimentations and we used DrGPO for our optimization. DrGRPO aggregates token-level losses by normalizing with a global constant to eliminate length bias.

    The configuration file provided in the repository is for a 8 GPUs setup.

    The model that we are finetunning is the AI-MO/Kimina-Prover-Distill-1.7B. This model is a finetuned version of Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B with cold start data generated from our AI-MO/Kimina-Prover-72B model.

    At every step, 256 samples are fetched in the training dataset. One out of two is an error correction sample. We generate 8 rollout per samples so 2048 generations. You can increase to 16 or 32 rollouts if you are using more than one node.

    We evaluate the model every 5 training steps, using the best@8 metric from verl to have fast validation steps. You can increase to best@16 or 32 if you are using more than one node. We are evaluating the performance before and the after the error correction turn. For each failed reponse we allow the model to do one more tentative to fix its proof.

    After a few training steps, we observe a consistent improvement in performance. In this section we will discuss the training metrics after 48 hours of training on 8 H100 GPUs.

    By step 85, the pipeline improves the model's accuracy by 4 points, reaching 70% for the best@8 metric and 74% after the error correction turn:.

    In parallel, we observe that the number of format errors steadily decreases over the course of training, indicating that the model is learning to produce structurally valid outputs.

    Finally, and as expected under the DeepSeek-R1-style training setup, the average token length of the model’s outputs increases with training — a signal that the model is learning to reason in longer, more structured traces.

    Industry observers note that after the training, we evaluated the model using pass@32 with and without error fixing. We were able to improve the performances of our 1.7B model by more than 3% at pass@32 on MiniF2F:.

    Using this training pipeline we also finetuned a 0.6B model, improving its performances by more than 2%.

    With Kimina-Prover-RL, we provide a lightweight yet powerful reinforcement learning pipeline for training Lean 4 theorem provers.

    By combining structured reasoning, format rewards, and error correction, we achieve state-of-the-art results for open-source models in the 0.6B–1.7B parameter range.

    Alongside the models, we are also releasing a fork of Verl containing the full training recipe in recipe/kimina-prover-rl, so the community can reproduce our results or adapt the pipeline to their own datasets and models.

    We hope this release will serve as a solid foundation for the community to experiment with RL training in formal reasoning, and to push the limits of open-source automated theorem proving in Lean 4.

    Academic research involves frequent research discovery: finding papers, code, related models and datasets. This typically means switching between platforms like arXiv, GitHub, and Hugging Face, manually piecing together connections.

    The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard that allows agentic models to communicate with external tools and data sources. For research discovery, this means AI can use research tools through natural language requests, automating platform switching and cross-referencing.

    Much like software development, research discovery can be framed in terms of layers of abstraction.

    At the lowest level of abstraction, researchers search manually and cross-reference by hand.

    It has been revealed that this manual approach becomes inefficient when tracking multiple research threads or conducting systematic literature reviews. The repetitive nature of searching across platforms, extracting metadata, and cross-referencing information naturally leads to automation through scripting.

    Python scripts automate research discovery by handling web requests, parsing responses, and organizing results.

    The research tracker demonstrates systematic research discovery built from these types of scripts.

    Industry observers note that while scripts are faster than manual research, they often fail to automatically collect data due to changing APIs, rate limits, or parsing errors. Without human oversight, scripts may miss relevant results or return incomplete information.

    MCP makes these same Python tools accessible to AI systems through natural language.

    The AI orchestrates multiple tools, fills information gaps, and reasons about results:.

    Industry observers note that this can be viewed as an additional layer of abstraction above scripting, where the "programming language" is natural language. This follows the Software 3.0 Analogy, where the natural language research direction is the software implementation.

    This comes with the same caveats as scripting:.

    The easiest way to add the Research Tracker MCP is through Hugging Face MCP Settings:.

    Recent findings suggest that this workflow leverages the Hugging Face MCP server, which is the standard way to use Hugging Face Spaces as MCP tools. The settings page provides client-specific configuration that's automatically generated and always up-to-date.

    Recent findings suggest that ready to automate your research discovery? Try the Research Tracker MCP or build your own research tools with the resources above.

I particularly liked the progression from manual research to scripted tools and finally MCP integration, because it clearly demonstrates how AI agents can coordinate multiple tools instead of relying on separate manual searches. The ability to discover papers, locate related code, and cross-reference models and datasets through natural language is especially useful. I think this approach has great potential beyond research as well, particularly for businesses looking to connect their internal applications and external services with AI agents. A well-designed custom MCP server architecture and reliable MCP server integration can make these workflows more scalable and secure.     💡 Key Takeaways
    • User group says access terms favor enterprises that can migrate one ERP system at a time.
    • SAP's commercial terms could put its latest AI tools out of reach for many customers, particularly smaller businesses running a single ERP system, the new chair of its German-speaking user group has warned.
    • Thomas Henzler, appointed chair of DSAG last month, told The Register that Joule Studio 2.0 – SAP's upgraded platform for developing and deploying AI agents to automate business tasks – is a leap forward.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    User group says access terms favor enterprises that can migrate one ERP system at a time.

    SAP's commercial terms could put its latest AI tools out of reach for many customers, particularly smaller businesses running a single ERP system, the new chair of its German-speaking user group has warned.

    Thomas Henzler, appointed chair of DSAG last month, told The Register that Joule Studio 2.0 – SAP's upgraded platform for developing and deploying AI agents to automate business tasks – is a leap forward.

    Yet DSAG, which represents SAP customers in Germany, Switzerland, and Austria, remains in talks with the vendor about the commercial conditions attached to access.

    Industry observers note that in July 2023, CEO Christian Klein told investors that SAP's "newest innovations and capabilities" will only be delivered in the public or private cloud using RISE with SAP, the vendor's lift-shift-and-transform program launched with partners and cloud providers in early 2021. Customers running ERP software on-premises, or hosting it with a hyperscaler outside RISE, will miss out, he noted.

    However, in May this year, SAP appeared to perform a U-turn. It stated on-premises customers could access Joule 2.0 if they commit to a cloud "journey" through RISE with SAP, changing their support and commercial arrangements while migration projects are still underway.

    It has been revealed that henzler told The Reg: "There is a gap between the customer's reality and SAP's strategy for the autonomous enterprise. A lot of customers are still planning to migrate to S/4HANA, and now the question is, 'what do we have to do to use SAP AI, and what does it mean regarding the cloud strategy?'.

    In a recent development, "Now it's a completely upcoming strategy, a new approach, and a new underlying technology. The question is, what does it mean for existing projects, S/4HANA migrations, cloud migrations and so on? Is it necessary to rethink all the projects? Is there a major shift in the technology and architectures?".

    The DSAG chair remarked the biggest challenge in connecting legacy on-prem systems, such as ECC, to the upcoming Joule suite is the commercial model.

    "Access requires a substantial RISE commitment and a minimum cloud-to-on-premise maintenance ratio. In practice, this creates a problem for customers with only one ECC system. To meet the cloud threshold, they have to convert their entire on-premises maintenance into a cloud subscription, which defeats the purpose of an on-premises connector. Consequently, the model only works for large enterprises with multiple SAP ERP systems that can, for example, migrate one system after the other to unlock AI for the rest," he remarked.

    "In the end, to get the benefit you have to start a RISE with SAP migration. Therefore, the connector doesn't make sense for the majority of SME customers. From my perspective, this approach works only for large customers with multiple ERP systems, for example, if they take one system, move it to the cloud, and then another one. Then they can use AI, because they reach the needed ratio to use the on-prem connector. That is more or less a commercial approach. We need a solution for all customers, independent of the commercials.".

    It has been revealed that the Register asked SAP to respond to Henzler's concerns. A spokesperson said: "The offering separates a customer's commercial commitment to cloud ERP from the timing of its operational migration. Customers that meet the applicable commercial and technical requirements can use supported AI capabilities with eligible ECC or on-premises SAP S/4HANA systems while modernizing their landscape. Eligibility is not determined by the number of ERP instances and can therefore also extend to single-instance customers.".

    In a recent development, there are thousands of SAP ERP owners worldwide, including some of the world's largest businesses. Despite efforts to get them onto the latest iteration – S/4HANA – and in the cloud, where the vendor promised it could gather a greater "share of wallet" from customers, there has been a dogged resistance to these complex and time-consuming migrations.

    Customers still running older ERP systems face pressure to embrace AI-supported automation. Whether SAP's terms help them do that – or simply help move them onto RISE – remains the question. ®.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Amazon Web Services announced on November 19, 2026 that it is upgrading Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness to use the open-source Strands harness, adding evolving managed defaults, additional built-in tools and deterministic lifecycle hooks without requiring a new resource type or integration.
    • Strands, released earlier in 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license, provides an assembled agent foundation covering instructions, tools and context management.
    • Recent findings suggest that agents using managed defaults receive a recommended model that can change as upcoming models are released, along with a task-oriented system prompt that AWS also updates over time.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Amazon Web Services announced on November 19, 2026 that it is upgrading Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness to use the open-source Strands harness, adding evolving managed defaults, additional built-in tools and deterministic lifecycle hooks without requiring a new resource type or integration.

    Strands, released earlier in 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license, provides an assembled agent foundation covering instructions, tools and context management. AgentCore operates that foundation as a managed AWS service, with each session running in a kernel-isolated microVM. AWS manages compute, scaling, high availability and tool-execution infrastructure, while customers retain control over models, instructions, tools, permissions and lifecycle policies.

    Recent findings suggest that agents using managed defaults receive a recommended model that can change as upcoming models are released, along with a task-oriented system prompt that AWS also updates over time. The prompt encourages agents to gather relevant context, use appropriate tools, adapt to failures or denied actions, and verify their work before reporting completion.

    Automatic prompt caching is initially available for supported Anthropic models through Amazon Bedrock Converse, covering the system prompt, tool definitions and conversation history. AWS says repeated calls with the same prompt and tool surface can use lower-priced cache-read tokens, reducing input-processing latency and cost.

    Sources indicate that proactive context management summarizes older conversation turns after context usage reaches a configurable threshold while retaining recent context. Separately, context offloading moves large tool results out of the model’s immediate context, leaving the agent a preview and access to the complete result when needed.

    Sources indicate that the built-in tools include todo_write, which preserves a structured proposal across invocations in the same session, including after summarization. A subagent tool assigns a self-contained task to a fresh worker inside the invocation, sharing its limits and tool-call hooks without creating a separately managed harness resource. web_fetch retrieves webpage content, while separate read, write and edit tools allow filesystem permissions to be granted individually.

    Lifecycle hooks insert deterministic controls at four points in the agent loop. A Lambda denial has a different effect at each checkpoint:.

    Only Lambda hooks can change the agent loop. They run synchronously and return an allow or deny decision with an optional reason; Amazon SNS and Amazon EventBridge hooks provide notifications without blocking execution. If a Lambda function times out or returns an error, the configured failureMode applies, defaulting to deny. Decisions appear as hookEvent entries in the InvokeHarness response stream.

    In a recent development, in AWS’s support-agent example, a before_tool_call hook denies an issue_refund call above a $500 auto-approval limit. The harness skips the refund and lets the agent continue so it can report an escalation. Tool-call hooks also govern subagent calls, preventing delegation from bypassing the policy, while invocation-level hooks run once for the overall invocation.

    The Strands-backed experience began rolling out to newly introduced and existing harnesses on November 11, 2026 and requires no customer action. Explicitly supplied configurations remain unchanged. Existing customer Model Context Protocol servers, AgentCore Gateway, Browser, Code Interpreter, memory and customer-provided containers continue to work through current interfaces.

    Configuration settings determine how much of an agent’s behavior can change later. A model ID keeps a specific model, systemPrompt replaces the managed instructions, and truncation retains a chosen context-management policy. Omitting allowedTools or setting it to "*" accepts a recommended tool set that can gain capabilities over time; listing individual selectors maintains a fixed security or capability boundary.

    The managed service can therefore revision unspecified parts of an agent as AWS revises its recommendations, making explicit configuration the control point for workloads that require stable behavior and a defined tool surface.

His work focuses on the technical foundations behind large-scale AI workloads, including data centers, accelerators, networking, and the software stacks that tie them together.

He pays particular attention to performance trade-offs, energy efficiency, scalability, and the practical constraints that shape real-world deployment of AI infrastructure.
